News.title: Love Island final LIVE: Jasmine 'horrified' as she learns public's nickname for her and Lorenzo
News.content:
Yesterday's final of Love Island crowned Lorenzo and Julia as the 13th season's winners, with Jasmine and Kavan coming second, and Simba and Angelista in third

Love Island final LIVE: Jasmine 'horrified' as she learns public's nickname for her and Lorenzo

The Love Island has officially ended with Lorenzo Alessi and Julia Majchrzak announced as winners, beating out stiff competition from Kavan Murphy and Jasmine Muller.

However, it wasn't without drama as one Islander was noticeably absent from the proceedings, while fans were convinced that there was drama brewing between others.

Since their win, some fans have voiced their doubts about Julia and Lorenzo's relationship, but Lorenzo has hit back at those comments, saying that he understands where they're coming from, as he and Julia have not been as quick to go through milestones on TV, but that pressure would have "ruined things" for him.

This hasn't been helped by lingering beliefs that Lorenzo and Jasmine had feelings for each tother. When Jasmine learned that the public were calling her and Lorenzo 'Jarenzo', she visibly cringed and looked horrified as she covered Kavan's ears.

Here's everything else that went down as the new champions were crowned...

News.title: Trump live: Rambling Donald veers off script and falls asleep during Graham eulogy
News.content:
Donald Trump once again made it all about himself during a funeral in Washington DC for Senator Lindsey Graham

Donald Trump once again found himself unable to stick to the script during a eulogy for Sen. Lindsay Graham, veering off-topic to claim the deceased Senator wasn't actually liked by everybody.

"Virtually everyone, Republican or Democrat, liked Lindsey," Trump said during a eulogy for his former rival turned close political ally.

"Well, not everybody," he quipped. "But it sounds good. He was a tough cookie. I have to be honest. I have to veer from this for a second."

Elsewhere during the funeral service, the 80-year-old president was spotted struggling to stay awake following closed-door meetings with both Benjamin Netanyahu and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

In a post on X following the meeting, Zelenskyy confirmed the pair had discussed the US president's recent pledge to allow Ukraine to produce Patriot missile interceptors as well as “several other ideas that could help” as the war with Russia enters its fifth year.

The Israeli president meanwhile hailed the meeting as "one of the best conversations I’ve had with the President of the United States," despite Trump claiming that Israel "wouldn't survive" without the US just a day earlier.

Following the discussions, White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt wrote on X: “Both meetings were positive and productive!”

News.title: Andy Burnham invites Tory and Lib Dem leaders for urgent talks to fix crisis-hit social care sector
News.content:
Andy Burnham invites Tory and Lib Dem leaders for urgent talks to fix crisis-hit social care sector

Tory chief Kemi Badenoch and Liberal Democrat leader have been asked to meet with the new Prime Minister Andy Burnham to tackle a problem governments have kicked into the long-grass for decades

View 3 Images New PM Andy Burnham has invited political rivals to talks to fix social care sector (Image: Aaron Chown/Pool PA via AP)

Andy Burnham has invited opposition leaders for urgent talks to fix the crisis-hit social care sector and give people the dignity and support they deserve.

‌



Tory chief Kemi Badenoch and Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey have been asked to meet with the new Prime Minister on Wednesday to tackle a problem governments have kicked into the long-grass for decades. The proposed summit would be an unprecedented chance to grip the issue once and for all.

‌



It comes as Mr Burnham warned ahead of a major speech on Wednesday that the creaking system can no longer be treated as a political football while the NHS and families count the cost.

‌



He said: “Politicians might have different views but I’m serious about fixing this issue and to do that, we have to find common ground and listen to others to find a way forward.”

He added: “It’s time to draw a line under people playing politics when the human cost of that means carers struggling, families paying the price and our NHS buckling under the strain.

“This comes down to a choice. We can carry on passing the problem to the next generation, or we can face it head on and work together to build a care system that gives people dignity, security and the support they deserve.

‌



"This is about bringing back hope that we can finally fix the difficult issues that have been ignored for too long, and making Britain believe again. That's why I’m making this choice and I'm prepared to put everything I've got behind it."

Andy Burnham issues dire warning NHS will collapse if social care isn't finally fixed READ MORE :

Streeting backs Burnham to sort out Britain's social care crisis with dig at Starmer READ MORE :

View 3 Images Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey has been invited to the talks with Andy Burnham (Image: ANDY RAIN/EPA/Shutterstock)

'The NHS will collapse without reform to social care'

Referring to his first speech outside No10 last week, he said: “Last week I said we needed a different kind of politics: problem-solving, not point-scoring. Nowhere is that more urgent than social care.”

‌



A Tory spokesman told The Mirror on Tuesday evening: "Kemi Badenoch is unable to attend and Stuart Andrew, Shadow Health Secretary, will be attending in her place.”

Sir Ed accepted Mr Burnham’s invitation saying “we need to do things differently”. The Lib Dem leader added: “Our priorities are clear: family carers must be at the heart of any proposals, everyone should be able to get care regardless of means, and no-one should lose their home or life savings on catastrophic care costs.”

It comes after Mr Burnham warned earlier this week the NHS will “collapse” without reform to social care and said he wants to bring in substantial changes before he leaves office. He has frequently cited his personal experience of the care system, as his father lives with Alzheimer’s in a care home.

‌



He has described as “not defensible” a system which can see people lose their homes and savings to pay for care.

According to government figures, an average of 13,600 people a day were stuck in hospital beds in June 2026 despite being medically fit to leave, including some delayed because of a lack of adult social care availability.

The PM - who will also visit a care home on Wednesday - is set to appear alongside Baroness Louise Casey, who has been tasked with leading an independent review into the issue.

‌



It is expected Mr Burnham will announce he is speeding up the Casey Commission - launched by Keir Starmer last year - that had been due to report in 2028, rather than set out a full plan.

Baroness Casey will also launch a ‘Big Conversation on Care’ and invite the pubic to share their views on fixing a problem through an online platform.

She said: “For too long, we have been stuck in the same cycle: crisis, promises of reform, another review, and then retreat, while the people who need care, and their families, bear the brunt. Fixing adult social care is about far more than money.

‌



“People are already paying for failure through council tax, pressure on the NHS, their savings, giving up work, and the forced sale of their homes."

View 3 Images According to Age UK, an estimated 17% of older people have an unmet need for care – equivalent to 1.9 million (Image: Getty)

No plans for 'death tax'

Baroness Casey added: “The choice is whether we keep putting money into a system that is unfair, unpredictable and broken, or have an honest conversation about how to build something better. That is why we need a public conversation on care that tackles the tough questions. It’s only by facing up to this problem together that we can fix social care once and for all.”

‌



Mr Burnham’s speech also follows a row over funding after Mr Burnham appeared to fail to rule out introducing a care levy on all estates earlier this week.

As Health Secretary under Gordon Brown, Mr Burnham previously backed replacing traditional inheritance tax with a 10 per cent levy on all estates. But plans were ripped up at the time after the Tories accused Labour of a “death tax” to pay for the proposed new care service.

But a government spokesman said earlier this week: “There are no plans for this. Fixing our social care system will require building a broad consensus. The old way of doing politics has held up social care reform for decades.

‌



“Our immediate focus is on working together to find common ground and deliver the reforms needed to fix the future of social care – not imposing one particular solution or tax.”

Care system 'no longer fit for purpose'

According to Age UK, an estimated 17% of older people have an unmet need for care – equivalent to 1.9 million.

In 2024/25, there were 1.3 million requests for social care support from people aged 65 and over in England. In the same time period in England, 880,000 (67%) requests for social care support from people aged 65+ resulted in no further action.

‌



Age UK’s Caroline Abrahams said the creaking care system “is no longer fit for purpose”.

She added: "Commentators constantly talk about the challenges of social care reform but less often talk about the prize: knowing that if we develop care needs and disabilities as we get older, we will not be abandoned to struggle alone - as happens to almost two million of us at present.

“A reformed system would ensure that there would be some help for us, and hopefully it would be properly joined up with the health care that we typically require as we get older too.

Article continues below

"At Age UK we hear far too many older people who are desperate for good care and support but simply cannot secure it, creating misery and heartache for them and for their families. It's high time this ended. The Prime Minister is right: we can and we must do better.”

News.title: France wildfires live: 184 arsonists arrested as 'all regions' at risk of further fires
News.content:
Flames are nearing the French Atlantic Coast with raging wildfires now nine miles from Bordeaux as the city's mayor says he's prepared for 'all eventualities'

All regions of France are potentially at risk of wildfires tomorrow as the country grapples with what President Macron has claimed is the "most difficult situation" his country has dealt with since World War Two.

“We are facing two particularly critical days, with the heatwave and the very dry forest,” Gironde mayor Blandine Sarrazin. told local media. "This is the third fire to start here in the last two and a half days, it's really difficult," she added, telling residents it was not yet safe to return home.

Holidaymakers have been forced to leave campsites, tourist homes, holiday villages and leisure parks around Lacanau, which is around 40 miles from Bordeaux. The order comes as firefighters race against time to bring the fires under control before the country's south-west is blasted by a forecast 40C heatwave tomorrow (Wednesday).

Officials say the largest blaze has "stabilised" but have warned it could still burn out of control again as temperatures rise and humidity falls.

But a number of additional fires continue to burn with no end in sight, as local officials warn that the inferno could continue for months before it is fully contained.

France's Interior Minister Laurent Nunez claimed wildfire season is "far from over," and said authorities have arrested 1 84 suspected arsonists since the start of the summer.

Meanwhile in Spain, 63,000 people have been evacuate from their homes near Madrid, with the country's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez calling it "the most painful expression of the climate emergency".

News.title: Japan earthquake live: Dozens still missing as search for survivors continues overnight
News.content:
Multiple people have died while more are missing after a shopping centre collapsed following a huge 7.1 magnitude earthquake on the Japanese island of Kyushu

Dozens of people are still reported missing following the horror collapse of a shopping mall in Japan that caused 'many fatalities' after being struck by a powerful earthquake.

Up to 30 others remain missing at the Aeon Mall in Kumamoto, while employees are also missing at the nearby Nippon Paper Industries Yatsushiro Plant. Several people travelling in a high speed train were also injured after a chimney stack from the paper company fell on them during the quake, local media reports.

“People are coming in with burns and fractures from being trapped under objects due to the earthquake, and ambulances are constantly bringing in injured people,” a hospital employee told national broadcaster NHK.

“Inside the hospital, there are water leaks and electrical system failures,” they added.

The massive quake measured at the highest possible level seven on Japan's own Shindo "scale of shaking" and has left tens of thousands without power. Kumamoto Airport has been closed indefinitely after the earthquake rocked its runway.

Kumamoto was hit with a deadly quake in 2016 that left more than 50 people dead, 1,800 injured and tens of thousands of homes damaged or destroyed.

News.title: Man, 80, faces lethal injection 40 years after brutal murder of ex-girlfriend's parents
News.content:
Man, 80, faces lethal injection 40 years after brutal murder of ex-girlfriend's parents

Dominick Anthony Occhicone, 80, will make history today when he is put to death by Florida authorities - 40 years after he was sentenced for the killings of his ex-girlfriend's parents

View 4 Images Dominick Anthony Occhicone will die by lethal injection (Image: Florida Department of Correction)

An 80-year-old man will become the second-oldest to be executed in modern US history - decades after he brutally murdered the parents of his ex-girlfriend.

‌



Dominick Anthony Occhicone is scheduled today to become the oldest person in Florida history - and the second in US national history - to be executed by the state as it continued a deadly streak of killing condemned prisoners. The country has carried out 17 executions in total this year, with Florida carrying out more than every other state combined.

‌



The elderly man, who was convicted of killing his ex-girlfriend Anita Gerrity's parents in 1986, is set to die by lethal injection at 6pm local time, barring any last-minute developments.

‌



I was a death row executioner and quit with PTSD after watching sickening 15-minute botched killing of inmate READ MORE :

View 4 Images Occhicone's execution is set to take place at Florida State Prison (Image: Douglas R Clifford/Tampa Bay Times/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock)

Occhicone had made a last-ditch appeal to the US Supreme Court to intervene in his death sentence, which was denied by Florida's Supreme Court last week. His lawyers had argued that the inmate was suffering from a series of age-related ailments, among them kidney and prostate problems, which would make his execution especially painful.

This, they argued, would constitue a cruel and unusual punishment, prohibited under Florida's state constitution, which bars officials from inflicting a "superaddition" of terror, pain, or disgrace on an executee.

‌



A Florida prison official said on Tuesday morning that the department was confident in its readiness to carry out Occhicone's execution. All Florida executions are by injection of a sedative, a paralytic and a drug that stops the heart, according to the Department of Corrections.

View 4 Images Ron DeSantis has overseen an exploion in the number of executions carried out in Florida (Image: Jefferee Woo/Tampa Bay Times/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock)

If his execution proceeds as planned, Occhicone would become the state’s oldest inmate to be executed just weeks after two 74-year-old men briefly held that spot, the second man just a week older than the first at his time of death.

‌



Occhicone also would become the second-oldest prisoner known to be put to death in modern US history after 83-year-old Walter Moody Jr was executed in Alabama in 2018 for a wave of southern mail bombs in 1989 that killed a federal judge and wounded a Black civil rights attorney.

Occhicone sat on death row for 40 years, and is the last remaining member of his immediate family, members of whom previously said they noticed in him a rage they believed made him a "time bomb" following his conviction for murder.

View 4 Images Occhicone will become Florida's 12th execution (Image: Birmingham Mail)

‌



In 1986, he had told Ms Gerrity he would harm her parents, Raymond and Martha Artzner, or children after appearing at her home in Holiday, Florida. Ms Gerrity refused to speak to him, and when her father went outside their home to confront Occhicone, he grinned at Ms Gerrity while murdering him.

Attorneys wrote in a statement of fact presented to the court: "Occhicone pointed a gun at Artzner, turned to Anita, and grinned as he shot Artzner in the neck."

Occhicone then broke through the home's locked door in pursuit of Gerrity, who escaped with her daughter. Occhicone then turned the gun on her mother Martha, shooting her four times and killing her at the scene. The killer was arrested on the same day, and was sentenced to life in prison and death for their murders in 1986.

Article continues below

His execution was condemned as "cruel and unusual" by the Floridians For Alternatives to the Death Penalty, who opposed it on the basis of his persistent health troubles.

Grace Hannah, executive director of the organisation, said in a statement the move was an "affront to the conscience" of those involved, saying: “This is cruel and unusual punishment and an affront to the conscience of everyone involved. He is 80 years old. He looks like he is 80 years old and has the health problems of an 80-year-old.”

News.title: Couple paid £37.5m by eBay after they were sent cockroaches and bloody pig mask
News.content:
Couple paid £37.5m by eBay after they were sent cockroaches and bloody pig mask

David and Ina Steiner, from Massachusetts, have received a huge payout from eBay after they told of being threatened and targeted in a campaign to "intimidate" them

View Image A massive payout has been agreed by eBay (Image: Bloomberg via Getty Images)

A couple have been paid nearly £37.5million by eBay after claiming former company employees threatened and targeted them with deliveries including insects and a bloody pig Halloween mask.

‌



The online commerce site agreed the pay out to David and Ina Steiner, from Massachusetts, having reached the basis of a settlement in February as it headed towards trial.

‌



And now a final agreement has been reached with the Steiners, founders of EcommerceBytes, a newsletter covering the e-commerce industry. The deal includes an additional £5.27 million in charitable donations,

‌



Lawyer Christopher Murphy said the resolution sends "a warning that attempts by big business to suppress speech and the press will not be tolerated."

France wildfires map shows vast infernos as thousands of tourists told to leave READ MORE :

The Buck Moon: Rare chance to catch glimpse of spectacular Full Moon this week READ MORE :

"This was not only an attack and campaign of harassment against two people; it was also an attack on free speech and freedom of the press," said Murphy. He added that his clients insisted on being able to speak openly about what happened to them in the settlement.

It resolves more than six years of criminal and civil proceedings stemming from the harassment campaign.

‌



In their 2021 lawsuit filed in a Boston court, the Steiners said that the company engaged in a conspiracy to "intimidate, threaten to kill, torture, terrorize, stalk and silence them" in order to "stifle their reporting on eBay."

The couple, who report on the e-commerce industry in their newsletter, said they were subjected to cyberstalking, death threats and in-person surveillance by former eBay workers.

The settlement also requires eBay to issue a public statement addressing the conduct of former executives involved in the case. When the lawsuit was filed, the company said "the misconduct of these former employees was wrong," and that it would "do what is fair and appropriate to try to address what the Steiners went through."

‌



And eBay reiterated its apology today, saying, "What the Steiners were subjected to by former eBay employees in 2019 was wrong, reprehensible and should never have happened."

The company also accepted "the unprofessional tone in internal communications" by former CEO Devin Wenig, former Chief Communications Officer Steve Wymer and former Senior Vice President Wendy Jones.

eBay said the conduct "is not representative of eBay's culture" and said it has since changed leadership and strengthened its policies, procedures and ethics training.

‌



In 2020, prosecutors charged seven former eBay employees, alleging they carried out a coordinated harassment campaign against the couple after becoming angered by coverage in the couple's online newsletter.

Most of the defendants pleaded guilty to charges including conspiracy and cyberstalking and were later sentenced to prison terms or home confinement.

In 2024, eBay Inc. agreed to pay a $3 million criminal penalty under a deferred prosecution agreement with federal authorities.

‌



Prosecutors have said the harassment included anonymous deliveries of items like live cockroaches and spiders, a funeral wreath, and a bloody pig face mask to the couple's home.

The employees also sent pornographic magazines with the husband's name on them to a neighbour's home and planned to break into the couple's garage to install a GPS device on their car.

In a statement, Murphy cited the payout and the absence of a confidentiality provision in a system where "wrongdoers too often hide their misdeeds by dangling compensation in front of those they victimised and trading that compensation for confidentiality".

Article continues below

He added: "We believe this resolution sends a clear message that corporations and their executives cannot engage in this type of misconduct without facing significant consequences."

News.title: UK heatwave: Met Office names 9 areas facing up to 35C heat on Wednesday - see full list
News.content:
UK heatwave: Met Office names 9 areas facing up to 35C heat on Wednesday - see full list

The Met Office has warned temperatures could reach 35C in nine areas on Wednesday, as amber heat health alerts remain in place across the Southeast of England

View 3 Images Wednesday will be warm and sunny, including here in Folkestone, Kent (Image: Gareth Fuller/PA Wire)

Brits are set to bake on Wednesday with temperatures likely to reach 35C.

‌



Forecasters say Wednesday will be the warmest day of the week and, as a result, amber heat health alerts have been issued for the East Midlands, East of England, London and Southeast of England. Yellow heat health alerts have also been put in place for the same period across the South West, West Midlands and Yorkshire & The Humber.

‌



The Met Office says it will remain hot for the rest of the week, and so the heatwave threshold will likely be met across most regions of the UK. The warmest counties on Wednesday should include Berkshire, Surrey and Buckinghamshire.

‌



Although it was warm on Monday, the mercury only peaked at 28C at Heathrow Airport in west London. Wednesday's figures are expected to be much hotter than that, particularly in the capital.

The Buck Moon: Rare chance to catch glimpse of spectacular Full Moon this week READ MORE :

View 3 Images Temperatures are again set to rise (Image: Getty)

But the sweltering temperatures will increase the threat of wildfires, which have happened frequently in the UK this month — and across Europe to devastating effects. Hundreds of thousands of people have been evacuated from their homes across France, where Emmanuel Macron says the blazes have put the country in its most difficult situation since the Second World War.

‌



And here, firefighters battled a raging wildfire in the Cairngorms for at least 10 days. Families there were also ordered to leave their properties. Temperatures across Scotland this week, though, are not anticipated to be as hot as parts of England and Wales. Southern parts of Scotland and most of Northern Ireland may in fact see showers throughout Wednesday.

Come Thursday, temperatures will ease across much of the country, though those in the Southeast of England will continue to feel the heat for a little longer, with the mercury still forecast to reach 29C, matching the heatwave threshold, reports the Express.

Met Office Deputy Chief Forecaster Gregory Wolverson said: "This is a short-lived spell of heat, but temperatures will climb quickly through the first half of the week, particularly in the southeast.

‌



"By Wednesday, some areas could see temperatures in the mid-30Cs, and while the heat will not be widespread across the whole of the UK, it will be enough for parts of the southeast to likely meet official heatwave criteria by Thursday.

"Elsewhere, the weather will be more changeable, and the change to cooler, more unsettled conditions will arrive sooner from the north and west, with a mix of sunshine and showers. Across northern areas, it is possible there will be heavier showers with a small risk of isolated thunderstorms through the week."

News.title: Some parents on benefits to get up to £4,500 for child starting apprenticeship
News.content:
Some parents on benefits will be given up to Â£4,500 a year to encourage their children to start apprenticeships, the government has said.

Under plans to encourage young people into work, families will be offered a bursary to replace Universal Credit payments lost by starting jobs.

The payment is expected to benefit an estimated few thousand households, who currently face losing between Â£17 and Â£330 a week if their children start apprenticeships.

The Conservatives welcomed Prime Minister Andy Burnham's support for apprenticeships, but criticised his plans to fund the bursaries.

The bursary will be paid for from a Â£30m pot, funded through the growth and skills levy, a tax on employers with annual wage bills over Â£3m.

It followed the publication of a Social Security Advisory Committee report, external which warned of the "perverse effects" of the benefits system on young people's employment choices.

It said, for example, single parents with a disabled child could lose up to Â£340 per week in benefits if their child started an apprenticeship, exceeding the expected apprenticeship salary of Â£258 per week.

Because they are classed as paid employment, benefit payments are reduced to households where young people take on apprenticeships.

The committee said the system was hampering government efforts to reduce the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet).

In a recent report, former Health Secretary Alan Milburn warned that one in six young people could be Neet in the next five years unless urgent action is taken.

Official figures show more than a million people aged 16 to 24 are currently Neet.

The government said its new bursary would remove a barrier to young people taking on apprenticeships, allowing them to "earn and learn".

Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said: "By providing bursaries to those who need them most and fully funding apprenticeship training, we are making sure cost is not the reason someone misses out."

It is part of a wider package of support for apprenticeships, including funding for apprenticeship training for under-25s and additional support for employers taking on apprentices.

Helen Whately, the Shadow Work and Pensions Secretary, said: "I'm glad Burnham agrees: apprenticeships are a good thing, and we need more of them."

But she said the plan was "uncosted".

"It is spending money already committed elsewhere. So, either it is another unfunded announcement, or Andy Burnham is not being straight with us about his plans."

Burnham has said he is "on a mission" to reduce the number of Neets.

"The trend is rising at the moment, so the first thing I've got to do is to stop that rise," he said.

As he continues a flurry of early policy announcements, Burnham on Tuesday set out plans to strike a balance in the education system between prioritising academic and technical skills.

News.title: Zelensky and Netanyahu meet Trump as wars in Ukraine and Iran drag on
News.content:
President Donald Trump has held separate meetings with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, which the White House described as "positive and productive".

The two leaders were in Washington to attend the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham, a staunch supporter of Israel and advocate for US aid to Ukraine, who died earlier this month.

Zelensky and Trump discussed Kyiv's hope that the US would help bolster its air defences, although no formal commitment has so far been announced.

Netanyahu, for his part, arrived at a time when the US-Israel ties have been frayed by diverging views on Iran.

Ahead of the visit, Zelensky was expected to press Trump to follow through on a promise he made at this month's Nato summit to grant Ukraine a licence to produce Patriot interceptor missiles.

Ukraine has long sought American Patriot missiles, which Kyiv says could be used to defend Ukrainian cities from escalating Russian drone and ballistic missile attacks across the country.

But the closed-door meeting ended without any firm announcement over US military assistance to Ukraine.

News.title: French Navy carries out 'shooting drill' during MP's BBC interview
News.content:
A French Navy patrol boat appeared to fire a round of gunshots "without warning" in the English Channel during a BBC interview with the UK shadow home secretary.

Conservative MP Chris Philp was being interviewed about small boat crossings by BBC journalist Michael Keohan as a French warship passed by at 09:15 BST (10:15 CET), about three miles from the French coast.

Keohan said there were 17 shots but "no warnings" from the boat about 300m away, which left Philp believing it was an intimidation tactic to "stop us covering migrant crossings".

The French authorities said it was part of a training exercise, unrelated to the presence of a British ship, which it said was out of range of fire.

Philp dismissed this claim as "not credible", adding: "There were no warnings in place about live firing training exercises.

"It looked and sounded exactly like deliberate intimidation."

News.title: Grieving mum was told baby's ashes were animal remains
News.content:
Ness suffered a miscarriage just before she was due to have her 12-week scan on April 20 2021.

She told how she had treasured the ashes for three years.

"They had sat on my shelf next to my baby scan," said Ness.

In court, prosecutor Chris Paxton KC said "the ashes that Lucy was given could not have been those of her baby".

The barrister did not state that they were of animal origin.

Ness was clear to the BBC, however, that police had told her the ashes were animal remains.

Her disgust at Bush was clear.

She said: "How can somebody with a duty of care do this to my family?"

She and her partner, Callum Ellerby, were told their baby was cremated on 10 May 2021.

"We didn't know the gender," said Ness. "We were not going to know the gender."

The day after the cremation was meant to have taken place, Bush, from Legacy Independent Funeral Directors, rang her and asked her to collect the ashes, which she did.

They were contained in a white china urn with a teddy bear embossed on it, Ness recalled.

When Humberside Police announced they were investigating Legacy in March 2024, Ness rang the helpline set up for anyone concerned.

The force then contacted her to say the ashes she had in her home could not be that of her baby, she said.

Officers explained to Ness that they had checked records at the crematorium and found Bush collected the baby's ashes on 13 May - two days after he had presented Ness and Ellerby with the urn.

She said: "I have felt very up and down. This has definitely impacted on my mental health."

News.title: Naga Munchetty to leave BBC Breakfast after 17 years
News.content:
Munchetty, 51, is among the best-paid presenters on the BBC's star salaries list, earning about Â£360,000 a year, according to the latest accounts.

She has interviewed major celebrities and politicians on the programme over the years ranging from Hillary Clinton and Michelle Obama to Sir Keir Starmer, Sir David Attenborough and Sir Rod Stewart.

In 2016, she appeared on the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing.

She has also been at the centre of some controversies during her time on BBC Breakfast.

In 2019, she was initially found to have breached the BBC's guidelines over comments she made about a social media post from Donald Trump about four female politicians of colour.

However, the BBC's director general then reversed that finding after deciding her words were not "sufficient to merit" upholding part of the complaint.

In 2021, Munchetty and co-presenter Charlie Stayt were "spoken to and reminded of their responsibilities" after complaints about their reaction to a government minister's flag. Munchetty apologised for liking "offensive" tweets about the exchange.

In June 2025, the Sun reported details of two alleged incidents which the paper said caused BBC bosses to speak to Munchetty about her conduct.

That came amid reports of behind-the-scenes tensions on the show, and at the same time as the programme's editor Richard Frediani took extended leave following allegations about his behaviour.

Frediani returned to work two weeks later and remains editor of BBC Breakfast.

At the time, the BBC said it did not comment on individual cases but took all complaints about conduct at work extremely seriously. Munchetty and Frediani did not comment on the reports.

The programme won a Bafta TV Award last year for best news coverage for a special about the Post Office scandal.

News.title: Powell says student loan system at top of in-tray
News.content:
Lucy Powell has said she wants to make sure the student loans system is "fair" and that the issue is at the top of her in-tray as the new education secretary.

Labour's deputy leader told the BBC she stood by comments she made in February that the interest rates graduates with Plan 2 loans were paying were "egregious".

She said she was committed to looking at the issue, although acknowledged she "can't make any promises" about changes.

Plan 2 loans were taken out by students in England between September 2012 and July 2023, and are still issued in Wales. Graduates pay back what they earn above the repayment threshold at a rate of 9%.

In November last year, then-Chancellor Rachel Reeves said the repayment threshold for students with Plan 2 loans would be frozen at Â£29,385 between 2027 and 2030, instead of rising with inflation.

The change would result in students starting to repay their loans sooner than they would otherwise have done, and their rising salaries leading to greater repayments.

Campaigners have called for that decision to be reversed.

Reeves later said the government's measures were "fair and proportionate" for getting "the balance right between tax and spending".

In April, the government said interest on some student loans in England - including Plan 2 - would be capped at 6%.

Speaking to Matt Chorley on BBC Radio 5 Live, Powell said she was "very familiar" with the issue as her eldest child has a Plan 2 loan.

She said: "I think it's not just about the threshold of when people start to pay it back, but also the interest rate which is RPI [retail prices index] plus 3%.

"I think I've called it in the past egregious and I'm not going to change my opinion on that just because I'm now the secretary of state.

"The government has committed to a review of that, it's very much at the top of my in-tray as the secretary of state, and I want to make sure we look at this so it's fair for students."

Powell described it as a "real cost-of-living issue" for young people, adding: "They're paying high repayments and never, ever paying off the capital of their student loan."

Pressed on whether it is something she will look at, Powell replied: "Yes. I can't make any promises, but it needs looking at."

MPs on the Treasury Committee this month said comparing student loan repayments to phone contracts or cinema tickets "amounted to mis-selling" by government.

It came after a BBC investigation found the government compared student loan repayments to Â£30-a-month phone contracts in promotional presentations to teenagers a decade ago.

Earlier this year, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said she would cut the rate of interest charged on Plan 2 loans, capping it at RPI only. The current RPI rate is 3%.

News.title: Richard Hammond fined £999 for  speeding offences
News.content:
Former Top Gear presenter Richard Hammond has been fined Â£999 after being caught speeding twice in three weeks while driving luxury cars.

The 56-year-old was captured driving his Porsche Taycan Cross Turismo at 68mph in a 50mph limit on the A40 in Pencraig, Herefordshire on 2 December.

He was later clocked driving his Bentley Continental GT at 82mph in a 70mph limit on the M50 Rudhall Overbridge, also in Herefordshire, on 22 December.

Hammond pleaded guilty to two speeding charges through his solicitor. Two further charges that he had ignored the police letters and failed to identify himself as the guilty driver were withdrawn by police.

He was also given seven penalty points for his licence at the hearing last week.

Magistrate Ann Minton ordered him to pay a total of Â£1,771, comprising two fines of Â£333 and Â£666, Â£240 in costs and victim surcharges totalling Â£532.

News.title: Fourth heatwave grips parts of UK with 35C forecast
News.content:
A fourth heatwave of the year is now under way for parts of the UK, with temperatures expected to climb into the mid-30s Celsius later this week.

This latest spell of heatwave threshold-level temperatures is expected to peak on Wednesday in the south-east and east of England.

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has warned the rising temperatures could increase health risks, particularly for vulnerable groups.

It has issued amber heat health alerts, external for much of eastern England that come into force on Wednesday.

News.title: Laughter and tears at Dame Penelope Keith funeral
News.content:
Dame Penelope Keith's funeral has been hailed as "wonderful, beautiful and absolutely amazing" by her friends.

The actress, who starred in The Good Life and To The Manor Born, "died peacefully whilst living with cancer at her home" on 29 June at the age of 86.

Crowds lined the streets to say their goodbyes to the "very special lady" as her coffin travelled through her home town of Milford in Surrey before the service at Guildford Cathedral.

Broadcaster, writer and former politician Gyles Brandreth said the funeral was "filled with a mixture of sadness but laughter and gratitude as well because we were celebrating a great actress".

"It was a wonderful way to remember a remarkable person," he told BBC Radio Surrey.

Posting on X later, he said: "There was laughter and tears at Guildford Cathedral this morning - a truly beautiful and deeply moving funeral service for Dame Penelope Keith - what a lady and what a perfect service.

"It caught her completely. She was very special."

News.title: Unsolved Suzy Lamplugh case 'haunts' detectives
News.content:
Police officers investigating the disappearance of estate agent Suzy Lamplugh in west London say they remain "haunted" by the case, four decades after she went missing.

Lamplugh, 25, vanished after leaving her Fulham office to meet a client on the afternoon of 28 July 1986. She never returned and her body has never been found.

As the Metropolitan Police investigation is due to be mothballed next year, cold case detectives say they are troubled by the continuing mystery.

To mark the 40th anniversary of her disappearance, the Lamplugh family has released previously unseen photographs featuring her siblings Lizzie, Tamsin and Richard and her parents Paul and Diana.

In releasing the intimate family images, her siblings described her as "a truly beautiful person inside and out".

News.title: Two-Michelin-star chef brings fine dining to town football club
News.content:
Football fans will have the chance to swap their traditional match day pint and pie for a pop-up dining experience created by a renowned two-Michelin-star chef.

Gareth Ward, the chef behind Ynyshir Restaurant and Rooms near Machynlleth, Powys - which has an almost Â£500 per head tasting menu - has partnered up with Aberystwyth Town Football Club, in Ceredigion.

The collaboration will bring supporters different match day dining experiences, hospitality packages and corporate events throughout the season.

Ward, who has featured as a guest judge on MasterChef: The Professionals, said he was "excited" for the new venture.

The chef-patron said football clubs should be at "the heart of their communities".

The club's team is in the Novira Cymru South division, the second tier of Welsh football.

He added: "I see a real opportunity to bring people together through food and unforgettable matchday experiences and corporate events."

News.title: Schools to offer technical subjects to pupils from age 14 in England, Burnham says
News.content:
Secondary school pupils in England will be able to study subjects like manufacturing and AI in addition to core academic learning under reforms outlined by Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

The government said the courses, which would be available from Year 10, would be linked to local industries and designed to give children a clearer pathway into work.

Data published this year showed more than one million young people across the UK were not in education, employment or training, the highest level in more than 12 years.

Few details have been published about how the new vocational courses would work in practice and it is not clear how they would operate in areas with low industrial activity.

The BBC understands that the government expects the new pathways into work to be up and running in some areas by 2028.

Later on Tuesday, the government also announced a new bursary of up to Â£4,500 for some families who would lose out on money if their children wanted to do an apprenticeship, because the child benefit they would lose out on would be worth more than the apprenticeship starter salary.

Speaking at a train manufacturing site in Derby, Burnham said: "We've had a system built for too long around the university route and it sends a message to some young people that they're some kind of second-class citizens, and it's just not right.

"They need an education system that works for them as well, that offers a path to all young people, that's balanced between academic and technical."

The prime minister said he was "on a mission" to reduce the number of young people not in education, employment or training - known as "Neet" - but declined to put a target date on his ambition.

"The trend is rising at the moment, so the first thing I've got to do is to stop that rise," he said.

"It's hard to put a firm date on the moment when you can say there are fewer than now."

However, shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said while there was a "broad consensus" on improving vocational education, it was "not a big bold announcement".

She told BBC Breakfast: "What's going on there is a drastic shortage of jobs because Labour's policies over the last couple of years have killed job opportunities for young people. This announcement will not solve that."

News.title: Hundreds of thousands of women get morning-after pill via free pharmacy service
News.content:
The morning-after pill, known as emergency contraception, external, is medication designed to prevent unwanted pregnancies. It usually has to be taken within three to five days of having unprotected sex. The sooner it is taken, the more effective it is.

It works by delaying or preventing the release of an egg, but will only prevent pregnancy if ovulation has not already happened.

Alternatively, women can visit a doctor or nurse to have a coil or intrauterine device (IUD) fitted to prevent pregnancy at any time during their menstrual cycle. To be effective, it needs to be fitted within 120 hours or five days of unprotected sex.

The government said making the morning-after pill available free from pharmacies would end the "unfair" barriers and postcode lottery some women faced - with access varying dramatically depending on where they live.

Under the scheme, women can visit their local pharmacy and have a confidential consultation with a pharmacist or trained pharmacy technician, before receiving the medication on the same day.

Prior to this, women had to book an appointment with their GP, sexual health clinic or pharmacy to get the morning-after pill. Women could also access it privately, as they still can now.

In 2024/25, there were around 150,000 NHS prescriptions for the morning-after pill - far fewer than under the new service.

Dr Sue Mann, NHS National Clinical Director for Women's Health, said the pharmacy service was a "major step forward for women's health", with "no appointment, no waiting and no judgement".

"This service is already making a real impact, particularly for women living in more deprived communities, by making contraception easier to access closer to home," she added.

Women can check online, external to find their nearest participating pharmacy. All pharmacists and pharmacy technicians delivering the service have received specialist training to provide emergency contraception and wider contraceptive care.

News.title: Man guilty of murdering two men found in woods
News.content:
Desborough stood to listen to the verdicts with his hands behind his back.

He was wearing a grey T-shirt and glasses, and maintained a neutral expression while listening.

He was told he should "be alive" to the prospect of a whole life sentence when he is sentenced by Mr Justice Pushpinder Saini on Wednesday.

Witness impact statements would also be read out at the hearing, the court was told.

After the verdict, Coleman's family said in a statement: "We as a family would like to thank the police, prosecution and everyone involved in getting justice for Dan.

"Dan was a loving, caring and compassionate man who will be forever loved and sadly missed."

Aquilino's family said: "We are completely and utterly mortified in the violent murder of Claudio and the manner in which his body was disposed.

"Claudio will always be in our thoughts and we now pray he is at peace."

They said they had faced a "profoundly sad ordeal".

Det Supt Rachael Bentley, of Devon and Cornwall Police's major crime investigation team, described the killings as "callous and cold-blooded", as "both men were vulnerable and trusted James Desborough as their friend" before he brutally murdered them and "savagely desecrated their bodies".

She paid tribute to the victims' families, saying they "conducted themselves with a quiet dignity throughout this investigation and who have had to listen to, and see, some harrowing evidence".

Desborough was previously found guilty of strangling his 65-year-old cellmate Steven Kempster in September 2025, while on remand awaiting trial over the deaths of Coleman and Aquilino.

That trial had heard Kempster's snoring had annoyed Desborough.

Bentley said Desborough's taking of Kempster's "in this way was cowardly".

Helen Phillips of the Crown Prosecution Service said after the hearing that it had been a "large and extremely complex case".

"We worked closely with police from the very start of their investigation in Paramoor Woods, and then later with a second police team on the investigation into the murder at HMP Exeter, which ran in parallel," she said.

"The families of Claudio and Daniel have been so dignified throughout the investigation and trial process, even when faced in court with awful descriptions of what happened to their loved ones, and Desborough's attempts to blame Daniel for somehow being involved in the disposal of Claudio's body.

"As Desborough faces justice for his actions, my thoughts remain with the families and friends of his three victims."

News.title: Chairman stole £22k from junior football club to fund cocaine habit
News.content:
A former junior football club chairman stole Â£22,491 from accounts and faked HMRC documents to feed his cocaine habit.

Karl Morecroft, 45, lied to club members at RTB Ebbw Vale while taking home the payments over the course of 15 months.

The club in Blaenau Gwent supported 330 children and relied on the goodwill of fundraisers, parents and volunteers to raise the money to keep going after the fraud.

Morecroft was given a 20-month jail term suspended for two years at Cardiff Crown Court on Monday, and must complete 180 hours of unpaid work and 50 rehabilitation days.

He was also ordered to pay Â£21,259 within three years and a default order of 12 months in prison if he failed to do so was imposed.

Discrimination remains "deeply embedded" within English football, according to the chief executive of Kick It Out, as reports of abuse surged by 25 per cent last season.

The anti-discrimination charity recorded 1,744 reports in the 2025-26 campaign, a significant rise from 1,398 in the previous year. For the first time, the number of distinct incidents surpassed 1,000, reaching 1,255.

Kick It Out clarified that while one incident can generate multiple reports, the reports-per-incident ratio for the past season stood at 1.39. The increase was widespread across various platforms and levels of the game.

Reports of online discrimination rose by five per cent to 650, while incidents in the professional game and at grassroots level both saw a 41 per cent increase, reaching 636 and 458 reports respectively.

The charity's data revealed alarming increases across all types of abuse. Islamophobia reports soared by 88 per cent, homophobia by 46 per cent, and anti-Semitism by 43 per cent. Racism reports were up 19 per cent, sexism by 12 per cent, and ableism by 20 per cent.

open image in gallery Kick It Out chief executive Samuel Okafor commented on the latest figures (Handout pic from Kick It Out/PA)

Samuel Okafor, Kick It Out’s chief executive, stated: "These figures show that discrimination remains deeply embedded across the game at a time when we’re also seeing rises in hate crime and divisive political rhetoric in Britain. But they also show that people are more willing to stand up to abuse when they see it, and it’s encouraging to see professional players set that example last season."

Mr Okafor added: "While we recognise that there is a lot of good work ongoing in football to tackle discrimination, we will continue to work with football authorities, clubs, leagues, regulators and Government to ensure we match the courage shown to report abuse with clear and consistent action so that football is welcoming to everyone."

The season also saw a 41 per cent increase in reports of discriminatory mass chanting, reaching a record 142 instances. This included rises in racist, sexist, homophobic, transphobic, and ableist chants.

Furthermore, Kick It Out noted a concerning rise in anti-immigrant language, with terms such as "stop the boats" and "send them back" reported at all levels. The 39 reports of this nature in 2025-26 was more than the 37 in the previous two years combined.

Despite the stark figures, Kick It Out marked a milestone during the season, delivering its 500th fan education session to individuals found to have discriminated in football, with a reoffending rate of just 1.25 per cent.

British singer Myles Smith has cancelled an upcoming concert in Vancouver, Canada, citing a "major family health issue."

The show, which was scheduled for August 4, was part of his ongoing tour.

Smith had recently released his debut album, My Mess, My Heart, My Life last month, and had embarked on a promotional tour.

He shared a statement regarding the cancellation.

Posting on Instagram, he said: “To everyone who was planning on coming to the Vancouver show. You may have received a notification that the show has been cancelled. I wanted to explain why, because I never want to leave you in the dark.

“There has been a major family health issue at home, and important appointments are taking place on that date. I simply can’t not be there. Family has to come first, and this wasn’t a decision I made lightly.

open image in gallery ( Myles Smith/Instagram )

open image in gallery ( Myles Smith/Instagram )

“I know many of you have spent your hard-earned money, made travel plans and set aside time to be there. The fact that you continue to show up for me means more than I can put into words, and I never want to take that for granted or lose the trust we’ve built together.”

He continued: “I also want to reassure everyone with tickets for the shows after Vancouver that this decision is specific to this date because of those appointments. As things stand, the rest of the shows are going ahead as planned, and I can’t wait to see you. Thank you for your understanding, your patience, and for always supporting me. It truly means the world.”

Smith then shared another post in which he said he wanted to “say one more thing”.

He wrote: “I will always try to be as open and transparent with you as I can. I respect you all too much not to be. I would never cancel a show unless I absolutely had to.

The singer went on to say that over the past four years he has been “lucky enough” to play more than 400 shows and had only ever cancelled four – which he said were “all for reasons completely out of my control”.

open image in gallery The UK leg of Smith’s tour will start in Kingston on October 1, eventually wrapping up in London on November 20 ( Matt McNulty/Getty Images For MOBO )

“I don’t say that to make excuses, but to show you how seriously I take the commitment of showing up for you.

“I’ve already seen some of the frustration and disappointment, and I completely understand it. If you’d booked time off, travelled, or spent money to be there, I’d feel exactly the same. I’m not asking for anybody to feel sorry for me! I just wanted to give you as much information as I could, because I believe that’s what you deserve. Whilst trying to maintain the privacy of the circumstances back home.”

He concluded: “I’m truly sorry and I’ll be back as soon as it’s feasibly possible. Thank you for continuing to support me. It means more than you’ll ever know.”

Earlier this month, Smith shared a post on Instagram in which he explained that he had gone home for a few days to “be with the people I love”.

“There’s a lot going on in my personal life right now. I’ll probably talk about it when the time feels right, but for now I’m just trying to take things one day at a time,” he wrote.

“Before I left, the people closest to me told me something I won’t forget: don’t rob yourself of the dream you’ve worked so hard for just because life is heavy back home.”

Smith then thanked his fans for “carrying him through” a show the night before.

He is next due to play in Sacramento, California, on Tuesday night.

The UK leg of his tour will kick off in Kingston on October 1, eventually wrapping up in London on November 20.

Smith is best known for his 2024 singles Stargazing and Nice To Meet You.

He received three nominations at the 2025 Brit Awards and also won the Rising Star award.

A judge has issued a preliminary injunction sought by the city of Santa Monica, preventing overnight operations at the two Waymo LLC Broadway recharging stations, finding they are public nuisances.

"While the evidence shows that the parties have attempted to mitigate the noise, lights and traffic, it does not show that those efforts have been sufficiently successful to eliminate the public nuisance that is created," Santa Monica Superior Court Judge Bradley S. Phillips wrote in his final ruling issued Monday.

The judge said Waymo is prevented, pending trial, from operating the Broadway Lots between the hours of 11 p.m. and 6 a.m. Phillips had heard arguments July 22 and taken the case under submission.

In their court papers, attorneys for the city stated that those living near the stations have used such terms as "mini-Las Vegas," "living next door to a spaceship," "a circus" and "a city that never sleeps" to describe their plight.

The group Santa Monica for Renters Rights backed the requests for injunctive relief sought by the city and the City Council.

"SMRR is deeply disturbed by the disruptions and the burdens imposed on residential neighbors as a result of Waymo's current operation of the lots," a letter written on the group's behalf stated. "It simply is not acceptable that residents should be forced to endure sleepless nights in their homes."

According to the city's court papers, residents are disturbed by Waymo lot workers talking in the middle of the night as well as the sounds of the Waymo vehicles, which the city contends "echo off buildings along the alleys like a canyon."

( Getty )

Although the alleged nuisances have cost residents the peace and quiet enjoyment of their homes, repeated requests from the city to abate the problem have been rejected, the city alleged.

In a sworn declaration, resident Paula Achter, who works from home, said she had to adjust her sleeping habits and do her job from a different location in her apartment due to the noise from the Waymo vehicles passing by her building. She further said that humans are not the only ones being bothered.

"I used to hear birds singing in the morning from my apartment,” 69-year-old Achter said. "I've noticed I don't hear them anymore. I believe that they have nested elsewhere due to the Waymo frequency."

Victoria Benchuk, a single mother of a 5-year-old son with autism, said in her declaration that the Waymo lot near her building opened a few months after she and her boy moved into their apartment in October 2024.

"When there are multiple Waymos stopped in the alley, the noise from the motors, the beeping and the people talking and working in the Waymos lot wake up my son two to four nights a week and he has trouble getting back to sleep," Benchuk said. "I often have to bring my son into the living room where I sleep to help him settle back down."

Benchuk further said her son did not have the same sleeping issues before the Waymo lot opened or when they lived in their prior apartment.

In its own lawsuit filed against the city, Waymo denies a public nuisance existed and contended the company hired more staff, implemented software updates to reduce noise levels and frequencies, installed light and noise barriers and modified "vehicle behaviors" in the area.

"These changes resulted in a material decrease in noise and light levels during Waymo's overnight operations and traffic congestion in the surrounding areas was reduced," according to the Waymo suit.

Waymo also contended that the nuisance was actually created by local residents' interference with the company's operations during the relevant hours.

A Guatemalan man who was deported from the United States and his wife, who later left the country voluntarily to join him, were found dead in a sugarcane field in southwestern Guatemala, authorities said Tuesday.

Their 1-year-old daughter was found alive beside their bodies.

Nixon Giovanni Perez, 43, and Glendy Marisol Gonzalez, 25, were discovered with their hands tied behind their backs in a field outside Retalhuleu, a city about 112 miles (180 kilometers) west of Guatemala City, according to photos reviewed by Reuters.

Guatemala’s prosecutor’s office said in a statement that the couple’s infant daughter and their two other children were placed in the care of relatives. Local media reported that the couple had been reported missing the previous week.

The deaths highlight the risks and challenges faced by some immigrants after deportation from the United States, as President Donald Trump’s administration continues its large-scale deportation campaign.

open image in gallery The deaths highlight the risks and challenges faced by some immigrants after deportation from the United States ( Guatemala Prosecutor’s Office (MP)/Handout via Reuters )

The couple's troubles began last year when Perez and his brother were detained by immigration agents in Overland, Missouri, on their way to roofing jobs, Perez's brother Rolando told St. Louis Public Radio.

Perez, who had fled violence and poverty in Guatemala, was deported last year. Gonzalez self-deported to Guatemala in recent weeks to join her husband, Rolando said.

Representatives for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Overland police did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The Missouri Workers Center said it will hold a vigil on Sunday for Perez and Gonzalez, who was a member of an immigrants' rights organizing committee of the workers' group.

"Glendy came to our Fuerza meetings three weeks after giving birth. She was working two jobs, bringing new members, showing up — even as her world was being torn apart," they said on social media. "In June, to protect her daughters and keep the rest of her family together — and fearing she might lose custody of the girls — Glendy made the impossible decision to go back to Guatemala, even with an asylum court date set for 2027."

Nearly 32,000 people have been deported to Guatemala in the first six months of 2026, according to U.N. data, a 47 percent increase from the same period last year. More than 90 percent of deportees were sent from the United States, and the rest from Mexico.

Guatemala's government, which attributes a wave of murders that spiked over the last week to organized crime, on Monday announced a plan to strengthen the country's security measures.

Andy Burnham has challenged his opponents to join him in putting aside political point scoring to find a solution to England’s social care crisis.

The new Labour prime minister is set to hold a summit in Downing Street on Wednesday with Tory leader Kemi Badenoch and Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey to begin the process of thrashing out a way to deliver social care before it forces the NHS to collapse.

Ahead of a speech he is set to deliver at a care home in north London on Wednesday morning, Mr Burnham said: “Last week I said we needed a different kind of politics: problem-solving, not point-scoring. Nowhere is that more urgent than social care.

“For decades, governments have kicked this issue down the road because they’ve seen it as too risky, too difficult, and too complicated.

“Politicians might have different views but I’m serious about fixing this issue and to do that, we have to find common ground and listen to others to find a way forward.

open image in gallery Andy Burnham has appealed to opposition leaders to help him find a solution ( Reuters )

“It’s time to draw a line under people playing politics when the human cost of that means carers struggling, families paying the price and our NHS buckling under the strain.”

However, the initiative comes amid growing concerns about the state of the economy and the government’s ability to pay for Mr Burnham’s initiatives.

Already there are major questions about how he will fund £2bn of commitments on removing VAT of energy bills, capping bus fares at £2 and reducing business rates of pubs and clubs by 20 per cent.

Added to that, a major think tank is set to warn that inflation will hit almost 4 per cent next year and the government’s capacity to borrow has maxed out meaning everything will need to be funded through tax rises and spending cuts.

This will hit defence in particular, where Mr Burnham will need to find between £5bn and £18bn to meet the UK’s commitments and it has been suggested wants to issue war bonds, another form of borrowing to fund the gap.

Ahead of the summit on Wednesday Sir Ed, who has ensured that the Lib Dems have prioritised demanding solutions to the care crisis, has said his party is willing to work with Mr Burnham. Ms Badenoch has also offered to work with Mr Burnham, but warned she will not support new tax rises to fund it.

open image in gallery Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch will not support tax rises (Jonathan Brady/PA) ( PA Wire )

In 2009, when Mr Burnham was health secretary, he tried to find a common solution on care with a levy on assets when people died. But the Tories turned against him and accused him of trying to create a “death tax.”

Mr Burnham has not invited Reform to take part in the talks, even though they had been leading the polls for 15 months until Labour passed them this week.

However, Reform UK launched a preemptive attack, accusing Mr Burnham of wanting to revive his “death tax” plan, a claim that was immediately denied by Downing Street.

In a bid though to reach across the political divide, Mr Burnham said: “This comes down to a choice. We can carry on passing the problem to the next generation, or we can face it head on and work together to build a care system that gives people dignity, security and the support they deserve.

“This is about bringing back hope that we can finally fix the difficult issues that have been ignored for too long, and making Britain believe again.

“That's why I’m making this choice and I'm prepared to put everything I've got behind it.”

Visiting a care home on Wednesday, the prime minister will say he is making the choice to fix the broken social care system by finding common ground across party lines to tackle the big issues.

open image in gallery Reform have not been invited to the summit ( Reuters )

He will attempt to draw a line under decades of decline and a refusal to tackle these problems head on, calling on all political parties to focus on solving problems and find solutions together.

He will reiterate the need for a new kind of politics that puts differences aside in order to come together and face up to the challenges that Westminster has left unaddressed for too long.

He will be joined by the new health secretary Yvette Cooper and Baroness Louise Casey, who is leading the Independent Commission on Adult Social Care which will draw up recommendations to deliver a National Care Service.

Baroness Casey will also launch the Big Conversation on Care, which will give the public their chance to share their views and help shape the future of adult social care in England so that it is designed for the people it is there to serve.

It will be open to everyone through a new online platform, starting off the conversation by asking people about the values and principles we should all expect from a care system.

Baroness Casey said: “For too long, we have been stuck in the same cycle: crisis, promises of reform, another review, and then retreat, while the people who need care, and their families, bear the brunt.

“Fixing adult social care is about far more than money. People are already paying for failure through council tax, pressure on the NHS, their savings, giving up work, and the forced sale of their homes. The choice is whether we keep putting money into a system that is unfair, unpredictable and broken, or have an honest conversation about how to build something better.

“That is why we need a public conversation on care that tackles the tough questions. It’s only by facing up to this problem together that we can fix social care once and for all.”

Responding, Tory shadow health secretary Stuart Andrew said: “Andy Burnham and Labour cannot rely on vague promises of reform without a clear plan for implementation and detail on what will happen when.

“The Conservatives are ready to work with Labour on measures that improve social care provided they are not reliant on yet more tax rises and borrowing.”

Sir Ed said: “"There have been 22 failed attempts at reforming social care since 1997. To see the 23rd effort work, we need to do things differently.

"My party has been pushing for cross-party talks on care for years, because it is the only way to build a solution that actually works. For carers and for our country, nothing matters more, so I look forward to meeting the prime minister to begin these talks.”

The spacecraft rushing to the rescue of an aging and sinking NASA telescope has run into its own problem.

Katalyst Space Technologies said Tuesday that its Link satellite is experiencing thruster problems and has gone into an uncontrollable spin that is disrupting communication.

The trouble struck over the weekend, three weeks after the three-armed robotic spacecraft blasted into orbit.

The startup company said it's working nonstop to get Link back in action so it can capture Swift and boost the telescope to a higher orbit. Swift will crash back to Earth this fall without help. NASA is paying $30 million for the rescue effort, which was thrown together in under a year.

Launched in 2004, Swift is descending faster than expected because of recent solar activity. It needs a lift as soon as possible in order to continue scanning the universe for some of the biggest explosions, including gamma ray bursts and exploded stars. Scientific observations are on hold until then.

Neither Katalyst nor NASA is giving up hope. All of Link's other major subsystems appear to be doing fine, according to the company.

"The mission remains active and we continue to believe that with these changes, Link has a viable path to rendezvous with Swift," Katalyst said in a statement.

Ed Miliband is set to embark on his inaugural visit to Europe as Foreign Secretary this Wednesday, with a clear agenda to bolster ties with the EU.

His trip to France and Spain comes as both nations grapple with devastating wildfires, which have forced the evacuation of approximately 330,000 people.

Mr Miliband will extend the UK's solidarity in the wake of the destruction, while also emphasising that the crisis serves as a potent reminder of the climate emergency, demanding unified international action.

In Paris, he is scheduled to meet his French counterpart, Jean-Noel Barrot, to discuss crucial matters including the defence of European security, continued support for Ukraine, and efforts to secure peace in the Middle East.

Co-operation on migration is also expected to feature in their discussions.

Following his engagements in France, the Foreign Secretary will travel to Madrid to confer with Spanish foreign minister Jose Manuel Albares.

Firefighters battle a blaze in Madrid ( Getty )

Their talks are anticipated to cover the ongoing UK-EU Gibraltar treaty negotiations and broader collaboration on security issues.

The pressing issue of the climate crisis is slated for discussion during both high-level meetings, underscoring its global significance.

French authorities have ordered 4,000 more people to leave tourist sites along the country’s Atlantic coast, expanding what may be France’s largest peacetime evacuation as a vast wildfire west of Bordeaux raged.

A renewed heatwave was threatening firefighters’ fragile hold on the blaze, and fresh flames have erupted near Grand Crohot, a popular Atlantic beach on the Lège-Cap-Ferret peninsula, local authorities said.

French meteorological agency Meteo-France placed Gironde and Landes under a yellow heatwave warning.

President Emmanuel Macron said France was facing its most difficult situation since the Second World War, urging fire crews to “stay strong”.

More than 360,000 people across France and Spain in total have been forced to flee.

The new heatwave is forecast to last until at least Sunday.

News.title: Recovery aids and building muscle: Welsh weightlifter Laura Hughes answers your questions
News.content:
Laura Hughes first discovered weightlifting while training at her local Crossfit gym, making the transition from amateur gym-goer to competitive lifting.

Now a member of the Welsh national weightlifting squad, the 33-year-old holds the Welsh record for both the snatch and the clean and jerk (the two official competitive lifts in weightlifting) and is currently third overall in the women’s Welsh rankings. Hughes won bronze at the 2018 Commonwealth Games in Australia and was selected again for this summer’s Games in Glasgow.

We caught up with her for our Readers Ask series, where industry specialists answer questions from our Telegraph Recommended Reader Panel.

Who inspired you to get into weightlifting?

Olamilekan, South East

Originally, it was lots of different people, particularly general gym goers who were doing weightlifting at my gym. As I’ve grown as an athlete and become more competitive, I’ve had other inspirations.

Most notably, coming into [the Commonwealth Games], it has to be Gareth [Evans], our coach. Looking back at his performance in 2018 when he won his gold medal is so inspiring. [English lifter] Emily Godley was another competitor in 2018. She won the gold medal in my category and I just remember thinking that she was on fire that day.

What are the best exercises for you to build muscle mass?

Norman, Wales

We spend a lot of time doing our main lifts, so snatches, clean and jerks, but we also do lots of pulls and squats. I spend a lot of time doing accessory work to make sure that my body stays healthy, especially being an older athlete. I’ve put on quite a lot of muscle in this last block just from going heavier and pushing my limits with my main lifts.

What advice would you give to people who want to improve their strength?

David, North West

The most important thing is consistency. As long as you’re doing something, do it regularly, even if it’s twice a week. Don’t be afraid of picking up some dumbbells. If you’ve got somebody that can teach you how to lift weights properly, that’s going to be the best option. Do it safely, do it consistently, and don’t be afraid to try new strength exercises.

News.title: Explosive mpox outbreak causes 3,000 cases in Madagascar
News.content:
More than 3,000 cases of mpox have been recorded in Madagascar after the virus spread from a single port city to some of the country’s busiest coastal hubs.

A total of 3,022 cases and 20 deaths have been recorded as of this week, with cases in Toamasina and Taolagnaro accounting for more than half of all diagnoses.

The outbreak has been linked to Clade 1b mpox, a strain that emerged in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2024, prompting the World Health Organization (WHO) to declare a global public health emergency at the time.

“The main factor driving the continued spread of the disease is human mobility, seeding new outbreaks in areas where the virus has not circulated before,” Professor Carlos Maluquer de Motes of the University of Surrey told The Telegraph.

“Under-reporting is likely, with the real number of cases exceeding what is being reported.”

News.title: Chelsea in 10-goal thriller as ‘Alonso ball’ brings risk and reward
News.content:
Chelsea’s first match under the management of Xabi Alonso was a 10-goal thriller in Australia, as the Premier League side eventually showed their class in a 6-4 win over Western Sydney Wanderers.

Star striker João Pedro, who was controversially left out of Brazil’s World Cup squad, scored a nine-minute hat-trick after coming off the bench with half an hour of the friendly remaining.

Alonso had selected a youthful team for the first hour before bringing nine senior players, including João Pedro, into the side in the second half. According to Transfermarkt, Chelsea’s squad is valued at over £1.3bn while their opponents a more modest £5.86m.

Teenage signing Dastan Satpayev, midfielder Dario Essugo and winger Jamie Gittens also found the net for Chelsea, who were defensively vulnerable for long spells for the game.

Here are five things Telegraph Sport learned from Alonso’s first match.

João Pedro picks up where he left off

João Pedro scored 13 goals in the second half of last season and his impressive performances resulted in the 24-year-old being named Chelsea’s player of the campaign. It was something of a surprise, then, when he was left out of Carlo Ancelotti’s Brazil squad this summer.

The good news for Chelsea is that João Pedro’s absence from the World Cup has given him plenty of time to recover ahead of the new campaign, and he looked thrillingly sharp in his second-half performance against Western Sydney Wanderers. The difference in class between João Pedro and Liam Delap, the man he replaced, was clear for all to see.

Two of the Brazilian’s three goals were classy, composed finishes — and he also created a goal for Gittens after surging past three defenders on the left wing. João Pedro looks like he means business.
