World.title: WNBA media predictably embarrasses itself again by ignoring Sophie Cunningham story over All-Star Weekend
World.content:
The WNBA media had every opportunity to show it could cover the league like a serious professional sport over All-Star Weekend in Chicago.

It blew it.

Reporters had access to the league’s biggest players and Commissioner Cathy Engelbert just days after Sophie Cunningham said biological males should not compete in girls' and women's sports. Yet not one public answer emerged from the weekend about whether the league’s stars agreed with her.

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SPEAKS OUT TO PROTECT GIRLS AS WNBA ALL-STAR INITIATIVE BACKS ‘GENDER-EXPANSIVE’ GROUP

The outcome was, sadly, predictable.

Before the event, I wrote on X:

It did not.

One important disclosure: OutKick and Fox News Digital attempted to cover All-Star Weekend in person, and I planned to ask the players and Commissioner Cathy Engelbert about Cunningham’s comments (if given the chance). We applied for a credential through the NBA/WNBA credential portal, but the league denied the request because it was submitted 10 days after its June 16 deadline.

The portal was still open and accepted the application, which was submitted four weeks prior to the event.

I had not received the WNBA’s original credential advisory or either of the two reminder emails the league said it sent. We asked the league to reconsider, noting that OutKick and Fox News Digital were approved to cover last year's All-Star Game, but the WNBA stood by its decision.

So, no, OutKick did not ask the players in Chicago because we didn't have access to do so.

That left the job to the reporters who received credentials.

After reviewing the publicly available press conferences, interview videos, transcripts and coverage from All-Star Weekend, I could not find one instance of a WNBA All-Star or Commissioner Cathy Engelbert being asked about Cunningham’s statement.

Sophie Cunningham created an obvious story for WNBA reporters

Cunningham’s comments came in an ESPN profile published just before the All-Star break.

"I got a lot of negative feedback about me hating trans. And I’m like, ‘I never once said that,’" Cunningham said. "I think that I am here to extend love. But I also think with that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn’t have to go against biological men."

Reporters grilled Cunningham just before the break. She did not retreat.

"I said what I said. I think it’s kinda common sense," Cunningham said.

The story quickly moved beyond Cunningham.

Las Vegas Aces forward Brianna Turner publicly defended transgender participation in women’s sports. The White House backed Cunningham. The Associated Press identified the transgender-athlete debate as one of the major cultural issues hanging over All-Star Weekend.

In other words, this wasn't an obscure social media controversy that reporters could credibly claim they hadn't seen.

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SEES SUPPORT SURGE AFTER STAR PUTS CAREER ON LINE FOR GIRLS SPORTS

An active WNBA player had taken a clear position on one of the biggest debates in women’s sports. Her comments drew a response from another player and reached the White House. The league’s most prominent athletes were about to gather in the same city for several days of media availability.

The questions practically wrote themselves.

Do you agree with Cunningham?

Should women’s sports be reserved for biological females?

Do Cunningham’s comments conflict with the values of the WNBA?

Apparently, that was too much to ask.

WNBA All-Stars were available, but no one produced an answer

The WNBA assembled 22 All-Stars in Chicago, including Caitlin Clark, A’ja Wilson, Breanna Stewart, Paige Bueckers and Cunningham’s Indiana Fever teammates Kelsey Mitchell and Aliyah Boston. Players participated in practice interviews, informal scrums and official press conferences throughout the weekend.

There is always a chance that a reporter asked someone about Cunningham during a scrum that was not recorded or published. It is impossible to prove that the topic never came up once over the weekend.

But journalism is not a private conversation between a reporter and an athlete. The point is to provide information to the public.

No outlet appears to have produced an answer from an All-Star. No videos surfaced, no quote appeared in a story and no reporter posted a player’s response on social media.

If someone asked, the answer apparently was not important enough to publish. The practical result is the same.

The public still has no idea what the WNBA’s most prominent players think about trans-identifying biological males competing in women's sports and using women's locker rooms.

The irony is that All-Star Weekend included the inaugural WNBA Media & Innovation Summit. The event’s stated theme was "From Participation to Power," and organizers promoted it as a discussion about who will shape the future of women’s sports.

Evidently, asking female athletes whether women’s sports should be reserved for females didn't fit the program.

Cathy Engelbert was standing in front of the entire WNBA press corps

The failure to question Engelbert was particularly glaring.

The commissioner began her All-Star press conference by addressing racism, misogyny, homophobia, harassment and threats against players. She said the league is built on "inclusion and respect" and pledged to make every player feel safe and supported.

That provided a natural opening to ask about Cunningham.

Does the commissioner believe Cunningham’s comments are consistent with the WNBA’s values?

What is the league’s position on transgender eligibility?

Does Engelbert believe supporting a female-only athletic category is exclusionary?

No one asked.

Instead, reporters questioned Engelbert about the new replay center, international games, the Las Vegas Aces investigation, the relationship between the league and its players, officiating, security, her future as commissioner, coaching diversity, HBCU internships and her communication style.

Several were legitimate questions. The problem is not that reporters asked about officiating or league operations. The problem is that the full press conference ended without anyone addressing the controversy involving one of Engelbert’s players.

Engelbert even talked about young girls viewing WNBA players as role models.

Cunningham’s entire argument was that young girls deserve protection in locker rooms and athletic competition. Still, no one in the room made the connection. Or, possibly, no one in the room wanted to make the connection.

WNBA COMMISSIONER VOWS TO CRACK DOWN ON 'RACISM, MISOGYNY,' DODGES BIG QUESTIONS AT ALL-STAR PRESS CONFERENCE

WNBA media was comfortable judging Cunningham from a distance

Some reporters had plenty to say about Cunningham. They just didn’t appear interested in asking WNBA players about her.

The Guardian published an All-Star Weekend feature that characterized Cunningham’s comments as "transphobic language." The story included fresh quotes from Courtney Williams, Becky Hammon, Jessica Shepard and A’ja Wilson on other subjects.

Yet the published article contained no response from any of them about Cunningham’s comments.

That captures the problem with much of the media covering this league.

A reporter was comfortable delivering a moral judgment about Cunningham’s statement. Getting a prominent WNBA player on the record about that statement was apparently less important.

The Associated Press also included the controversy in its scene-setting story from Chicago. But the article relied on Cunningham’s previous ESPN quote and Turner’s social media comments rather than producing a response from an All-Star attending the weekend.

The media knew it was a story. They wrote about it. They just decided not to do any actual reporting.

This is what passes for WNBA journalism

None of this should be surprising.

In 2024, Caitlin Clark went through a massive media tour before entering the WNBA. Reporters asked her the same safe questions repeatedly, but no one asked the most influential young woman in American sports what she thought about transgender athletes competing against females.

Later that year, USA Today reporter Christine Brennan asked DiJonai Carrington whether she intentionally poked Clark in the eye. It was a completely reasonable question about something that happened during a basketball game.

The WNBA Players’ Association responded by calling on USA Today to discipline Brennan and suggesting that she should lose access.

Then came the Brittney Griner controversy last season. A viral video showed Griner saying something after fouling out against the Indiana Fever. Many viewers believed she made a racially charged remark.

For nearly three weeks, no WNBA reporter asked Griner what she said. OutKick sought credentials specifically to ask the question and was denied by multiple teams before the Washington Mystics eventually granted access.

When we finally asked Griner, she denied using the phrase attributed to her. The controversy largely died because an athlete finally answered the actual question.

That should have been a lesson for everyone covering the league.

Instead, All-Star Weekend showed that nothing has changed.

The WNBA and its players say they want the attention, revenue and stature afforded to major professional sports leagues. That comes with real media coverage. Sometimes athletes have to answer questions they would rather avoid.

A reporter didn't have to agree with Sophie Cunningham to ask about her comments. In fact, anyone who believed her statement was offensive or harmful had an even stronger reason to ask other players for their views.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

OutKick sought access because we intended to ask.

The league denied our credential request, and the reporters who were admitted apparently decided the answer was better left unknown.

The WNBA and its media cheerleaders spent All-Star Weekend celebrating the growth of women’s sports while avoiding the most basic question about who should be allowed to compete in them.

World.title: Ex-FDA commissioner confronted on 'outrageous' Fauci diaries by CNBC host
World.content:

Scott Gottlieb, a former FDA commissioner, was confronted about former National Institutes of Health (NIH) Director Anthony Fauci's diaries on Monday in a back-and-forth on CNBC, which host Joe Kernen called "outrageous."

"How about your buddy Fauci, that I've asked you about in the past. You've defended him quite a bit," Kernen said. "I've asked about whether he orchestrated a cover-up of the lab origin because of his involvement in making gain-of-function research possible again in China, which he did. He knew that would come back to haunt him and then basically told his colleagues go with the natural origin. It was obvious three years ago, Scott, to me anyway, and everybody else, that he orchestrated that."

Fauci’s diary entries were released on Saturday by Senate Homeland Security Committee Chairman Rand Paul, R-Ky., detailing the doctor’s role during the COVID-19 crisis through conversations with President Donald Trump, governors, world leaders, media appearances and his personal observations as the pandemic unfolded in 2020.

"Well look, and I've looked through the emails, some of them have been online, I think it's disappointing to see him trying to suppress alternative opinions, and that clearly was evidence from the emails. I thought it was disappointing. The part of it that also disappointed me was how much he enjoyed the media associated with the event and his own appearances," Gotlieb said.

ABC, NBC, CBS, CNN AND MS NOW IGNORE FAUCI DIARY ENTRIES THAT REVEAL FIXATION ON FAME DURING COVID

"I think a lot of us went on to media out of a sense of obligation," he continued. "It was a hard time for all of us. I know it was a hard time for you. I think a lot of us felt an obligation to inform the public. And it wasn't particularly enjoyable. I mean, I got a lot of threats, others did as well, associated with that, and so to see those emails where he is evidencing some pleasure in the notoriety that he achieved, that's disappointing."

Kernen pushed back and said it was "outrageous."

"Does having a reputation totally in the toilet at 85 years, does that hold him to account for what he was responsible for?" Kernen asked.

Gottlieb said the Fauci he knew over the years was not the one he saw in the emails, and said the former NIH head was always careful and thoughtful.

Kernen specifically brought up Fauci's relationship with members of the liberal media. Fauci’s closest media ally appeared to have been CNN anchor Jake Tapper, who was mentioned 41 times in the diary.

FAUCI'S DIARY SHOWS HE FED QUESTIONS TO JOURNALISTS, BUILT FRIENDSHIPS WITH MEDIA FIGURES

"Did you figure out the obsession with mainstream media in defending him and Jake Tapper having multiple dinners and best friends? What did that come from? And I know people around here that would call Tony Fauci a hero," Kernen said.

Gottlieb said he couldn't dissect the relationship, but again said he was disappointed by the emails.

Fauci did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

According to the diary, Tapper texted Fauci to mock rival cable news hosts and other doctors. On one occasion, Tapper called to check on Fauci after an appearance on his show irked Trump supporters.

"Jake wanted to make sure the interview did not cause me any problems," Fauci wrote on April 13, 2020.

EXCLUSIVE: BIDEN PARDON WON'T SHIELD FAUCI IF HE LIES TO CONGRESS, COMER SAYS

In July 2020, Fauci gushed that he was forming a friendship with Tapper.

"Had dinner over Jake Tapper and Jen Tapper’s home in DC. Terrific couple. Friendship building," Fauci wrote, according to the diary.

Later that month, Fauci wrote that he "gave Jake some questions to ask" pediatrician Brett Giroir during an interview on CNN’s "State of the Union." But Tapper would later express frustration, waking Fauci up in the process.

"Tapper woke me up at 11:23 AM (I went to bed early) furius [sic] at POTUS for tweeting about the fact that Jake severly [sic] questioned Brett Giroir on SOTU CNN show today. Jake was really pissed at the craziness of it all," Fauci wrote.

The national stage wasn't kind to Jalen Carter at the start of the 2025 season when we saw him get kicked out of the regular-season opener for spitting at Dak Prescott, but the start of this season is getting off on much brighter note.

As in, a Brink's truck full of $100 notes.

PATRICK MAHOMES LEAPS PAST DAK PRESCOTT AS NFL'S HIGHEST-PAID QB WITH RECORD CHIEFS EXTENSION WORTH $504.75M

That's, shall we say, nothing to spit at.

Carter is now under contract with Philadelphia through 2031.

The No. 9 overall pick of the 2023 draft, Carter finished second in the Defensive Rookie of the Year voting behind Will Anderson Jr.

Carter was instrumental in helping the Eagles win Super Bowl LIX to cap the 2024 season. Last year he only played in 11 games until he required shoulder surgery in both shoulders.

World.title: ESPN's Dan Orlovsky weighs in on Florida coach Jon Sumrall's pedicure preferences, immediately gets roasted
World.content:
While last week's SEC Media Days saw plenty of coaches putting themselves in the spotlight with a litany of quotes, one coach from the Southeastern Conference rose above the rest.

Florida's Jon Sumrall made quite a name for himself in Tampa last week during his inaugural spin as a head coach in the SEC, creating a bit of a stink on social media with his comments regarding a reporter's cell phone going off.

Sumrall apparently wasn't done hogging the limelight, though this time it was his wife generating the headlines when she dropped the bombshell that one of the toughest coaches in the conference loves getting pedicures.

FLORIDA COACH BRINGS LAUGHS, NO FILTER AND LANE KIFFIN COMPARISON REBUTTAL TO FIRST SEC MEDIA DAYS

The internet once again reacted in kind, with fans and media members arguing both sides of the issue.

Some saw no problem with a man taking care of his feet - especially feet that used to play linebacker in the SEC - while others said the revelation that Sumrall gets his toes worked on pokes holes in his "tough guy act."

A few fans even suggested his wife was in the wrong for airing out his dirty laundry (and clean feet) and giving his rivals ammo to use against him.

One man who isn't necessarily a rival coach is ESPN analyst and former NFL quarterback Dan Orlovsky.

Orlovsky was asked about "Pedicuregate" on the show "Get Up" Tuesday morning, and the ex-Detroit Lion did not mince words.

"I have never gotten a pedicure, and I never will," said Orlovsky. "I am completely against pedicures for dudes."

ESPN PARTING WAYS WITH NFL ANALYST RYAN CLARK AHEAD OF NETWORK'S FIRST SUPER BOWL BROADCAST

Sumrall is pretty clearly a dude, so it sounds like Orlovsky is against the new Gators head coach getting a pedicure.

Orlovsky was roundly mocked by all of his co-hosts on "Get Up" during the segment, but that was nothing compared to what fans on X had in store for him.

One subset of fans - both Florida and otherwise - correctly pointed out that Orlovsky calling a guy out for getting pedicures while he wears makeup on the set of a TV show feels a tad bit hypocritical.

Another subset of fans took things on a bit more of a personal route, and brought up Orlovsky's very infamous trip out of the back of the end zone during the 2008 NFL season (a season in which the Lions notoriously completed an 0-16 campaign).

I also have to say, it is relieving that fans of teams other than the Florida Gators are hopping to Jon Sumrall's defense.

I thought I was going to have to defend this take as a massive Gator homer like that one scene in "Game of Thrones" where Jon Snow has to take on hundreds of soldiers all by himself in The Battle of the Bastards.

In all seriousness, I'm not a pedicure guy. I really don't like strangers touching me in general so that rules out massages, too.

But I am in no way going to shame a man for getting his feet taken care of.

Manicures, though? That's a different story.

I have to draw the line somewhere.

World.title: Leading economist warns of rise of 'Gen Z affordability socialism'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Artificial intelligence is fundamentally transforming the global economy at breakneck speed, but Diogo Costa argues that the real threat to prosperity isn't technological disruption; it's the return of bad economic ideas.

As the president of FEE (the Foundation for Economic Education), America's oldest free-market think tank, Costa is concerned that the affordability crisis is providing the perfect opportunity to tempt the next generation with the ideas of socialism, and argues that economic education is the antidote.

Recently, he sat down with Fox News Digital at Freedom Fest in Las Vegas for a discussion about the intellectual defense of free markets, the intersection of freedom and technology, and how his upbringing in Brazil brings a unique perspective to today's economic policy debates.

GEN Z IS WORKING HARD, BUT THE ECONOMY IS PUTTING THE AMERICAN DREAM OUT OF REACH FOR MANY

"The biggest challenge today is the different ways that ‘anti-economics’ keeps reappearing. And this time, it's reappearing through a new kind of socialism. So through the 20th century, we had different flavors of socialism, labor union socialism, environmental socialism, anti-globalization socialism. Now we see this cost-of-living socialism, affordability crisis socialism."

While young people are aware that they are better off in a market economy, Costa argues, they still want heavy-handed intervention if they perceive it benefits them.

"Young people, they want to live in a market economy. They don't want to move to Venezuela or Cuba, but they want price controls in everything. They want to freeze the rent, they want free rides in buses, they want to make sure that groceries are either run by the government or price controlled somehow. And this is not just a phenomenon in New York City or California. This is something that's happening globally.

"And this is the new kind of ‘anti-economics.’ So, Leonard Read [founder of FEE] understood that economics is always one generation away from turning prosperity into poverty. The good ideas need to keep being recycled, they need to be reframed, and this is a challenge that we have right now, the rise of this Gen Z affordability socialism."

He further argues that while the technology produced by vibrant market economies has incredible potential, the ideological foundation of capitalism is under attack like never before:

"We're in a golden age for technology, not necessarily for the ideas behind it…the ideas behind the market economy are not as well understood. And when you talk about AI, people are thinking all the jobs are going to be gone. Humanity is on the verge of extinction.

"So there is a lot of pessimism at the same time that you have these wonderful technologies. So the ideas that help us explain and help us work with technology are what's missing."

Costa's studies of the Austrian school of economics lead to separating the economic power of the free-market from its cultural power:

"Joseph Schumpeter, the Austrian economist, said that capitalism would be economically powerful and at the same time culturally weak because you have companies that will be doing amazing things, but capitalism makes things more abstract…and at some point people stop seeing exactly how they are part of this amazing complexity.

DEMOCRATS LURE ‘POLITICALLY HOMELESS’ GEN Z TOWARD SOCIALISM — A COUNTERATTACK IS TAKING SHAPE

"That's why with FEE we sometimes go back to a pencil. We just ask people ‘do you understand how a pencil is made?’ Because if you see the complexity, the network, the amazing, marvelous market system around... Just building a single pencil, you start to understand how you are part of the complexity and you benefit from it."

Costa's own experience growing up in Brazil during the economically chaotic 1990s was pivotal in shaping his outlook on policy and the need for economic education.

"I grew up in a country that had hyperinflation. When I was 10 years old, 11 years old, yearly inflation was above 1000%, 1200%, 1300%. That meant the prices were changing literally every day. And it's hard to understand how if you live in a society that is that economically chaotic all your life is designed around those problems.

"So as a child, when I was going to the grocery store because my mom gave me a $1,000 bill to buy a bag of chips, I had to think, ‘Oh, I need to get there before the price tagger starts changing the prices’."

"My parents had to turn a bedroom in our house into a pantry because when they got their paychecks the first thing they did was go to the grocery store and buy everything you can…So your life starts to be designed around these big issues. And this is something that some people take for granted."

But it was not only hyperinflation that opened Costa's eyes about economic education; he also first hand the effects of a fundamentally protectionist economic system:

"It's the same thing with protectionism…as a young boy in the early 90s, I wanted video games. Brazil had strict protectionism. So I could buy these dupe video games, but I couldn't get the real deal. And this was something that people now take for granted, but this was how the Brazilian economy was being shaped.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"And Milton Friedman has this saying that he thinks that we never actually learn economics as humanity, we learn as individuals, we learn maybe as generations, but now that we don't live under hyperinflation people forget what that's like, now that we don't live under hyperprotectionism people forget what it's like. So it's very easy to drift towards inflation, to drift towards protectionism, to drift towards anti-economics and economics needs to be re-taught every generation."

World.title: Netanyahu joins Trump for high-stakes meeting at the White House
World.content:
This month, the U.S. carried out strikes for nearly two straight weeks, while Iran struck ships and American targets in the region. The sit-down will be their first face-to-face meeting since Axios reported last month that Trump had called Netanyahu “f---ing crazy” during a heated phone call. Trump confirmed the report was accurate in an interview with the New York Post. “I was a little bit perturbed at his constantly fighting with Lebanon,” Trump said.

Asked about the confrontation, Netanyahu said he and Trump sometimes have “tactical disagreements.” “We always find a way to work them out, and we do so as great friends,” he said.

Trump has declined to say whether he supports Netanyahu for re-election. Earlier this month, he dodged a question, saying that Netanyahu has been “a great wartime president.”

“He’s been a great wartime prime minister,” Trump said this month. “I don’t know anything about his politics, I’m not sure. I would think he should be popular, because he did a very good job.”

The meeting also comes amid scrutiny from lawmakers over the administration’s handling of the war since the U.S. and Israel launched it in late February. Four U.S. soldiers were killed in recent days, bringing the total number of American troops killed during the war to 18.

NBC News has also previously reported that U.S. weapons stockpiles are diminishing and that U.S. military commanders are allowing some Iranian missiles and drones to pass U.S. defenses to preserve the weapons supply. At the same time, the Defense Department is requesting that Congress approve an additional $67 billion in supplemental funding to expand weapons production and speed up delivery.

Mike Waltz, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, argued in an interview on “Meet the Press” that the U.S. “has everything that it needs to conduct this campaign as effectively as it needs to be.”

Asked whether Trump had decided against escalating attacks on Iran, Waltz said that the president was giving talks between the two nations “some space” but that all options remained on the table.

In an interview Sunday on Fox News’ “Sunday Morning Futures,” Netanyahu said that the U.S. and Israeli intelligence services “are working so close together that it’s not that I’m going to present new information, but I think it’s a good thing to have the opportunity to sit with our good friend President Trump and to hear what he has in mind, because I think in many ways it’s his decision.”

“But let me say one thing, and I think that I should say it very, very clearly: If Iran attacks Israel, either directly or through proxies, either with ballistic missiles or UAVs or killer drones, it will make a terrible mistake, because our response, Israel’s response, will be very, very forceful,” Netanyahu said.

World.title: Apalachee High School shooter Colt Gray sentenced to life without parole
World.content:
WINDER, Ga. — The teenager who idolized mass murderers and used the assault-style rifle he got for Christmas to kill two students and two teachers at his Georgia high school will spend the rest of his life in prison.

Colt Gray, 16, was sentenced Tuesday to life without parole for the Sept. 4, 2024, shooting at Apalachee High School that also left another teacher and eight more students wounded, seven of them hit by gunfire.

Christian Angulo; Mason Schermerhorn; Cristina Irimie; Richard Aspinwall. GoFundMe; Instagram; Apalachee High School

Barrow County Superior Court Judge Nicholas Primm handed down the sentence days after Gray pleaded guilty to all 55 counts against him, including murder.

“You do not seem to be tormented by what you did, you seem to relish following in the footsteps of the murderers you idolize,” Primm told Gray. “You aren’t racked with guilt. You’re proud of yourself.”

Primm added, “There’s no joy here.”

“It’s only a measure of closure,” the judge said. “The slain will not return to life. The injured will not forget their wounds, and a 16-year-old, 16-year-old boy, will live and die in prison.”

Gasps could be heard in the courtroom when the judge handed down the sentence. Before he was led out in handcuffs, Gray glanced quickly up toward the gallery where his grandmother, Debbie Polhamus, had been sitting.

Gray, who was 14 at the time of the shooting, was charged as an adult. His trial had been scheduled to start in mid-October.

But Gray entered the plea without having reached a deal with prosecutors. That left it to the judge to decide whether Gray should be eligible for parole, after hearing victim statements and each side’s summary of a case that has loomed large over the Atlanta suburb of Winder.

Gray declined to address the court at his sentencing hearing Tuesday.

Prosecutors said Gray was obsessed with mass killers and played jailhouse phone conversations with his mother in which he appeared to revel in the attention he received for staging a massacre at the school.

“Four lives were stolen, two of whom were only just beginning,” Primm said. “And it wasn’t done out of fear or anger. You weren’t being bullied at Apalachee. It wasn’t done out of hatred — you didn’t even know anybody at that school. It was done for the infamy of it.”

Teachers Richard “Ricky” Aspinwall, 39, and Cristina Irimie, 53, and students Mason Schermerhorn and Christian Angulo, both 14, died in the shooting.

Their loved ones urged the judge to impose the maximum sentence in victim impact statements delivered in court Friday.

“It is a life sentence of grief and trauma for those left behind,” Aspinwall’s wife, Shayna, told the court. She said their daughters were 2 and 5 when their father was killed and their lives will be “forever marked by his absence.”

Breanna Schermerhorn, whose son Mason was killed, said that while Gray may have been failed by the adults in his life, it was his decision to commit mass murder.

“Those decisions were his and his alone,” she said.

The judge agreed. And he imposed on Gray the same sentence that another judge imposed on another mass murderer the 16-year-old revered — Nikolas Cruz, who was sentenced to life without parole four years ago for the 2018 shooting at a Florida high school that left 14 students and three staff members dead.

“Your plan was not hastily hatched,” Primm said. “It was a slow boil, simmering one in a year’s time. You savored the thought of it. You visualized it, and you fantasized about it.”

“The thought of mimicking these other mass murderers is what brought you joy,” the judge said.

Earlier in the sentencing hearing, a psychologist hired by the defense described the teenager as a “lonely, dysfunctional kid” who had a “chaotic” childhood.

“I thought he was kind of an odd kid,” Kevin Richards said at the sentencing hearing Monday.

His parents abused drugs, had financial problems and fought a lot, Richards said. The family moved frequently and there were long stretches when Gray wasn’t enrolled in school, he said.

So Gray immersed himself online with the “true crime” community and became obsessed with school shootings, Richards said.

Previously, investigators said they found in Colt’s bedroom what they described as a shrine to Cruz.

Gray, investigators said, also became obsessed with the gunmen responsible for the 1999 mass shooting in Colorado at Columbine High School, and the 2012 killings of mostly children at Sandy Hook Elementary School in Connecticut.

Gray was “kind of obsessed” with them, Richards said.

Ashley Gilleland, an investigator with the Barrow County District Attorney’s Office, testified Tuesday that Gray had more than 2,000 photos of Cruz saved on his phone and more photos of Cruz printed and posted on his bedroom wall.

But, Gilleland said, Gray had hoped “to gain some sort of fame or notoriety from” attacking his classmates at school.

To further buttress that argument, the state played recordings of jail calls between Gray and his mother, Marcee Gray, from October and November 2024 during which Gray sounded thrilled to be compared to Cruz and other mass killers.

“I’m in the big leagues, bro,” he said in one call.

Gray’s grandmother testified that her grandson spent long stretches of time with her because his parents were so unstable.

“Well, they always had issues,” Polhamus said. “They were doing a lot of drinking at that time, and then they got way behind on their bills.”

Polhamus said Gray’s dad, Colin Gray, kept dozens of guns in the house and not all of them were locked up. She said he bought Gray the gun he used to attack his classmates in order to bond with his son.

“He really wanted to find something that they could do together,” she said.

Colin Gray was convicted by a jury in March on charges including second-degree murder and involuntary manslaughter for giving his son what turned out to be a multiple murder weapon.

Just before 10 a.m. on the day of the shooting, Gray told his second-period teacher that he needed to see a crisis counselor but instead went to a bathroom to get ready to attack the school, police said.

When he was unable to re-enter his classroom, Gray marched down the hall to another classroom and opened fire and also shot at other people in the hallway, police said.

Gray surrendered to law enforcement officers. In the courtroom, prosecutors played a recording of his interview with investigators during which he sobbed hysterically and repeatedly apologized, calling what he did “horrible” and “the worst nightmare for everyone involved.”

The teenager also described having uncontrollable urges and said he was supposed to see a doctor. “I was so close to getting the help I need and the medication I need,” he told investigators.

But Gray, prosecutors said, had methodically planned the school shooting, and investigators described finding a notebook in which the teen detailed a step-by-step plan on how he would get himself ready in the bathroom.

It also came out in the pretrial investigation that sheriff’s deputies had interviewed Colt and Colin Gray in May 2023 about an online threat linked to the son. Colt Gray denied making the threat.

During Colin Gray’s trial, an investigator testified that he had sought help for his son from a counseling service weeks before the school shooting but failed to follow through.

Marcee Gray, who was separated from Colin Gray, told investigators she had urged her husband weeks before the shooting to secure his guns and restrict their son’s access to them.

Over time, Colin Gray bought the teenager ammunition, a gunsight and other shooting accessories, court records show.

Dan Gallo reported from Winder, Georgia, and Corky Siemaszko reported from New York.

World.title: How Ken Martin is holding on as DNC chair — for now: From the Politics Desk
World.content:
Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.

In today’s edition, Natasha Korecki digs into Ken Martin’s woes at the Democratic National Committee. Plus, Scott Wong and Frank Thorp V file a report from Sen. Lindsey Graham’s funeral in Washington.

Sign up to receive this newsletter in your inbox every weekday here.

— Adam Wollner

How Ken Martin is holding on as DNC chair — for now

Analysis by Natasha Korecki

Calls for Ken Martin to be replaced as Democratic National Committee chair are intensifying in certain corners of the party — except from the people who have the final say.

Since Martin won the chairmanship a year ago, he’s been enmeshed in a new firestorm seemingly every few months, from lagging fundraising to flip-flopping on the party’s autopsy of the 2024 election.

Over the weekend, the latest raft of negative news accounts surfaced, including a report from The New York Times that Martin threw a phone at an aide’s desk.

The resulting cycle was predictable: the consultant class erupted into a tizzy. They called for his resignation and even fought over who should replace him. This week, veteran Democratic strategist James Carville went as far as to suggest that David Hogg — the ousted DNC vice chair whom Carville last year labeled a “contemptible little twerp” — take the reins of the national party committee.

But as was the case in past episodes, that’s as far as it has gone. Martin is again digging in, his allies are circling the wagons and powerful Democrats are either standing by his side or staying out of it. On Sunday, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said Martin “has my full support.” Potential 2028 presidential candidates could also apply pressure, but none has called for his ouster.

That leaves the DNC members themselves holding the most consequential power over Martin’s future. It would take a majority of DNC members to remove a national chair, according to committee rules. But even as they prepare to convene in Austin next month, some of Martin’s biggest detractors tell us there’s no groundswell to remove him — though some acknowledge they’re exploring their options, including a potential no-confidence vote.

Michael Ceraso, a Democratic strategist who works with numerous DNC members and state party chairs, said he’s not seeing immediate evidence of a call for change from within.

“Based on my conversations that I had with chairs and DNC leaders, there’s no indication whatsoever that there is some mass mobilization to oust Ken,” Ceraso said.

But that may not hold. For party leaders, there’s little incentive to shake things up now, with the midterm elections just a few months away. Post-November may be a different story.

“All of that happens after the midterms,” said one DNC official who wasn’t authorized to speak on the record. While that person was rooting for Martin to “pull it together,” they added, “I wouldn’t be shocked if it were an end-of-the-year thing. Unless something truly horrific comes out, I don’t think a change happens before the midterms.”

Washington says goodbye to Sen. Lindsey Graham, a ‘true American original’

By Scott Wong and Frank Thorp V

President Donald Trump, congressional colleagues and world leaders said their final goodbyes to Sen. Lindsey Graham, the influential and colorful foreign policy hawk whose sudden death this month at age 71 stunned Washington and reverberated in capitals around the globe.

Eulogizing Graham at his funeral service at the Washington National Cathedral, Trump called him “a respected statesman, a giant of the United States Senate, and a true American original who left us much too soon.”

“Lindsey rose from a small town in rural South Carolina, a place he loved so much, to become a constant fixture of American politics at the highest level, and a force to be reckoned with all over the world,” Trump told those gathered. “For more than 30 years, nothing of consequence happened in this capital without Lindsey Graham knowing about it. Nothing of significance happened anywhere in the world without Lindsey Graham having a view on it, and no bill became law in the most exceptional republic in human history without Lindsey Graham having a say in it.”

Graham had been a vocal critic of Trump’s when the two men ran against each other in the 2016 presidential race. But Graham became one of the president’s closest and most trusted allies on Capitol Hill and a frequent golf partner.

Senate colleagues, past and present, Cabinet members and Graham’s family and staffers packed the Capitol rotunda. Among those paying tribute were former Sens. Bob Corker and Lamar Alexander, both Tennessee Republicans; Rob Portman, R-Ohio; Richard Burr, R-N.C.; Jeff Flake, R-Ariz.; Pat Toomey, R-Pa.; and Kelly Ayotte, now New Hampshire’s GOP governor.

“It’s such a loss in terms of his voice on foreign policy and America’s role in the world,” Ayotte, who traveled regularly with Graham on Senate trips around the world, told NBC News, adding: “He loved life, he had so much fun, and no one could make you laugh more than Lindsey Graham.”

World.title: Americans face higher back-to-school costs. Here's what's pricier.
World.content:
As back-to-school season approaches, families will face higher prices for supplies and other costs for the upcoming academic year, a new analysis found.

The cost of a typical basket of school items, including notebooks, lunch boxes and index cards, is up nearly 8% this year compared to 2025, according to research from The Century Foundation, a progressive think tank, and Groundwork Collaborative, a progressive advocacy group. Americans will also pay 11% more for a typical school lunch, the groups found.

Families will spend roughly $4,000 per student on school supplies and lunches this year, including about $175 on school items and $3,800 on packed lunches, according to the analysis.

"It's the second-biggest shopping event of the year after Christmas, and families are going to be facing a lot of pain this school year," Lindsay Owens, executive director of Groundwork Collaborative, told CBS News.

"Higher gas prices have filtered through to food and clothing, and tariffs are hitting these items heavily, too, because most school supplies are not made in the U.S. — they're imported, " she added.

Inflation across the U.S. slowed in June, easing to an annual rate of 3.5%, from 4.2% in May, as fuel costs fell. Yet gas prices have flared in July amid renewed conflict in the Middle East.

Among the products that are costlier this year, according to The Century Foundation and Groundwork:

School supplies

Lunch box: $18.91 (up 27% from 2025)

One-subject notebook: $4.92 (up 23%)

Index cards: $3.86 (up 22%)

Glue sticks: $7.68 (up 7.6%)

Lunch box staples

Blueberries: $4.89 (up 48% from 2025)

Sandwich bread: $4.36 (up 22%)

Apple juice: $4.14 (up 20%)

Animal crackers: $6.49 (up 15.7%)

What's driving up costs?

Steeper U.S. tariffs on a range of imports have driven up the price of binders, pencils and other school supplies, the groups' research shows. Many school essentials, such as pens, markers, notebooks and glue, are manufactured overseas, making them subject to higher tariffs.

For example, Newell Brands, the maker of Sharpie pens, Elmer's glue and other classroom products, said in an earnings release earlier this year that it would hike prices to offset sharply higher tariff costs.

Matteo Anversa, the chief financial officer of Logitech, which makes electronics like headsets and keyboards, in May also cited stepped-up tariffs for a "sizable" increase in its U.S. prices.

Other school-supply companies also blame higher energy costs due to the Iran war for having to raise their prices. Acco Brands, the parent company of notebook and binder brands Mead, Five Star and Trapper Keeper, said in a May earnings call that higher oil prices stemming from the conflict have driven up the company's costs and led to price hikes for consumers.

A recent survey of more than 1,000 parents by Credit Karma found that 45% expect to take on debt to cover back-to-school costs. Half of families plan to cut back on household expenses to cover those costs, according to Deloitte.

"Parents do what they can to try to get their kids to school with the essentials, so it's not surprising folks are cutting back to make sure their kids have what they need," Groundwork's Owens said.

World.title: Kenya investigates deaths of 15 elephants in Amboseli National Park
World.content:
The deaths of 15 elephants over the past month in Kenya's Amboseli National Park have sparked an investigation, wildlife officials said Tuesday.

The Kenya Wildlife Service said 10 of the pachyderms showed signs of partial paralysis before dying within two days, while the remaining five were found dead, with their carcasses partially consumed by scavengers.

Most of those affected were female elephants and their calves, with only one male among the dead. The deaths happened in the Kimana Sanctuary and Kuku Ranch areas surrounding the park, the authority said.

Kenya has previously recorded incidents of elephants being poisoned as a result of poaching and human-wildlife conflict. But officials say it's the first time in decades the region has recorded elephant deaths on this scale, according to CBS News' partner network BBC News.

KWS said there was currently no evidence pointing to a single cause of death, BBC News reported.

Preliminary tests on samples collected from the elephants by a laboratory at the University of Nairobi detected a "potential toxic substance," while separate analyses by Kenya's Government Chemist were negative for the toxins tested. KWS said further tests are underway.

"Environmental investigations are also being undertaken, including the analysis of water sources and other potential environmental contaminants within the affected areas, to establish whether the elephants were exposed to a common source," KWS said in a statement.

Officials sought to reassure the public, saying there was no evidence the condition could be transmitted to humans.

The Amboseli National Park is located near the Tanzania border at the northwestern foot of Mount Kilimanjaro. There were more than 2,000 elephants in the Amboseli ecosystem as of 2025, according to BBC News.

World.title: "60 Minutes" announces new correspondents and contributors
World.content:
Ross Douthat, Sebastian Junger, Gianna Toboni and Trevor Phillips will all join "60 Minutes" as correspondents or contributors, the show's executive producer Nick Bilton announced Tuesday.

They join veteran correspondents Lesley Stahl, Bill Whitaker and Jon Wertheim. Norah O'Donnell, who had been a contributing correspondent, will be doing even more for the broadcast, Bilton said.

"Norah is a powerhouse," Bilton wrote in his announcement. "You've seen her all over the network. She's launched a new podcast. And you'll see much more of her in our halls because Norah will be a correspondent on 60 Minutes."

Douthat, well known as a New York Times Opinion columnist, joins the show as a correspondent.

"Ross is one of the preeminent public intellectuals in America today, a thinker of uncommon rigor and a journalist of deep empathy," Bilton said. He described Douthat's interviews with leading figures including Vice President JD Vance, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, Supreme Court Justice Amy Coney Barrett, political commentator Hasan Piker and former Senator Ben Sasse, among others, as "expansive and probing and news making."

Junger, author of "The Perfect Storm" and an award-winning documentary filmmaker, will join "60 Minutes" as a contributor.

"We all remember The Perfect Storm," Bilton said. "It landed with an electric charge in the world of reported nonfiction, defining an intense and intimate form of storytelling and establishing Sebastian as a generational talent. It was a bestseller, as were his next six books. Sebastian carried that intensity and that ethos of deep reporting to his work as a documentarian, broadcast journalist and war correspondent."

Toboni will also join "60 Minutes" as a contributor. She previously worked with VICE News and CNN.

"Gianna is a journalist with extraordinary range," Bilton wrote in the announcement. "She's interviewed members of ISIS and investigated cartel violence in Mexico. She's also been recognized for her compassionate and incisive reporting on complex social and cultural issues, including America's mass shootings and the death penalty, about which she wrote an investigative book, The Volunteer: The Failure of the Death Penalty in America and One Inmate's Quest to Die with Dignity."

Phillips, until recently a Sky News presenter, was previously announced as CBS News' new senior global affairs correspondent. He'll also contribute to "60 Minutes."

"Trevor is one of the most respected and trusted voices in the United Kingdom for his ability to ask the toughest questions and hold anyone in power to account," Bilton said. "He will bring that same passion for the pursuit of the truth to 60 Minutes."

World.title: Trump meets with Zelenskyy and Netanyahu amid wars in Iran, Ukraine
World.content:
Washington — President Trump met with both Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu separately at the White House Tuesday amid the war with Iran and Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

Neither meeting was open to reporters. Zelenskyy and Netanyahu are attending the funeral of Sen. Lindsey Graham, a staunch supporter of both Ukraine and Israel. Graham had just returned from a trip to Ukraine before his sudden death at 71. His last public words were in Kyiv.

Zelenskyy said his meeting with Mr. Trump was "good" and that they discussed the licenses for the production of Patriot missile interceptors, critical in Ukraine's efforts to combat Moscow. Mr. Trump and Zelenskyy most recently met earlier this month on the sidelines of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization in Turkey, where Mr. Trump announced the U.S. would allow Ukraine to build its own Patriot missiles.

"A good meeting with President Trump at the Oval Office," Zelenskyy wrote on X. "Thank you for everything we do together to protect the lives of Ukrainians and advance peace. First and foremost, I offered President Trump our condolences on the passing of Lindsey Graham. He was a true friend of Ukraine.

"The president and I discussed licenses for Patriot interceptor production and several other ideas that could help. We also spoke about diplomacy – it's important that the diplomatic process be reinvigorated. Our teams will arrange the details of their further communication. I am grateful to the United States for its firm support."

Immediately following the Zelenskyy meeting, Mr. Trump met with Netanyahu behind closed doors. Neither the White House nor the Israelis have yet released a readout of that meeting. It was their first known face-to-face meeting since the U.S. and Israel launched the war with Iran.

ראש הממשלה בנימין נתניהו נפגש כעת עם נשיא ארה״ב דונלד טראמפ בבית הלבן. pic.twitter.com/9UWM8rsn97 — ראש ממשלת ישראל (@IsraeliPM_heb) July 28, 2026

Mr. Trump, who has typically been one of Netanyahu's staunchest supporters, has put distance between himself and the Israeli prime minister of late. Although he's called Netanyahu a good wartime president, Mr. Trump hasn't said whether Netanyahu should continue as prime minister in the future. Netanyahu, Mr. Trump has said, needs to apply a "softer touch" and "be more responsible with respect to Lebanon."

In an interview with Fox News Tuesday morning, Mr. Trump pushed back when he was asked about reports that Netanyahu planned to discuss information related to Pickaxe Mountain in Iran, an underground nuclear site. Mr. Trump said he doesn't need someone else to tell him what's happening there.

"I don't need Bibi to tell me that," Mr. Trump responded, adding that Netanyahu is "telling me that because he wants me to stay involved."

World.title: People trapped and injured after powerful earthquake strikes Japan
World.content:
Tokyo — A major earthquake collapsed buildings and sparked fires in Japan's southwest, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said Tuesday, with authorities in the hard-hit Kumamoto region saying at least nine people remained missing in a heavily damaged shopping mall.

Public broadcaster NHK said at least 50 people were taken to hospitals and local emergency services, and CBS News' Japanese partner network TBS cited the regional Kumamoto government as saying five people had been rescued from the Aeon Mall in Kashima city but nine remained unaccounted for. Police in the city earlier told TBS that there were "a lot of deaths" in the mall, but that it would "take time to confirm the exact number."

There were 11 people trapped inside the Nippon Paper Industries Yatsushiro Plant in Kumamoto prefecture after a chimney collapsed during the quake, though two had been rescued, TBS reported. The two people were found without vital signs, according to NHK.

Video aired by NHK showed several blazes, damaged bridges, a derailed cargo train and cracked roads after the temblor struck at the far southern end of Japan's main Kyushu island. NHK said at least 12 houses had collapsed, and the national Kyodo news agency said one person was killed in a damaged home.

An aerial view shows damage to the Aeon Mall in Kashima City, after an earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 7.1 struck Japan's southern Kumamoto prefecture, July 28, 2026. Kyodo/REUTERS

The quake at 4:27 p.m. (2:27 a.m. Eastern) had a magnitude of 7.1, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency, but reached the highest possible level of 7 on Japan's Shindo scale of shaking. The U.S. Geological Survey measured the quake — one of hundreds that strike Japan every year — at 6.8. The vast majority cause little damage.

"We are still assessing the extent of injuries and property damage, but I have been informed that there have already been several injuries," Takaichi said. "Power outages and fires are happening in some areas, and roads and bridges have been damaged and buildings collapsed."

Workers conduct search and rescue operations at Aeon Mall, which was seriously damaged by an earthquake on July 28, 2026, in Kashima, in Japan's southern Kumamoto prefecture. Kyodo/REUTERS

In "Kashima town, a shopping complex's second floor collapsed, leaving many people trapped inside," the fire department said in a statement.

Police said earlier they had received reports of what sounded like an explosion at the Aeon Mall, but they did not publicly confirm the TBS report of multiple fatalities at the damaged retail outlet in Kashima.

The Japan Meteorological Agency initially issued an alert for a possible tsunami of up to three feet, but withdrew the warning after a couple hours.

An aerial view shows fire crews spraying water into a building on fire in Kumamoto, Japan, after a powerful earthquake struck the area on July 28, 2026. Reuters/Nippon TV

No immediate abnormalities were recorded at nuclear power plants, the Nuclear Regulation Authority said.

About 45,000 households and facilities have no power in the Kumamoto region, according to local utility Kyushu Electric Power.

The firm added that three nuclear reactors operating in the region at the time were functioning normally.

The exterior wall of a shop is seen collapsed following a strong earthquake, in Kumamoto City, Japan, July 28, 2026. JIJI Press/AFP/Getty

A local NHK staffer wearing a helmet reported live on air that the shaking was continuing around half an hour after the quake, with the newsroom rocking so violently that it was difficult to remain standing.

"Shaking is continuing as I speak. Including myself, there may be some people who feel their hearts racing," the staffer said.

"When the quake struck, the shaking was so big that I could not stand up. Please be aware of possibility that shaking might continue after this."

A map shows the epicenter of a major earthquake that hit southwest Japan's Kumamoto region on July 28, 2026. Mehmet Yaren Bozgun/Anadolu/Getty

Kumamoto was hit by two devastating earthquakes in 2016 — one of magnitude 6.5, followed two days later by one of magnitude 7.3 — which killed 273 people and injured more than 2,800.

A quake with a magnitude of 7.2 hit northern Japan on June 25 but caused no deaths or major damage.

Japan is one of the world's most seismically active countries, sitting on top of four major tectonic plates along the western edge of the Pacific "Ring of Fire."

The archipelago, home to around 125 million people, typically experiences hundreds of jolts every year and accounts for about 18% of the world's earthquakes. The vast majority are mild, although the damage they cause varies according to their location and the depth below the Earth's surface at which they strike.

Japan's positioning on the "Ring of Fire" between the Philippine and Pacific plates leads to many earthquakes. CBS News

Japan is haunted by the memory of a massive 9.0-magnitude undersea quake in 2011, which triggered a tsunami that killed or left missing around 18,500 people and wrecked the Fukushima nuclear plant.

A tremor measuring 7.7 hit the country's north on April 20 this year, injuring at least 10 people and shaking large buildings in Tokyo.

That prompted authorities to issue a special advisory warning of an increased risk of earthquakes of magnitude 8.0 or stronger.

The advisory was lifted after a week.

World.title: Keiko Fujimori is inaugurated as Peru's president following a narrow election victory
World.content:
Keiko Fujimori is inaugurated as Peru's president following a narrow election victory

toggle caption Martin Mejia/AP

LIMA, Peru — Conservative leader Keiko Fujimori was sworn in as Peru's president on Tuesday after winning the June presidential runoff by a margin of fewer than 50,000 votes, a victory that confirmed a regional shift in South America toward the conservative wing.

With the ceremony, Fujimori, a four-time presidential candidate and leader of Peru's largest political party, officially takes office as the country's ninth president in a decade. The 51-year-old is hoping to stabilize Peru's turbulent politics, reduce crime and boost economic growth.

Sponsor Message

Over the past decade, only three of Peru's presidents have been elected by popular vote. The rest have come into office after their predecessors resigned or were removed by congress amid corruption scandals.

Fujimori's Popular Force party and its main ally, Popular Renovation, will hold half the senate seats once the new legislature is installed, making it harder for opposing legislators to attempt to remove her as president.

An incoming president with a political past and promises for the future

Fujimori centered her campaign around promises to improve security in a nation where extortion rackets have become a significant problem. She has also promised to develop infrastructure by making it easier for government agencies to form partnerships with private investors.

She is the daughter of former President Alberto Fujimori, who led the country in the 1990s and stabilized its economy while defeating terror groups, but was later imprisoned for human rights abuses committed under his rule by the Peruvian military as his government took an authoritarian turn. He was pardoned in December 2023 and died in September the following year.

During her campaign, Keiko Fujimori pledged to fight crime with an "iron fist," implementing some policies adopted by Salvadorean President Nayib Bukele, and also build a megaprison modeled after the notorious Cecot penitentiary in El Salvador.

Sponsor Message

To guarantee judges their safety, she has said she will implement reforms to enable them to hide their identities as they oversee criminal trials.

She also said on Tuesday she would reorganize social services to fight malnutrition in rural communities and announced a 15% increase in the nation's minimum wage.

Fujimori said that the nation's military will "temporarily" lead security operations in crime afflicted areas. And said she will focus on preparing the South American nation for the latest onset of El Niño, a weather pattern that warms ocean temperatures and often leads to flooding along Peru's coast.

"My goal is not only to administer the state" Fujimori said. "My main objective is to narrow the enormous social deficit that affects millions of Peruvians."

Opposition leaders remember those killed in protests

Opposition leaders have asked Fujimori's incoming government to reverse a series of laws approved by Peru's last legislature, which critics say weaken efforts to fight organized crime.

The laws eliminate preventive arrests and stop prosecutors from processing political parties involved in corruption under the same statutes as criminal groups. The laws also make it harder for police to confiscate the goods of criminal groups.

Opposition leaders are also asking the incoming government to create a commission to investigate the deaths of 50 civilians during anti-government protests in late 2022 and early 2023 following the removal of former President Pedro Castillo.

During Fujimori's swearing-ceremony, some opposition lawmakers protested outside the parliament, holding photos of people killed during the protests. Relatives of the dead have said they do not recognize Fujimori as president and that they are protesting her inauguration.

Fujimori will lead a deeply polarized country

Fujimori was widely backed by voters in Peru's capital and along the Pacific coast, but voters in the highlands, where there is a larger Indigenous population, overwhelmingly supported left-wing candidate Roberto Sanchez, an ally of Castillo.

Sponsor Message

Sanchez challenged the election results, arguing there were irregularities in how votes were counted at Peruvian consulates abroad, but electoral authorities dismissed his complaints.

Despite the political friction, Peru continues to be one of the most stable economies in Latin America. Its central bank has long kept the benchmark interest rate below 5%, and the government is known for a conservative approach toward public spending.

But critics point out a growing gap in living standards between coastal areas and communities in the Andean highlands.

Fujimori's June election victory, along with those of Abelardo de la Espriella in Colombia and José Antonio Kast in Chile, underscored South America's shift toward the conservative wing, a stark contrast from the panorama of a few decades ago when left-wing leaders such as Hugo Chávez in Venezuela or the current Brazilian president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva emerged.

Conservatives have won seven major presidential elections in Latin American in the past few years, most of the them since the January 2025 inauguration of U.S. President Donald Trump, in a winning streak propelled by concerns over crime, immigration and slow economic growth

World.title: Ukraine negotiator: 'We have the upper hand'
World.content:
Ukraine negotiator: 'We have the upper hand'

toggle caption Paula Bronstein for NPR

KYIV — When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022, Sergiy Kyslytsya was in New York serving as Ukraine's ambassador to the United Nations.

That day, Kyslytsya leaned into his microphone at the U.N. and looked straight at his Russian counterpart Vasily Nebenzya. Kyslytsya did not hold back.

"There is no purgatory for war criminals," he said. "They go straight to hell, ambassador."

Russia's invasion severed diplomatic relations between Kyiv and Moscow. That made Kyslytsya's posting at the U.N. a particularly unique one: the only place where a Ukrainian diplomat engaged directly with his Russian counterpart.

Sponsor Message

"My fellow ambassadors in all capitals around the world would not talk to them," Kyslytsya says. "So by the time I was part of our negotiating team (for peace talks), I already knew how to control my feelings and attitude."

toggle caption Spencer Platt/Getty Images

Official negotiations mediated by the U.S. have stalled since early this year as the Trump administration has focused on the U.S. war on Iran. Yet Ukraine continues to talk with American and, occasionally, Russian envoys, says Kyslytsya, who has been a key member of Ukraine's negotiations team since 2025.

"Dialogue," he says, "is active and ongoing."

NPR spoke to Kyslytsya, who also serves as the first deputy head of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's office, inside the well-guarded presidential compound in Kyiv. His office is decorated with wartime artwork and shelves of history and current-affairs books, including one by Jared Kushner. Standing guard is DeZi, Kyslytsya's 13-year-old Jack Russell terrier.

In a wide-ranging conversation, Kyslytsa reaffirmed Kyiv's current position on stopping the war: freeze the fighting along the current frontline.

"Of course, that does not entail illegal or de facto recognition of the territories occupied by the Russians as Russian territories," he says.

The Kremlin, he says, continues to make unrealistic demands. He points to the "3+2" proposal, also known as the "Anchorage formula," which Russian officials have described as a U.S.-backed diplomatic framework that emerged from an August 2025 summit in Alaska between President Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Sponsor Message

Under this proposal, Russia is seeking recognition of its claims over five Ukrainian regions—three that it fully occupies and two that it partially occupies. U.S Secretary of State Marco Rubio said this proposal had failed because Ukraine rejected it, and that he wants a deal acceptable to both sides.

"The Russians are obsessed, and Putin is obsessed with taking full control of the Donetsk region, the 15 to 20 percent that's not occupied," he says. "And (the Russians) have been feeding the Americans with the line that in two or three months, they will take full control."

toggle caption Marharyta Fal/Frontliner/Getty Images

Even when it's clear, he says, that this is no longer solely a war of infantry and artillery.

"It is a war of the 21st century," he says. "And we have the upper hand."

Ukraine's long-range drones are repeatedly hitting Russian oil and gas facilities, causing fuel shortages, and weakening the Kremlin's ability to wage war. Kyslytsya argues the Russian army is no longer making meaningful advances on the battlefield.

"And that has become very apparent not only to Ukrainians but also to our partners and to the United States," he says.

President Trump praised Ukrainian troops at the NATO summit in Ankara last month.

In June, Zelenskyy wrote a pointed open letter to Putin proposing face-to-face talks between the two men.

"In Russia, this war is a decision of just one person," Kyslytsya said. "In Russia, this war can be stopped at any given time by just one person."

Kyslytsya says he believes it's likely such a meeting could happen even later this year and yield in a "major breakthrough."

Last month, Putin said he saw no point in such a meeting. But if the war continues on its current trajectory, Kyslytsa says that could change.

toggle caption Paula Bronstein for NPR

"Because, see, if we keep doing what we do, with long-range strikes, sooner or later, the Russian leader would have only one choice: to sit down and discuss how to stop this war."

Sponsor Message

He says he believes even Putin has realized that Ukraine now has all the cards.

World.title: In a day of tributes, Lindsey Graham is remembered as a tireless Washington mainstay
World.content:
In a day of tributes, Lindsey Graham is remembered as a tireless Washington mainstay

toggle caption Jim LoScalzo/Pool-Getty Images

President Trump heralded the late Sen. Lindsey Graham as a "legend" and "giant of the U.S. Senate" during a funeral service at the Washington National Cathedral on Tuesday.

Trump's remarks came on the first of two days of remembrances for Graham, who died earlier this month at the age of 71.

Trump expressed fondness for the man who once had harsh words for him when the pair competed for the GOP presidential nomination in 2016. He recalled sharing Graham's personal cell phone number in a particularly heated moment with millions of people – "something I shouldn't have done," he admitted, before once again reciting the digits during the ceremony, to much laughter in the sanctuary.

Sponsor Message

"But it was Lindsey who had the last laugh because while I blew up his phone for one day, we became great friends, and Lindsey did not stop calling me for the next 10 years," Trump said with a smile.

Graham, a legislative powerhouse for over three decades in Congress, grew to become one of the president's closest confidantes, particularly on matters of foreign policy.

"He never saw a war that he didn't like," Trump said of the hawkish senator. "Only friends would understand that. But he wanted it for the good of our country."

toggle caption Pool/Getty Images

Trump spoke about Graham's role in shepherding his signature tax and spending bill through the Senate last summer, quipping: "a lot of Lindsey goodies in there, I can tell you."

He recalled a lesson Graham said he learned from his parents' pool hall business that included a liquor store: "You have to be funny enough that people will keep coming back, and you have to be tough enough that you can stay in business and thrive. A very difficult combination. For his entire storied career, that's exactly who Lindsey Graham was. He was the first person to make you laugh, and one of the last people that you really ever wanted to fight."

Sponsor Message

"He died doing the work he was born to do," Trump said, referencing Graham's trip to Ukraine one day before his death. Graham announced a newly-brokered deal with the White House on a sanctions deal he believed would compel Russia to end its assault on Ukraine.

That sanctions bill has been a priority for Republican leaders in the Senate, who plan to hold a procedural vote on the legislation on Tuesday after the end of services in Washington.

'A family man'

Dozens of members of Congress, along with members of the Cabinet, attended the funeral. Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh was also in attendance; Graham was one of Kavanaugh's most vocal defenders during his confirmation process.

Several of Graham's staff members served as honorary pallbearers for the South Carolina senator.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy were both in attendance — a reminder of Graham's longtime advocacy for both nations, and his interventionist foreign policy approach.

toggle caption Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images

Among the other speakers was Emillie Boggs Roberts, who gave an emotional tribute to her uncle.

"Lindsey was, without a doubt, a family man. His world revolved around my mother, his family, and those he considered such," she said.

She shared the story of how after Graham's parents died, he became the primary caretaker for his teenaged sister Darline Graham, who has now been appointed to serve out the remainder of his term.

"Lindsey became brother, father and mother to my mother overnight," she said. "My mother said Lindsey would come home to visit every weekend from the University of South Carolina in Columbia while she was living with their aunt and uncle in Seneca. That is over a two-hour trip, one way, every weekend, as a young man in college. And that was only the beginning. Without a second thought, Lindsey made sure that he was there for his little sister, and he never stopped. Lindsey was always there for all of us."

Sponsor Message

Congress says goodbye to Graham at the Capitol

Earlier Tuesday, with a flag-draped coffin at the center of the Capitol Rotunda, Republican senators past and present remembered Graham in remarks that celebrated his far-reaching influence — from his home state of South Carolina to the international stage.

Graham's former colleagues shared memories of him as a friend, a congressional mainstay and a leading voice in U.S. foreign policy.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., highlighted the scope of Graham's work over his three decades in Congress, from his role in judicial confirmations to his fierce defense of Ukraine to his support of the anti abortion rights movement.

With Graham's death, a "powerful voice" and a magnetic friend of the Senate was gone, Thune said.

"There was no one — no one — who took his job more seriously than Lindsey Graham. But also, no one was more capable of cracking up a room," Thune said. Graham was often the first call for joint Senate dinners, where "the conversations and the laughs always flowed at any meal where Lindsey Graham was present."

Vice President J.D. Vance, who served alongside Graham in the Senate, said it was impossible not to like his former colleague. Vance described a heated argument the two once had over funding for Ukraine.

toggle caption Pool/Getty Images

Vance assumed Graham would never support another piece of his legislation. But he was wrong.

"It was impossible not to like him — that swashbuckling, infectious laugh, that attitude, that passion that so many others have talked about," Vance said.

New Hampshire Gov. Kelly Ayotte, a close friend who served with Graham in the Senate, said he was exceptional at developing personal relationships with those who disagreed with him. Ayotte, who comes from a military family, said his work for the armed forces will never be forgotten.

An alum of the University of South Carolina's law school, Graham served in the U.S. military for more than three decades, including as an Air Force judge advocate. Ayotte said he often joked about her status as a freshman senator.

Sponsor Message

"Lindsey never missed an opportunity to remind me that he outranked me — not only in service but also in his office in the upper chamber," Ayotte said. "And you know what, he had earned that right."

Graham's remains will be flown back to South Carolina for a funeral service on Wednesday at the First Baptist Church in Columbia.

World.title: Photos: Spain and France battle record wildfires
World.content:
Photos: Spain and France battle record wildfires

toggle caption Philippe Lopez/AFP via Getty Images

From Spain to southwestern France, around 330,000 people have been forced to flee their homes and holiday sites as some of Europe's worst wildfires of the summer spread across the Iberian Peninsula and the Atlantic coast.

In France's Gironde region near Bordeaux and in wildfire-hit areas of Spain, flames are being fueled by extreme heat — and scientists say some fires are now creating their own weather systems, making them even harder to control.

"You cannot stop a storm, so you will not stop a firestorm," says Jean-Baptiste Filippi, a fire-weather expert at France's Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique (CNRS), or National Centre for Scientific Research.

Sponsor Message

Europe, the world's fastest-warming continent, is facing increasingly frequent and intense fire seasons, heating at more than twice the global average according to the European Union's Copernicus Climate Change Service.

The Gironde wildfire alone has burned land equivalent to four times the size of Paris and displaced 220,000 people.

The devastation across Spain and France continues to reshape communities and landscapes, serving as a stark reminder of the growing threat posed by climate change.

"The evidence is clear: the climate emergency kills. That is why it is not enough simply to deal with the consequences. We must tackle the root causes, anticipate the consequences and better prepare our country to protect people's lives," said Pedro Sánchez, prime minister of Spain.
