World.title: Japan Tops Global Waste Index 2025; U.S., Israel, and Chile Rank as Worst Polluters
World.content:
Japan has emerged as the world leader in waste management, while Israel, Chile, and the United States rank among the worst-performing countries, according to the Global Waste Index 2025 released by Slovak-based waste technology company Sensoneo.

The report, which ranks all 38 OECD member states based on their waste generation and disposal practices, highlights significant disparities in global waste management. Sensoneoâs index evaluates countries on per capita waste generation, recycling, incineration, and landfill use.

Israel and Chile ranked last and second-to-last, respectively, primarily due to their heavy reliance on environmentally damaging landfilling practices. Israel sends 524 of the 650 kilograms of waste it generates per person each year directly to landfills. Chile recycles just 1% of its waste and sends more than 95% to landfill.

The United States, which increased its per capita waste generation from 811 to 951 kilograms since 2022, remains the highest generator of municipal solid waste globally. The U.S. disposes of nearly half of that â 447 kilograms â in landfills annually. Neighboring Canada also performed poorly, landfilling 67% of its annual 694 kg per capita waste.

At the other end of the spectrum, Japan ranked No. 1, followed by South Korea and Estonia, all of which combine relatively low waste generation with efficient disposal methods. Japan sends only 3 kilograms per capita to landfill, relying heavily on incineration (245 kg) and maintaining a controlled recycling rate.

European countries dominated the top 10 rankings, with Austria, Germany, Finland, Belgium, Sweden, Norway, and Switzerland all demonstrating strong waste management systems. Austria topped the recycling chart with 334 kilograms of municipal waste recycled per person annually â accounting for 42% of its total waste.

Meanwhile, Spain fell four places to 27th despite minor improvements. The country reduced its landfill and incineration rates slightly while increasing recycling by 10 kilograms per capita. However, its overall waste generation rose by 10 kg compared to the 2022 index.

The index revealed that in 12 of the 38 countries, over half of all waste is still landfilled â including in developed nations like Australia, New Zealand, and Canada. By contrast, Switzerland was the only country to report zero landfill disposal, while Belgium, Finland, Estonia, and Japan landfilled less than 3 kg per person.

Other key findings include:

New Zealand , Finland , and Iceland posted the largest reductions in waste generation per capita.

, , and posted the largest reductions in waste generation per capita. From an environmental standpoint, incineration is considered preferable to landfilling, but excessive reliance on either suggests a need for stronger waste reduction and recycling strategies.

About the Index and Sensoneo

First launched in 2019, the Global Waste Index is published every three years by Sensoneo, a company specializing in digital transformation for waste management systems. The 2025 edition is based on the latest available national data.

Sensoneo operates in 87 countries and provides waste monitoring solutions to cities, industries, and governments. It is the only company to have successfully implemented deposit return systems (DRS) IT infrastructure in nine countries, achieving recycling rates above 90%.

In Madrid, Sensoneo is deploying 11,100 smart sensors, marking the worldâs largest smart waste monitoring installation to date.

World.title: South Korean Model and Actor Kim Jong Suk Dies at 29, Family Urges Respect Amid Speculation
World.content:
South Korean model and television personality Kim Jong Suk has died at the age of 29, his family confirmed on June 6. The news has shocked fans and colleagues across the countryâs entertainment industry, where Kim rose to prominence following his appearance on tvNâs 2022 reality dating show Skip Dating.

Kim, who began his career in modeling before transitioning to television, had been steadily gaining popularity in recent years. His sudden death has prompted an outpouring of grief and speculation online.

While the exact cause of death remains unconfirmed, some media reports have linked Kimâs passing to an incident in Hanam involving a violent altercation between a young man and his girlfriend. According to the reports, law enforcement responded to the scene, after which the man allegedly died by suicide after jumping from a high-rise building.

Amid widespread online discussion and conjecture, Kimâs family issued a public plea for restraint, asking the public and media to refrain from spreading misinformation or making disrespectful assumptions.

Kimâs older sister posted on social media, expressing the family’s devastation and emotional exhaustion. âWe ask for privacy and understanding during this difficult time,â she wrote, emphasizing the familyâs wish to grieve in peace.

Details regarding funeral arrangements have not been made public.

World.title: Trump and Netanyahu meet at the White House as contacts to negotiate with Iran advance
World.content:
Trump and Netanyahu meet at the White House as contacts to negotiate with Iran advance

28th Tuesday, July 2026 - 20:57 UTC Full article

Netanyahu described the meeting as one of the best he has had with Trump, and an Israeli source cited by specialist outlets said the two agreed that Iran must never obtain a nuclear weapon

US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu met on Tuesday for about 90 minutes at the White House, in their first encounter since the joint offensive against Iran began in February. The meeting was held behind closed doors, with no appearance before the press, as Washington seeks to revive negotiations with Tehran.

Netanyahu described the meeting as one of the best he has had with Trump, and an Israeli source cited by specialist outlets said the two agreed that Iran must never obtain a nuclear weapon. The White House called the meeting positive. The encounter came, however, after weeks of public differences between the two governments over the direction of the war.

Hours earlier, asked about the intelligence the Israeli prime minister planned to present to him regarding an Iranian nuclear facility, Trump played down the matter: “I don't need Bibi to tell me. We know perfectly well what is going on,” he told a US television channel. He also brushed off calls to intensify the strikes.

Their priorities differ. For Washington, the central issue is the Strait of Hormuz and its impact on energy prices; for Israel, Iran's nuclear and ballistic missile programs. US bombing ceased last week after two weeks of uninterrupted strikes, and mediators from Pakistan, Egypt, and Qatar are working to define the navigation regime through the strait, one of the issues that sank June's ceasefire. Iran and Oman have reportedly endorsed a proposal, though the Iranian government warned the waterway will remain closed if its security conditions are not addressed. Brent crude fell 2.9% on Tuesday, to around $86 a barrel, on expectations that talks would resume.

Two other matters were on the Israeli agenda: the potential US sale of F-35 fighter jets to Turkey, which Israel sees as a threat to its regional military superiority, and the nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia, which Washington has made conditional on Riyadh recognizing the State of Israel. On the first point, Trump had been blunt days earlier: “Nobody tells me what we should sell,” he said, describing Turkey as an ally.

Both leaders face demanding electoral calendars: Trump, November's midterm elections; Netanyahu, a reelection bid in October. Criticism of the US involvement in the conflict has grown among the president's supporters: former White House strategist Steve Bannon questioned the frequency of the Israeli prime minister's visits and said Trump's staunchest backers are angry.

Israel signed a framework peace agreement with Lebanon weeks ago, though it refuses to withdraw all its troops from the country's south without Hezbollah's disarmament. As a gesture ahead of the meeting, it carried out a first partial withdrawal in one area of southern Lebanon. Netanyahu used his trip to attend the funeral of Republican Senator Lindsey Graham, also attended by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who held a brief meeting with Trump.

World.title: Fujimori takes office in Peru and announces the armed forces will join the fight against crime
World.content:
Fujimori takes office in Peru and announces the armed forces will join the fight against crime

28th Tuesday, July 2026 - 20:54 UTC Full article

At 51, Fujimori is the first woman to reach Peru's presidency through the popular vote

Keiko Fujimori was sworn in as president of Peru on Tuesday and announced that the armed forces will temporarily assume internal control during states of emergency to confront organized crime, in coordination with the National Police. The ceremony took place at Congress on July 28, the anniversary of the country's independence, opening a five-year term.

“We will use every tool the Constitution provides us. During states of emergency, the armed forces will temporarily assume internal control in close coordination with the national police until the authority of the state is fully restored and those territories are returned to citizens,” the president said in her first address to Parliament, in which she placed particular emphasis on extortion.

At 51, Fujimori is the first woman to reach Peru's presidency through the popular vote. She takes office on her fourth attempt, after three consecutive runoff defeats, having beaten left-wing candidate Roberto Sánchez by fewer than 50,000 votes in June's runoff.

In her speech she pledged to govern for “all Peruvians, without exception,” with particular attention to those who “have remained for too long on the margins of the country's growth and progress,” and said she inherits a “state adrift” in “a country marked by abandonment.” She said she had not come “to offer miracles, but method and a clear route,” and set as her first priorities citizen security and preparation for the El Niño phenomenon, for which she announced a contingency plan aimed at moving “into the era of timely prevention.”

The inauguration marks the return to power of the movement founded by her father, Alberto Fujimori, who governed between 1990 and 2000, was convicted of crimes against humanity and of corruption, and died in 2024 at liberty following a humanitarian pardon. The new president publicly invoked his memory on the day of her inauguration. That legacy continues to divide Peruvian society: outside Congress, human rights organizations, student groups, and victims' relatives called a national mobilization. Among them are the relatives in the La Cantuta and Barrios Altos cases, for which her father was convicted. “We are not going to sit down and talk with her and we will never publicly recognize her as president,” said Gisela Ortiz, a relative of one of the victims and a former culture minister.

The day began with the traditional Te Deum at Lima's Cathedral Basilica, where Cardinal Carlos Castillo used his homily to criticize those who “use religion for their partisan position and thus obtain votes,” and remembered the victims of state repression in recent years.

Three cabinet appointments were confirmed: Luis Galarreta as president of the Council of Ministers, Elmer Cuba at Economy and Finance, and Carlos Espá at Foreign Affairs. The final composition will be among the first signals of the new government's direction.

The ceremony drew a broad international presence, led by Spain's King Felipe VI and US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau. Attendees included presidents Javier Milei of Argentina, Yamandú Orsi of Uruguay, Santiago Peña of Paraguay, Daniel Noboa of Ecuador, José Raúl Mulino of Panama, and Nasry Asfura of Honduras, along with delegations from China and Japan. Mexico, Brazil, and Venezuela did not send high-level representation.

Fujimori takes office after a decade of institutional instability in which Peru had nine presidents, most of them serving interim terms.

World.title: Colombia: official accuses Petro of mistreatment and the president announces legal action against her
World.content:
Colombia: official accuses Petro of mistreatment and the president announces legal action against her

28th Tuesday, July 2026 - 20:00 UTC Full article

Rodríguez, once one of the president's closest officials, said he began to distrust her during her tenure at DAPRE and pressured her to resign

The manager of Colombia's Adaptation Fund and former director of the Administrative Department of the Presidency (DAPRE), Angie Rodríguez, publicly accused President Gustavo Petro of subjecting her to mistreatment during her time in government, in remarks to a local radio station. The president responded that the claims are “slanderous” and announced he will pursue criminal action. The exchange comes ten days before the handover of power to president-elect Abelardo de la Espriella.

Rodríguez, once one of the president's closest officials, said he began to distrust her during her tenure at DAPRE and pressured her to resign. She said he accused her of being allied with paramilitary sectors and of other offenses, and said she interpreted as threats certain remarks about the president's past in the guerrilla movement. “I think he is my greatest victimizer,” she said, adding that she fears for her safety. None of those claims has any judicial backing.

The president rejected the accusations and made his own. He said he removed her from DAPRE over what he described as “a subordinate relationship to political sectors that are heirs to paramilitarism,” and attributed her recent dismissal to “her disloyalty to the government program and the use of public office for private ends.” He said he had kept her at the Adaptation Fund despite having lost confidence in her. Those allegations have likewise not been brought before the courts.

Rodríguez also repeated corruption allegations she had made over the weekend. She said she had blocked a maneuver to divert more than 1.2 trillion pesos, some $380 million, from the Adaptation Fund to the National Disaster Risk Management Unit. She argued those funds should go to flood-control works in the La Mojana region, scheduled through 2029, rather than to the response to the El Niño phenomenon. The accusation has not been independently corroborated.

The president had said on Monday that the official is on medical leave for psychiatric reasons. Rodríguez responded that she is experiencing depression and anxiety stemming from the situations she faced in government, called those remarks “unfortunate and stigmatizing,” and said her diagnosis does not affect her professional capacity. Petro said the decision to remove her is unrelated to that diagnosis.

The official requested protection from the incoming government. De la Espriella said on social media that he had instructed his future interior minister, Rodrigo Lara, and the designated head of the National Protection Unit to guarantee her security. Lara later said he gives “very high credibility” to the allegations given how close the official had been to the outgoing president. Rodríguez was the fifth of six directors to pass through DAPRE during this administration.

World.title: “Who is that guy?”: Lula's response to Milei's remarks in São Paulo
World.content:
“Who is that guy?”: Lula's response to Milei's remarks in São Paulo

28th Tuesday, July 2026 - 10:55 UTC Full article

The remarks led to the sharpest diplomatic response between the two countries in years

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva addressed for the first time the remarks made against him by Argentine President Javier Milei, with a brief and ironic response that avoided escalating the controversy. Asked by reporters while preparing to receive South Korean President Lee Jae-myung, he replied: “Who is that guy?”

The reaction contrasts with that of the rest of the Brazilian government, which took a firmer stance. Foreign Minister Mauro Vieira described the Argentine president's remarks as “serious and unacceptable” and said they “constituted interference in internal affairs, in national affairs.” Speaking to TV Globo, he nonetheless defended the diplomatic route: “We must work to achieve understanding between nations, and diplomacy is based on that, on dialogue,” he said.

Finance Minister Dario Durigan questioned the Argentine leader's economic argument and compared the two countries' situations. In a radio interview, he said Milei had spoken about Brazil's situation despite Argentina posting a higher country risk, a larger public debt, and higher inflation. “One cannot fall for the narrative of those who claim the situation will become apocalyptic,” he said.

The episode began on Saturday, when Milei took part in São Paulo in the event formalizing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro's presidential candidacy for the October 4 elections. In a speech of about 25 minutes, the Argentine president avoided naming Lula and referred to him with terms such as “thief” and “convict,” while also using crude language about the region's left-wing governments. He argued that Brazil could face an adverse economic scenario if it does not change its political course.

The remarks led to the sharpest diplomatic response between the two countries in years. On Sunday, the Brazilian government recalled its ambassador in Buenos Aires, Julio Bitelli, whose return has no set date, and summoned Argentina's ambassador in Brasília, Daniel Raimondi, for explanations at Itamaraty. The president of the Supreme Federal Court, Luiz Edson Fachin, also issued an institutional note after Milei disparaged one of the court's justices.

In Argentina, a group of lawmakers filed a motion of censure over the remarks in the Chamber of Deputies. Argentina's foreign ministry had not issued an official response to the Brazilian statements as of this writing. Brazil and Argentina are Mercosur's two largest members and each other's main trading partners.

World.title: Fujimori's inauguration brings Southern Cone and Andean presidents together in Lima
World.content:
Fujimori's inauguration brings Southern Cone and Andean presidents together in Lima

28th Tuesday, July 2026 - 10:30 UTC Full article

Fujimori will become the first woman to reach Peru's presidency through the ballot box

The presidents of Bolivia, Paraguay, Chile, and Honduras arrived in Lima on Monday to attend the handover ceremony at which Keiko Fujimori will assume Peru's presidency for the 2026-2031 term. The leaders of Argentina, Javier Milei; Uruguay, Yamandú Orsi; Panama, José Raúl Mulino; and Ecuador, Daniel Noboa, are also expected to take part.

Interim President José María Balcázar hosted an official dinner for the delegations on Monday night at the Government Palace in the capital's historic center, and on Tuesday will hand the presidential sash to Fujimori on the anniversary of Peru's independence.

Several delegations arrived with defined bilateral agendas. Bolivia's Rodrigo Paz, on his first visit to the neighboring country, will hold a meeting with Fujimori with the stated aim of “restoring diplomatic dialogue between the two countries,” according to Foreign Minister Fernando Aramayo. La Paz's priorities include setting up a binational cabinet in the short term and advancing the use of the Peruvian port of Ilo, which for landlocked Bolivia holds “commercial, tourism and energy” significance.

Chile's José Antonio Kast had already held a video call with the president-elect on July 10, in which they discussed migration and coordination against transnational organized crime. The two also agreed on the need to revitalize the Pacific Alliance, a bloc in which both countries are full members and which they see as a key mechanism for commercial projection toward Asia-Pacific markets.

Paraguay's Santiago Peña, who arrived with his wife, has bilateral and business meetings scheduled, while Honduras's Nasry Asfura will meet with business leaders and officials to promote cooperation opportunities, according to their respective governments.

Fujimori will become the first woman to reach Peru's presidency through the ballot box, after winning by a narrow margin of 49,641 votes over left-wing candidate Roberto Sánchez in the June 7 runoff. She takes office on her fourth attempt, following three consecutive runoff defeats.

The incoming president assumes office facing two main challenges: citizen security, the population's foremost concern, and political stability in a country where no president has completed a five-year term over the past decade. Her electoral rival turned to the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights alleging irregularities, a request the National Elections Board dismissed before proclaiming the results.

World.title: Trump asks the Supreme Court to allow his mail-voting restrictions before the midterms
World.content:
Trump asks the Supreme Court to allow his mail-voting restrictions before the midterms

27th Monday, July 2026 - 22:26 UTC Full article

Trump has repeatedly maintained that mail-in voting facilitates electoral fraud

The US government on Monday filed an emergency request with the Supreme Court seeking authorization to implement President Donald Trump's executive order restricting mail-in voting, which lower courts have blocked. The request comes 99 days before November's midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress.

The filing followed by two days a decision by the First Circuit Court of Appeals, based in Boston, which refused by a two-to-one vote to stay the injunction issued on June 25 by a district judge. That ruling keeps the order blocked in twenty-three Democratic-led states and the District of Columbia, which sued the administration.

The order, signed in March, tasks the director of Citizenship and Immigration Services and the commissioner of the Social Security Administration with drawing up a list of eligible voters, and bars the Postal Service from sending ballots to anyone not on it. The plaintiff states argue that the Constitution reserves the conduct of elections to the states and Congress, not the executive branch, an argument accepted in the earlier rulings.

In its filing before the high court, the administration framed the order as “general policy guidance” and stressed that the Postal Service has not finalized any regulations. The appeals judges had noted, by contrast, that the measure sets rapidly approaching deadlines requiring states to reorganize their procedures immediately, while also ensuring that officials and the public understand the rules governing the September and November votes. A White House spokesperson said the lower courts' decision “is not the final say” and that the administration expects a favorable outcome.

Trump has repeatedly maintained that mail-in voting facilitates electoral fraud. Election officials, courts, and federal agencies concluded that there was no evidence of widespread fraud in the 2020 elections, when that method saw unprecedented use during the pandemic, and noted that the system includes multiple verification and audit mechanisms.

The initiative is part of a broader set of government actions on electoral matters. The administration is pressing Congress to pass the SAVE America Act, which would require documentary proof of citizenship to register on the federal roll and remains stalled in the Senate, and has sued twenty-nine states to obtain copies of their voter registries, which include dates of birth, driver's license numbers, and portions of social security numbers. Courts have blocked access in three states and have yet to rule in the rest.

World.title: Milei announces Starlink deal to bring satellite internet to 6,000 rural schools
World.content:
Milei announces Starlink deal to bring satellite internet to 6,000 rural schools

27th Monday, July 2026 - 22:20 UTC Full article

At the time of the announcement, neither the text of the agreement nor any public statement from the company about its terms had been released

Argentine President Javier Milei announced an agreement between the National Communications Agency (Enacom) and Starlink to provide satellite connectivity to 6,000 rural schools that currently have poor internet access or no connection at all. The announcement was made on Sunday during the main event of the 138th International Livestock, Agriculture and Industry Exhibition in Buenos Aires.

According to the president, Elon Musk's company will donate 6,000 complete satellite kits along with 24 months of its highest-capacity service, which includes priority access of up to five terabytes per month per site. “Yes, it's a huge amount. Thank you, Elon,” he said during the speech.

Once that period ends, the equipment will remain at the schools and the regulator will take on the cost of the service for an additional year, covering the subscription, installation, technical support, and monitoring. Enacom sources said those resources will come from the Universal Service Fund, made up of contributions from the telecommunications sector and earmarked for extending access to areas not covered by commercial provision.

At the time of the announcement, neither the text of the agreement nor any public statement from the company about its terms had been released. The president also said the initiative adds to the three million users who, he said, already use the company's services in the country.

Starlink accelerated its expansion in Argentina following the easing of the regulatory framework for satellite services introduced by the current government, and now operates across the entire territory. The Argentine market accounts for about 25% of the company's Latin American operation and ranks among the countries with the highest service penetration, with weekly user growth of around 2%. Most customers are households, a concentration that has led to episodes of saturation in certain areas, such as greater Buenos Aires, Córdoba, and the Vaca Muerta region.

The agreement fits into the relationship Milei has maintained with Musk since the start of his term. The two met in February 2025 in the United States and have kept in frequent contact since. In parallel, Tesla is advancing its commercial entry into the local market, after formally incorporating in the country and appointing its first manager for Argentina and Uruguay.

In the same speech, the president projected an expansion of agricultural output and said the country is in a position to double its grain harvest, though he announced no decisions on export duties, one of the sector's main demands.

World.title: Uruguay prepares protocols for the risk of El Niño flooding in the spring
World.content:
Uruguay prepares protocols for the risk of El Niño flooding in the spring

27th Monday, July 2026 - 22:00 UTC Full article

“The challenge we face now is preparing for what may happen in the spring as a result of this climate phenomenon,” the president said

Uruguay's government is drawing up a set of contingency protocols for the flooding risk associated with the El Niño phenomenon, which climate projections indicate will have its greatest impact on the region during the southern hemisphere spring. President Yamandú Orsi announced at the Congress of Departmental Governors that the measures will be presented in August, ahead of what may occur from September and October.

“The challenge we face now is preparing for what may happen in the spring as a result of this climate phenomenon,” the president said. He indicated that the protocols drawn up by the departmental emergency coordination centers will be put on the table and that a coordination space will be created with the National Emergency System. “We have a record, going back to 1998, of how floods play out and we know where they will hit hardest and where less. It will not affect every area in the same way,” he added.

The available projections are probabilistic. NOAA's Climate Prediction Center puts the probability of El Niño conditions during the June-July-August quarter at close to 100%, persisting at least through the end of the year. Uruguay's Meteorological Institute does not forecast specific flooding, but projects a higher probability of above-normal rainfall in the country's northeast, with that signal expanding toward the north and part of the center during the spring. Brazilian consultancy MetSul estimates a probability above 80% that accumulated rainfall will substantially exceed historical averages in southern Brazil, northeastern Argentina, and across Uruguay, placing the period of greatest risk between September and December.

A central concern is the effect of rainfall in southern Brazil on the flow of the Uruguay River, which runs along the country's western edge. Rio Grande do Sul has already recorded flooding episodes this month. National Party senator Sebastián Da Silva said management of the binational Salto Grande dam will be decisive and warned about the situation of the Río Negro dams, while identifying the Merín Lagoon basin, the Estero de Pelotas, and the Treinta y Tres lowlands as sensitive areas. He called for machinery and shelter space for potential evacuees to be arranged in advance.

Meteorologist José Serra said the movement of moisture from the equator toward southeastern Brazil and Uruguay has already begun to affect dams in the country's north, and put forward, as his own hypothesis, that a convergence between El Niño and a cooling of North Atlantic waters could amplify the phenomenon's effects.

The region is already going through a season of extreme events. Last week, Chile declared a state of catastrophe in the north of the country over a storm that left at least ten dead.

World.title: CFE: Power outages reduced by nearly 40% since 2024
World.content:
The Federal Electricity Commission (CFE) reported that power outages fell 39% during the first half of 2026 compared to the same period in 2024, attributed to a “historic investment” in the expansion and modernization of the country’s transmission and distribution networks.

Speaking at the Industrial Exhibition of the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), Mexico section, head of CFE Emilia Calleja said that system restoration times were also “significantly reduced,” typically resolved within one to three hours.

Calleja noted that improvements in electricity coverage respond to CFE’s updated strategy to enhance and modernize distribution network capacity, as attention had long been focused primarily on generation.

The head of CFE explained that “modern, robust and intelligent grids” allow for the integration of new energy sources, remote operation, anticipation of failures and, above all, a better response to natural disasters.

The latter has a direct precedent in the aftermath of Hurricane Otis, which in October 2023 devastated much of Guerrero’s electrical infrastructure, leaving more than 500,000 customers without power. It took the CFE a record time of seven days to restore service in that region.

“This experience showed us the importance of having a resilient infrastructure, qualified and well-trained personnel, and above all, technology that allows us to respond quickly,” Calleja said.

For this purpose, between 2024 and 2030, CFE is implementing a program exceeding 244 billion pesos, including 15 billion pesos (US $859 million) in 2025-2026 alone, to strengthen distribution with new poles, meters and conductors.

The move is enhanced by the renewable energy plan recently presented by Energy Minister Luz Elena González. In June, González explained that the government aims to add 32,475 megawatts of generation capacity to the national electricity system by 2030, of which approximately 22,376 megawatts — roughly 70% — will come from renewable sources.

Speaking at Sheinbaum’s mañanera, Calleja also highlighted the emblematic project of the Rafael Galván Maldonado Solar Park in Puerto Peñasco, Sonora, which upon completion of its four stages will reach 1,000 megawatts, becoming the largest solar installation in the Americas.

With reports from La Jornada and El Heraldo de México

World.title: Spain’s Repsol is selling half its Gulf oil project to Talos Energy, a US company
World.content:
Spanish oil company Repsol has agreed to sell half of its Block 29 oil and gas development project in the Gulf of Mexico to Talos Energy.

Repsol will bring the U.S. company into its project by selling it a 50% stake in exchange for two payments totaling more than US $50 million.

The transaction is subject to approval by Mexico’s Energy Ministry and the National Antitrust Commission.

Headquartered in Houston, Texas, Talos is acquiring a working interest in Block 29, located in the Salinas-Sureste Basin approximately 88 kilometers offshore of the state of Tabasco. This 3,254 square-kilometer area in the southern Gulf of Mexico has seen more than a dozen deepwater discoveries.

Block 29 contains the Polok and Chinwol oil discoveries, which together are estimated to contain more than 200 million barrels of oil equivalent in gross recoverable resources, along with multiple additional exploration prospects.

The block features a floating production, storage- and offloading-based development concept anchored by existing oil discoveries described by Energy-pedia news as “well-positioned to serve as a hub for future developments and nearby discoveries.”

The two payments offered by Talos are a contingent payment of US $30 million at the time of the final investment decision (FID) and a cash stake of up to US $20 million in the next exploration well. Talos will also be asked for the reimbursement of “certain pre-closing costs.”

Upon closing, Talos will hold a 50% working interest and, together with Repsol, will be the sole participants in the block. The partners expect to reach a FID early next year.

Repsol acquired 100% of the rights to Block 29 in 2025, assuming full operational and strategic responsibility for the asset, after Petronas (Malaysia’s national oil and gas corporation) and Harbour (the largest London-listed independent oil and gas company) relinquished their stakes.

In a statement, Talos Chairman and CEO Paul Goodfellow expressed confidence in working alongside Repsol as progress is made on Block 29.

“This stake adds a high-quality, large-scale development opportunity and significant exploration potential in a proven deepwater basin, further boosting the third pillar of our strategy and strengthening our long-term growth portfolio,” he said.

Talos said the “discoveries and identified prospects target amplitude-supported Miocene reservoirs analogous to fields [the company] has successfully developed and produced in the Gulf of America [sic].” The investment reinforces Talos’ “strategic focus on opportunities where its deepwater subsurface expertise provides a competitive advantage.”

With reports from El Economista, Economía Digital, Energy-pedia news and Offshore Engineer Magazine

World.title: Great escapes: Summertime adventures accessible from Guadalajara
World.content:
Guadalajara is the perfect location for people looking for a quick escape from noise and congestion on a fine summer day. The city is bordered to the north by gorgeous Oblatos Canyon and to the west by Bosque la Primavera, a magnificent pine and oak forest the size of 42,657 World Cup soccer fields.

Guadalajara also happens to sit at the center of an area where all five of Mexico’s main ecosystems converge. This puts tapatios (Guadalajara residents) within a day’s drive of mountains, beaches, deserts, rivers, slot canyons, hot springs and Mexico’s largest lake.

My wife and I described 90 of these sites in our three-volume series “Outdoors in Western Mexico,” no longer in print but available in digital form.

The importance of finding a good guide

These days, I suggest that hikers contact local guides to arrange for excursions out in the blue. The guides know the territory, the people who live there, the weather patterns and the feasibility of transit on a given day. On top of that, you’ll have a chance to contribute to the local economy.

One of those knowledgeable guides is outdoor enthusiast Mike Gallegos. Mike is the founder of Senderismo Guadalajara, which organizes hikes and climbs all over Western Mexico.

500 meters straight down

As I mentioned above, Guadalajara has some great outdoor sites located immediately adjacent to the city. For example, you can take a bus to Parque Puerta de la Barranca at the northern edge of town for a good look at magnificent, 500-meter-deep Cañon de Oblatos, also called Cañon de Huentitán. Very near the park, there’s a steep trail — once part of the famed Camino Real — which takes you to the Santiago River at the bottom. Here you’ll find graceful Puente de Arcediano, the second suspension bridge built in the Americas.

To get back up to the city, Senderismo Guadalajara offers two unforgettable, adrenaline-raising routes. One is via the Árbol de la Bruja (“Witch’s Tree”), while the other takes you up an abandoned cable-car track. Hang on to your hat!

Hot river, cool forest

At its Western edge, greater Guadalajara butts up against the Primavera Forest. Here, Senderismo Guadalajara has an exciting hike following the forest’s famed Río Caliente to the bizarre Cascada Esmeralda, which looks cold and alpine from a distance, but turns out to be hot and steamy up close. At its source, this river literally boils its way out of a spot you may be tempted to call the “Gates of Hell.”

For a totally different experience in this forest, you can hike seven kilometers atop mesas covered with pine and oak trees to reach Nejahuete Tower, better known as Torre Dos. Here you can climb up to a platform manned by forest-fire spotters 24 hours a day. The view from this tower is truly breathtaking.

‘The Tooth’

Another outstanding site on Guadalajara’s perimeter is “El Diente,” located only six kilometers north of the City’s busy Periférico or Ring Road. A veritable forest of giant rocks stands here in total silence except for the grunts of rock climbers who consider the monoliths ideal for perfecting their techniques. These hard rocks were once part of the Earth’s mantle and may be 30 million years old. You’ll enjoy taking Senderismo Guadalajara’s six-kilometer loop hike around the mass of monoliths.

Once you drive out of the city, you’ll find great summertime escapes at every turn.

Stargazing on Ceboruco Volcano

Ceboruco is a massive, still active volcano, 2,280 meters high, in the state of Nayarit, a two-hour drive from Guadalajara. The camino to the top is in good condition — and don’t be surprised if you see road runners along the way.

Senderismo Guadalajara will arrange for you to camp on the flat, grassy floor of an old crater a few meters below a billowing and hissing fumarole, with a spectacular view of the starry sky. The next day, you can hike to another of Ceboruco’s seven craters, from whose rim you can gaze down at a dramatic tongue of lava stretching off into the distance. Those “ants” you see crossing the rubble far, far away are actually buses and semi-trailers!

Comala Falls: Am I in paradise?

A two-hour drive to the southwest of Guadalajara brings you to the foot of an utterly spectacular waterfall. You can practically jump out of your car and straight into the delightful, bubbling pool at the foot of the cascade. “What more could I ask for?” you say, and Mike Gallegos replies: “More than you would ever believe.”

There are, in fact, 11 more waterfalls upstream. Welcome to paradise!

There are other falls and volcanoes near Guadalajara, too. But in case you get a yen for a jungle experience instead, you might drive to Huilotán Ecological Park, 90 minutes north of town, where you can camp next to spring-fed pools beneath mango and fig trees, your eyes peeled for military macaws flying overhead. Oh, did I mention the 100-meter-tall waterfall and the fish-fry dinner?

14 geysers and a psychedelic bell

Next, for something truly different, I recommend the 14 geysers of Los Patitos River, located 30 kilometers north of Huilotán. Of course, there are hot pools, too, so don’t forget your swimsuit.

Finally, how about a little mountain that stands in a category all its own? La Campana (“The Bell”), located 160 kilometers west of Guadalajara, features giant wave-shaped rock formations that look as if they could have been designed by Antoni Gaudí. Don’t forget your camera!

To start exploring Guadalajara’s natural wonders, contact Mike Gallegos at WhatsApp +52 (331) 136-8254.

John Pint has lived near Guadalajara, Jalisco, for more than 30 years and is the author of “A Guide to West Mexico’s Guachimontones and Surrounding Area” and co-author of “Outdoors in Western Mexico.” More of his writing can be found on his website.

World.title: MND Local: Balancing preservation and growth in Puerto Vallarta
World.content:
Puerto Vallarta has always known how to attract people. For decades, visitors have arrived searching for the same things: beautiful beaches, a welcoming community, incredible food and the feeling that life moves just a little differently here. But success brings its own challenges for the people living here year-round.

This week, three stories highlight different aspects of life in Puerto Vallarta: federal concerns about water quality at one of the city’s beaches, the arrival of electric buses aimed at modernizing public transportation, and the ongoing work of protecting the sea turtles that return to the region’s coastline each year.

Playa del Cuale flagged in federal water quality monitoring

One of Puerto Vallarta’s most recognizable beaches, Playa del Cuale, has been classified as unsuitable for recreational use following the latest federal water quality monitoring program.

The Federal Commission for the Protection against Health Risks (Cofepris) included the beach among five in Mexico that exceeded permitted bacteria levels during its most recent testing between June 15 and July 1. Cofepris tests beaches by measuring levels of enterococci bacteria, an indicator used to determine whether seawater meets health standards for activities such as swimming. Beaches that exceed established limits are classified as not suitable for recreational use until conditions improve.

The classification doesn’t mean Puerto Vallarta’s beaches as a whole failed inspection. Cofepris reported that 98.3% of beaches tested nationwide met the required standards for recreational use. However, the result draws attention to Playa del Cuale and raises questions about what contributed to the elevated bacterial levels and what measures will be taken to address the issue. Located near the mouth of the Cuale River, the beach is an area where factors such as rainfall runoff, drainage systems and coastal conditions can all influence water quality.

For residents, the report serves as a reminder of the importance of monitoring and maintaining the environmental systems that support a growing coastal city.

Puerto Vallarta receives first electric buses as public transport changes begin

Puerto Vallarta has taken its first step toward introducing electric public transportation, with the arrival of new electric buses designed to operate along one of the city’s busiest corridors.

The first units arrived as part of a state-backed electromobility project led by the government of Jalisco. Seven articulated electric buses are expected to serve the Francisco Medina Ascencio corridor, connecting important areas of the city, including the hotel zone, Marina Vallarta, Ixtapa and the Centro Universitario de la Costa area.

The buses are designed to carry high passenger volumes and include features such as air conditioning and accessibility improvements.

The introduction of electric buses represents one of the most significant changes to Puerto Vallarta’s public transportation system in years. For residents, however, the success of the project will ultimately be measured by how it performs in daily life.

Public transportation is a major issue for many people who depend on buses to travel to work, school and essential services. As Puerto Vallarta continues to grow, questions about traffic congestion, reliability and accessibility have become increasingly important.

The arrival of electric units marks the beginning of a transition, but residents will be watching how quickly the new system expands and what improvements it brings to everyday commuting.

Boca de Tomates turtle camp reports thousands of hatchlings released

While Puerto Vallarta continues to develop, conservation groups are working to protect one of the species that’s long been part of the region’s natural identity.

The Boca de Tomates turtle camp reported the release of 30,864 sea turtle hatchlings during the latest nesting season, following efforts that protected 521 nests containing more than 36,000 eggs.

The conservation program, located along the northern coastline of Puerto Vallarta, works throughout the nesting season to monitor beaches, protect nests from threats and help ensure hatchlings can safely make their way into the Pacific Ocean. The annual effort depends on the work of conservation staff, volunteers and community members who patrol nesting areas, relocate vulnerable nests when necessary and organize releases once the young turtles are ready to begin their journey.

For residents, the results highlight the role that local conservation organizations play in protecting Puerto Vallarta’s natural environment. While discussions about coastal growth often focus on development pressures, programs like Boca de Tomates demonstrate the ongoing work taking place to preserve local wildlife.

As Puerto Vallarta continues to change, the annual return of sea turtles and the thousands of hatchlings given a better chance of survival through these efforts remains an important part of the region’s environmental story.

Together, these stories offer a snapshot of a city continuing to evolve. Puerto Vallarta’s growth brings new opportunities, but it also highlights the importance of investing in the systems, services and natural resources that support the community that calls it home.

Charlotte Smith is a writer and journalist based in Mexico. Her work focuses on travel, politics and community. You can follow along with her travel stories at www.salsaandserendipity.com.

World.title: Mexico’s export revenue is up by 25% this year
World.content:
Mexico’s export revenue increased 24.6% annually in the first six months of 2026 to reach a record high of US $389.72 billion, according to the national statistics agency INEGI.

The year-over-year gain in percentage terms was the highest since 2021, when export revenue rose 29.4% in the first six months of the year.

México es una locomotora de exportación y pronto llegará a ser la novena potencia exportadora del mundo. El crecimiento anual de las exportaciones mexicanas al mundo fue de prácticamente 25% anual en el periodo ene-junio. Esto nos lleva al superávit comercial mas alto… pic.twitter.com/PjEm0SumEb — Luis Rosendo Gutiérrez (@LuisRosendo_) July 28, 2026

Published on Monday, INEGI’s data also shows that Mexico recorded a record high trade surplus of $9.85 billion between January and June, its export revenue exceeding its outlay on imports by that amount.

More than 80% of Mexico’s export earnings come from goods shipped to the United States. In 2023, Mexico supplanted China to become the world’s largest exporter to the United States and has remained in the top spot ever since. In 2025, Mexico sent goods worth more than $534 billion to its northern neighbor, while its total exports were worth almost $665 billion.

Non-automotive manufacturing exports surge 37% between January and June

INEGI’s data shows that 91.3% of Mexico’s export revenue between January and June came from the shipment abroad of manufactured goods.

On an annual basis, the value of manufacturing exports increased 25.8% to $355.9 billion.

That growth was the result of a 37.6% increase in earnings from the export of non-automotive manufactured goods and a 1% increase in the value of automotive exports, which are subject to tariffs when shipped to the United States. Non-automotive manufacturing exports were worth $263.64 billion between January and June, while automotive exports were worth $92.25 billion. The value of automotive exports to the U.S. in the first six months of 2026 fell 2.7% annually, but exports of those products to other markets rose 24%, according to INEGI.

Rodolfo Ostolaza, deputy director of economic studies at Banamex, said that technology-related investment in the United States, including in data centers and other infrastructure that supports the burgeoning artificial intelligence industry, is a factor in Mexico’s export dynamism. However, he said it wouldn’t be prudent to attribute all of Mexico’s export growth to technology investment in the U.S. because Mexico’s non-automotive manufacturing exports category is very broad.

For his part, Mario Correa, a former president of the economic studies committee of the Mexican Institute of Financial Executives, told the newspaper El Financiero that a good part of Mexican manufacturing sector exports have Asian content and therefore Mexico’s role in the chain, in some cases, is concentrated in assembly.

INEGI’s data also shows that the value of mining sector exports increased 78.6% annually to reach $11.2 billion between January and June.

Meanwhile, revenue from agricultural exports fell 4% annually to $11.74 billion, while oil export earnings declined 2.9% to $10.86 billion.

Exports increase 34% in June

Mexico’s strong export performance in the first half of 2026 was aided by a 34.4% annual increase in export revenue in June.

Mexico’s exports generated a record $72.55 billion in revenue last month, boosted primarily by a 48.8% increase in the value of non-automotive manufacturing goods that were shipped abroad.

Those goods generated earnings of $49.65 billion in June, accounting for 68.4% of total export revenue.

Mexico’s expenditure on imports grows by more than 20%

INEGI’s data shows that Mexico spent $379.86 billion on imports between January and June, a 22% increase compared to the same period of last year. Almost 80% of Mexico’s outlay on imports was spent on intermediate goods — i.e., inputs used in the production of finished goods.

Expenditure on intermediate goods, including oil-based intermediate goods, totaled $303.54 billion between January and June, a 26.7% annual increase.

Mexico’s outlay on imported consumer goods increased 9.8% annually in the same period to reach $48.65 billion, while expenditure on imported capital goods such as machinery and tools rose 1.1% to $27.65 billion.

In June, Mexico’s expenditure on imports totaled $68.46 billion, a 28% year-over-year increase. Mexico recorded a $4.08 billion trade surplus last month.

With reports from El Financiero and El Economista

World.title: Is Mexico a safe place for the gay community? A recalibration of a first impression
World.content:
I still remember sitting on my couch years ago watching a CONCACAF Gold Cup soccer game when I was in high school. It was a Mexico game. I was not a soccer fan at that time, and the game was mostly just background noise for whatever social media app I was more engaged with on my phone.

I heard the Mexican fans begin to wind up a chant, and I started to pay more attention. I watched as the fans built into a unifying crescendo while waving jazz hands in the air. Their harmony became louder and louder until it stopped, and they all shouted puto (male prostitute) so loud that it echoed throughout the stadium. The ref stopped play and warned the Mexican fans to stop the chant or risk a forfeit.

That was my introduction to the “puto” chant, a homophobic slur that has marred Mexico’s fan culture in controversy as it has become a staple at El Tri games around the world.

To me, chants from fans of national teams are representations of a nation’s culture, both on and off the pitch. So this became my first impression of how queer rights were treated in Mexico. To an outsider, it looked like a country coming together to insult an opposing team using a homophobic slur, and that the force behind it had only become greater as the world has increasingly told them to stop.

I had never been to Mexico until I arrived in San Miguel de Allende in late June to start a nine-week journalism internship with Mexico News Daily. Now I found myself with a chance to find out what the queer experience was actually like in Mexico — a country famous for its entrenched Catholic beliefs that is incongruent and often intolerant of gay rights.

My first impactful experience came just 10 days after I arrived when I embarked on a four-hour bus ride to Mexico City to experience the Mexico vs. Ecuador round of 32 game. I was surrounded by hundreds of thousands of fans in the Zócalo, Mexico City’s main square, in what immediately became one of the most memorable experiences of my life.

Despite the eruptions after both of Mexico’s goals, the deafening national anthem and witnessing nearly 1.5 million people take to the streets in celebration, the “puto” chant still stuck out. Nearly all of the hundreds of thousands of attendees in the Zócalo — ranging from more stereotypically conservative young men to middle-aged women and even children — partook in the tradition. It made me, a gay 21-year-old who has only lived in progressive areas of the United States, a bit uncomfortable.

As a lifelong sports fan, I am no stranger to hooliganism, racism and homophobia at sporting events. It is almost expected among certain people and at some games, but when a chant like this is belted by women and children and by those young and old, it makes you feel like maybe the entire nation subscribes to outward intolerance.

I returned to San Miguel and was continuously reassured by my colleagues that the word had changed in interpretation throughout the years, and more vulgar speech was popular in casual conversation in Mexico. I understood, but the word clearly still had a negative connotation, as it is used directly at opposing teams and players. So even if the meaning is no longer a direct slur towards gay people, it still had a negative connotation that evolved from that word.

However, the next three weeks did not produce any evidence of homophobia, despite me keeping a keen eye out for it. At a watch party for the Mexico vs. England round of 16 game, a large crowd that gathered in front of the Parroquia de San Miguel Arcangel church barely uttered the chant. My daily life in San Miguel went on without ever feeling unsafe or witnessing any blatant acts of homophobia.

This past weekend I found myself with some free time, so I decided to go read a book in Parque Zeferrino, a newer park a little over a mile north of San Miguel Centro. I was enjoying the weather and watching fish dart around the pond, but I started to notice something every time I looked up. Seemingly every minute, more and more people were showing up at the park adorned in pride flags.

I went over to ask what was going on and found out that I had coincidentally stumbled upon the starting point of the San Miguel de Allende Pride Parade.

Nearly one thousand people — both locals and foreigners — marched from the park down to the Parroquia. It was a celebration filled with dancing, singing and chanting. People waved flags and folding fans. They brought skeptical onlookers watching from the sidewalks to join in. It was a beautiful and colorful scene, especially in one of the most conservative regions in Mexico known for its strong ties to the church.

From everything I had experienced at the Zócalo, it felt like onlookers could have treated the parade with disdain. But that word was never yelled. No one in the parade felt unsafe. No one seemed like they had to be hyper-aware of their surroundings. They were just expressing their pride.

Same sex marriage was legalized in all of Mexico’s 32 states in 2022. Mexico City first legalized it in 2009. The San Miguel Pride Parade has only existed for a few years, but it has since grown into a signature summer event.

I may have found it by accident, but the parade — and all the locals watching and supporting from the sidewalks — showed me that Mexico, despite its insistence on belting a homophobic chant and its entrenched catholic beliefs, can still be prideful and a space that feels welcoming to people from all over the world.

This does not forgive the chant at the Zócalo or the meaning behind it. But the United States — which has championed itself as a safe haven for gay rights — continues to move backwards as half the country vies to eliminate gay marriage. Mexico may be comfortable spewing a homophobic chant at its sporting events, but as of today, it just might be a safer place for queer people than its northern neighbor.

World.title: Sheinbaum hits back at Miller’s ‘Mexico’s systems don’t work’ claim: Tuesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

📍 Miller, Ruffo and fracking: President Sheinbaum used her Tuesday press conference to respond to provocative remarks from White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller about Mexico, while also addressing the Ernesto Ruffo case and giving an update on the fracking feasibility assessment.

President Sheinbaum used her Tuesday press conference to respond to provocative remarks from White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller about Mexico, while also addressing the Ernesto Ruffo case and giving an update on the fracking feasibility assessment. 🎙️ Sheinbaum won’t debate Miller: Asked about Miller’s claim that Mexico’s justice, political and legal systems “don’t work” because parts of the country are “controlled and occupied by terrorist organizations,” Sheinbaum insisted there is “good coordination” between Mexico and the U.S. and asserted that “the people govern” in Mexico.

Asked about Miller’s claim that Mexico’s justice, political and legal systems “don’t work” because parts of the country are “controlled and occupied by terrorist organizations,” Sheinbaum insisted there is “good coordination” between Mexico and the U.S. and asserted that “the people govern” in Mexico. 🗳️ Midterms cited as motive: Asked why the U.S. official made the remarks, Sheinbaum pointed to November’s U.S. midterm elections.

Asked why the U.S. official made the remarks, Sheinbaum pointed to November’s U.S. midterm elections. ⚖️ Ruffo case is “criminal, not political”: Responding to a statement from 25 former Spanish and Latin American leaders — including ex-presidents Vicente Fox and Felipe Calderón — who called ex-Baja California Governor Ernesto Ruffo’s prosecution “political persecution,” Sheinbaum said the signatories should read the Attorney General’s evidence, calling it purely “a matter that has to do with a crime.”

Responding to a statement from 25 former Spanish and Latin American leaders — including ex-presidents Vicente Fox and Felipe Calderón — who called ex-Baja California Governor Ernesto Ruffo’s prosecution “political persecution,” Sheinbaum said the signatories should read the Attorney General’s evidence, calling it purely “a matter that has to do with a crime.” 🔥 Fracking assessment nearing completion: Sheinbaum said the expert committee studying “sustainable fracking” has reached internal agreements and is finishing its final assessment of energy needs through 2035–2040, with results expected within one to two weeks.

Why today’s mañanera matters

Today’s mañanera was important as President Claudia Sheinbaum responded to provocative remarks made by a senior Trump administration official. Given that the Mexico-U.S. relationship is currently strained, particularly in the areas of security and trade, any friction between the neighboring countries draws heightened scrutiny.

Also of note at the Tuesday morning press conference was Sheinbaum’s response to the view expressed by 25 former Spanish and Latin American political leaders regarding the criminal charges faced by a former governor of the northern state of Baja California.

In addition, today’s mañanera was significant as Sheinbaum provided an update on an expert group’s assessment of the feasibility of “sustainable fracking” in Mexico, a practice that, if approved, could allow Mexico to reduce its heavy reliance on natural gas imports from the United States. The results of the group’s assessment were initially expected in June, but now look likely to come in August.

Sheinbaum responds to Stephen Miller’s remarks about Mexico

A reporter asked the president about the Mexico-related remarks made on Thursday by Stephen Miller, White House deputy chief of staff for policy and a homeland security adviser to U.S. President Donald Trump.

Stephen Miller: There is a reason why, in Mexico, the justice system doesn’t work, the political system doesn’t work, and the legal system doesn’t work. It’s because you have territory controlled and occupied by terrorist organizations who kill or kidnap anybody who gets in the… pic.twitter.com/zCyp7aRnsV — Clash Report (@clashreport) July 27, 2026

Miller said that Mexican criminal organizations “not only export massive death in the form of narcotics to our country, but they also export sophisticated criminal enterprises whose objective is to destabilize our democracy and to end the rule of law in our country.”

“There’s a reason why in Mexico, the justice system doesn’t work, the political system doesn’t work [and] the legal system doesn’t work. It’s because you have territory controlled and occupied by terrorist organizations who kill, extort, kidnap or murder anybody who gets in the way,” he said, referring to Mexican cartels that have been designated as foreign terrorists organizations by the U.S. government.

Sheinbaum’s first response to Miller’s remarks was a declaration that “we’re not going to get into a debate.”

She subsequently said there is “good coordination” between Mexico and the United States, and declared that “they” — i.e., Trump administration officials — know that “the people govern” in Mexico.

“Nobody else governs, the people rule,” Sheinbaum said.

“We’re a government of the people. … We work every day for security and peace in our country and there are results,” she said.

“I’m not going to get into a debate with him,” Sheinbaum added, referring to Miller.

Asked what she attributed the U.S. official’s remarks to, the president noted that midterm elections will be held in the United States in November.

“We’ve always said that Mexico should not be a defining element in their campaign,” Sheinbaum said, apparently referring to the U.S. Republican Party.

“… The United States has to look at itself, particularly with regard to the issue of drug use and the distribution [of narcotics] and money laundering in the United States,” she said.

Sheinbaum: Ruffo case is a ‘criminal issue,’ not a political one

A reporter noted that a group of former Spanish and Latin American political leaders issued a statement regarding the criminal charges faced by ex-Baja California Governor Ernesto Ruffo, who is accused of organized crime, fuel theft and tax evasion.

In the statement, the ex-leaders who belong to the “Democratic Initiative for Spain and the Americas” (Grupo IDEA) — among whom are former Mexican presidents Vicente Fox and Felipe Calderón — claim that the situation of Ruffo, National Action Party (PAN) governor of Baja California between 1989 and 1995, displays “unmistakable features of a political persecution orchestrated by those in power.”

Sheinbaum said “it would be very good” if the signatories of the statement “informed themselves” about the ex-governor’s situation by reading the information released by the Federal Attorney General’s Office.

“I repeat, it has nothing to do with a political issue. It’s a criminal issue,” she said.

Ruffo is “a person who allegedly, according to all the evidence, committed serious crimes,” Sheinbaum said.

“… Those who signed [the statement] saying that it’s a political matter are mistaken,” she said.

“It’s a matter that has to do with a crime,” Sheinbaum said.

Sheinbaum provides an update on the fracking feasibility assessment

Sheinbaum told reporters that a group of experts tasked with assessing the feasibility of “sustainable fracking” in Mexico has been expanded.

“The committee was expanded with two additional points of view,” she said.

“One from people who have historically had opinions against the exploitation of unconventional gas,” Sheinbaum said.

She said that another “group of people from different academic institutions” was added to the fracking assessment committee in order to develop an “energy planning scheme considering other sources of energy.”

“This second part is what has slightly delayed the committee’s ability to come to the mañanera to provide a result [of the fracking assessment],” Sheinbaum said.

She said that the committee has made a lot of progress, adding that its members have “even reached “agreements” among themselves.

“What’s missing is the final assessment regarding the growth of energy use and energy sources to 2035, 2040,” Sheinbaum said, explaining that the assessment considers how natural gas can be replaced by “other energy sources.”

She said that assessment is likely to be completed next week.

Sheinbaum said that next week or the week after next, the government will be in a position to announce the committee’s “guidance” regarding the feasibility of sustainable fracking in Mexico.

The president said she believed that the committee’s conclusions will be “satisfactory for everyone.”

The experts, she added, “will also propose that other studies are needed.”

Sheinbaum said those studies would be carried out this year.

The president has acknowledged her previous opposition to fracking, but now asserts that it can take place safely via the use of new technologies.

A decision to allow fracking in Mexico — a practice that was largely paused by former president Andrés Manuel López Obrador — would increase domestic production of natural gas, a fuel that Mexico currently imports from the United States in large quantities.

World.title: In canceling La Parota dam, Sheinbaum details a different water plan for rural Acapulco
World.content:
President Claudia Sheinbaum announced Sunday the cancellation of the La Parota hydroelectric dam to instead double down on an alternative plan featuring radial wells, rehabilitated pumping systems and elevated tanks to supply water to the Acapulco area.

“Yesterday I informed the entire rural area of ​​Acapulco that we are no longer going to do [the dam project] because it would have greatly affected the communities,” Sheinbaum said.

The Federal Electricity Commission’s (FCE) proposed 900-megawatt La Parota dam was expected to flood between 14,000 and 17,000 hectares of land, impacting the municipalities of Acapulco, Juan R. Escudero, San Marcos, Chilpancingo and Tecoanapa. However, concerns over the land expropriation process and a lack of agreements with local communities drove Sheinbaum to cancel the project.

Sheinbaum’s water strategy for Acapulco includes three radial wells along the Papagayo River, the rehabilitation of aqueducts, the repair of the pumping system, the construction of elevated tanks and the replacement of leaking water lines.

The works were initially included in the January 2025 federal program “Acapulco Transforms with You,” established in response to the damage caused by Hurricanes Otis and John.

The radial wells are being built on tall towers — high enough to keep them safe from flood waters — and will draw from the Papagayo River through underground collection systems.

In addition, Sheinbaum said, the government will replace drinking water lines in the upper part of Acapulco, starting in the neighborhood of Renacimiento.

Cleanup work is now underway in the Papagayo River, and dredging is taking place to remove sediment and increase the capacity of the riverbeds.

The aim is to reduce obstructions and reduce the flood risk during heavy rainfall as part of Acapulco’s reconstruction and adaptation efforts following the two severe hurricanes.

Residents of towns bordering the river have voiced their concern that the water works will directly serve beachfront Acapulco, instead of increasing their supply.

With reports from El Imparcial, Expansión Política and Infobae

World.title: Vivo Brazil Profit Hits US$308M on Mobile, Fiber Growth
World.content:
Brazil · Business

Vivo Brazil earnings for the second quarter of 2026 showed a 17.0% jump in net profit, as Telefônica Brasil (B3: VIVT3), the country’s largest telecom operator, reported net income of R$1.57 billion (~US$308 million). The result, released on July 27, was in line with market expectations and marked the strongest EBITDA growth since the third quarter of 2023.

Key Facts —Net Profit. R$1.57 billion (~US$308 million), up 17.0% year-on-year in Q2 2026. —Operating Revenue. R$15.76 billion (~US$3.09 billion), a 7.6% increase from the prior year. —EBITDA. R$6.58 billion (~US$1.29 billion), rising 10.9% YoY with a 41.8% margin. —Growth Drivers. Mobile postpaid services, FTTH (fiber-to-the-home), and digital services. —Electronics Push. Appliance and electronics revenue jumped 27.8% to R$1.048 billion (~US$205 million), advancing Vivo’s move into consumer-electronics retail. Revenue and Profitability Drivers

Net operating revenue for Brazil‘s top carrier climbed 7.6% year-on-year to R$15.76 billion (~US$3.09 billion). The expansion was primarily fueled by its mobile postpaid segment, fiber-to-the-home (FTTH) broadband service, and a growing portfolio of digital services.

Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) reached R$6.58 billion (~US$1.29 billion). This 10.9% increase from the R$5.93 billion (~US$1.16 billion) recorded a year earlier pushed the EBITDA margin to a robust 41.8%.

For readers unfamiliar with the term, EBITDA is a widely used measure of a company’s core operating profitability. It strips out costs that can vary significantly depending on a firm’s debt structure, tax situation, and accounting choices around large asset purchases. A rising EBITDA margin, such as the one Vivo just posted, often signals that a business is gaining operating leverage — meaning each additional real of revenue is generating proportionally more profit. In Brazil’s high-volume, infrastructure-heavy telecom sector, this metric is closely watched because building and maintaining networks requires enormous upfront capital, and investors want to see those investments translate into efficient, recurring cash generation.

The Push into Consumer Electronics Retail

Beyond connectivity, Vivo is expanding into consumer-electronics retail – and it is already showing up in the numbers. Revenue from appliances and electronics jumped 27.8% year over year to R$1.048 billion (~US$205 million) in the quarter.

By selling devices through its large store network and digital channels, the carrier competes more directly with traditional retailers and captures higher-margin hardware sales alongside recurring service fees – a diversification foreign investors are watching closely.

This strategy mirrors a broader global trend among telecom operators seeking to become more than simple connectivity providers. By controlling the point of sale for smartphones, laptops, and smart-home devices, a carrier can bundle hardware with long-term service contracts, potentially reducing customer churn. In Brazil, where a significant portion of the population still buys electronics through installment plans, a trusted carrier with an existing billing relationship can position itself as a natural financing partner. The open question is whether Vivo can scale this retail push without the inventory risk and thin margins that typically challenge dedicated electronics chains.

Market Position: Vivo vs. TIM and Claro

Vivo operates as the market leader in Brazil’s competitive telecom sector, which is dominated by three major players. Its main rivals are TIM Brasil and Claro, the local subsidiary of Mexican telecom group América Móvil.

The company’s scale in mobile postpaid and fiber broadband provides a defensive moat. While all three carriers compete aggressively on 5G expansion, Vivo’s latest results underscore its ability to grow profitability while maintaining its number-one market share.

For context, Brazil’s telecom market is structured around a national regulatory framework overseen by Anatel, the country’s telecommunications agency. The three-way rivalry among Vivo, TIM, and Claro has shaped pricing and investment cycles for years. Postpaid mobile customers — those who pay a monthly bill rather than topping up prepaid credit — are particularly valuable because they generate more predictable revenue and tend to consume more data. Fiber-to-the-home broadband, meanwhile, has become a key battleground as millions of Brazilian households upgrade from older copper-based connections. Vivo’s ability to lead in both categories simultaneously is a central reason its financial results have drawn consistent attention from analysts covering Latin American equities.

Shareholder Returns and Capital Allocation

Telefônica Brasil has a well-established policy of distributing earnings to shareholders through dividends and interest on equity (JCP). The company continued this practice in the second quarter, though the exact per-share payout amount for the period was not specified in the initial earnings summary.

For expats and foreign investors holding VIVT3 shares on the B3 exchange, these regular distributions form a key part of the stock’s total return profile. The company’s free cash flow generation supports these payouts, even as it invests in network expansion.

Interest on equity, or JCP, is a Brazil-specific mechanism that allows companies to treat a portion of shareholder distributions as a tax-deductible expense, making it a tax-efficient way to return capital. For international investors, understanding the interplay between dividends and JCP is important because the tax treatment can differ depending on one’s country of residence and whether a double-taxation treaty applies. What remains to be seen is how Vivo will balance its capital allocation priorities going forward — specifically, whether the accelerating push into electronics retail will require heavier inventory investment that could temporarily pressure the free cash flow available for shareholder returns.

What It Means for Foreign Investors

For international readers, the results demonstrate the resilience of Brazil’s large consumer market. A net profit of ~US$308 million in a single quarter reflects the scale opportunity in Latin America’s biggest economy, where demand for premium data services continues to rise.

The US dollar figures, converted at a rate of 5.1 reais, offer a clear lens for portfolio evaluation. Vivo’s push into device retail adds a new growth vector, though execution risk remains a factor to monitor in future earnings calls.

Currency volatility is a permanent consideration when evaluating Brazilian equities. The real has historically swung widely against the dollar, meaning that even strong local-currency results can translate into uneven returns for foreign portfolios. Beyond the exchange rate, investors will likely be watching two broader themes. First, whether Brazil’s macroeconomic environment — including the trajectory of interest rates set by the central bank — supports continued consumer spending on telecom and electronics. Second, how the competitive dynamics with TIM and Claro evolve as all three players deepen their fiber and 5G footprints. These factors will help determine whether Vivo’s current margin strength proves durable or faces compression in the quarters ahead.

World.title: TIM Brazil Profit Hits Record US$203M on Fiber, Mobile
World.content:
Brazil · Business

TIM Brazil earnings reached a historic high in the second quarter of 2026, as one of the country’s largest wireless carriers reported a normalized net profit of R$1.036 billion (~US$203 million), a 6.2% increase from a year earlier and its strongest-ever result for a second quarter.

Key Facts —Record Net Profit. TIM Brasil’s normalized net profit reached R$1.036 billion (~US$203 million) in Q2 2026, up 6.2% year over year – its best-ever second quarter. —Net Revenue. Net revenue rose 5.5% to R$6.965 billion (~US$1.366 billion), led by mobile service revenue and fast-growing fiber broadband. —EBITDA & Margin. Normalized EBITDA climbed about 7% to roughly R$3.5 billion (~US$686 million), lifting the margin to 51.5%. —Shareholder Payout. The board approved R$400 million (~US$78 million) in interest on equity (JCP) for the quarter; 2026 remuneration guidance is R$5.3-5.5 billion (~US$1.04-1.08 billion). —Reported. Results were released on July 27, 2026. TIM (B3: TIMS3) is controlled by Italy’s Telecom Italia.
