World.title: Three-way deathmatch unearthed at 100-million-year-old 'crime scene'
World.content:
A prehistoric "crime scene" involving a marine reptile eating one of its flying cousins before being killed by the "T-rex of the ocean" has been uncovered in outback Queensland.

The 100-million-year-old bones of an ichthyosaur, pterosaur and kronosaurus were discovered in the state's fossil-rich north-west, which was once the formidable Eromanga Sea.

University of New England associate researcher Matt White, who had a leading role in the discovery reported this week in the Gondwana Research journal, said it was one of only a handful of palaeontological finds showing an interaction between three different species.

Palentologist Dr Matt White is the lead researcher for the three fossil discovery in Richmond. (Supplied: Dr Matt White)

"It is an extraordinary find … it will attract scientists from all over the world," he said.

Dr White also said the more-than 30 bite marks could be the most recorded in any marine fossil.

Travellers Mick and Cathy Freeman stumbled upon the first of the remains — a six to seven metre ichthyosaur, affectionately named "BOB", for "bag of bones" — in 2019.

The skull of the icthyosaur being uncovered in outback Queensland. (Supplied: Matt White)

The long-extinct marine reptile was "dolphin-like" and grew up to 3 metres in length.

Dr White said the importance of the find was unknown at the time, but three years later, Kevin Petersen, then the curator of Richmond's Kronosaurus Korner museum, began unearthing the "murder scene".

"When we had a closer look at it, all the vertebrae and bones in and around the trunk region of this ichthyosaur were shattered, but they had so many tooth and bite marks in it that I hadn't seen before," Dr White said.

"We had the skull and the tail preserved, but that whole midsection was just ravaged by a large predator."

Kevin Petersen (left) worked to unearth the find with Matt White. (Supplied: Matt White)

He said there could only be one perpetrator of such violence in that time and place.

"The only one that was capable of basically ripping into a carcass like that in that area was a kronosaurus," Dr White said.

The marine reptile could grow up to 14 metres in length and had more than 100 sharp teeth that could easily tear through smaller prey.

Kronosaurus Korner museum, formerly curated by kevin Petersen. (Supplied: Paul Stumkat)

"They're quite a formidable animal — basically the T-rex of the ocean," Dr White said.

But there was even more to the "unbelievable find".

"Some of the actual ichthyosaur's stomach remains were preserved, and this is also a world-first," Dr White said.

"It had pterosaur remains in its stomach … the first documented case."

Some pterosaurs had a wingspan of up to 12 metres.

100-million-year-old cold case

Dr White said the details of precisely what had happened had to be filled in by the imagination, but the fossils painted a picture of a gruesome attack by a top ocean predator.

"[It is] a marine reptile crime scene and it did take a bit of working out to tell that story," he said.

"But did the actual kronosaurus leap out of the water and smash the ichthyosaur? Or was the ichthyosaur breaching the water and snatching a pterosaur out of mid-air to eat?

"[We just know] this is what's happened to the fossil, and what happened in the exact term of events we don't know, but that's half the exciting thing of palaeontology."

The "BOB" discovery was sectioned into blocks and transferred to the museum in Richmond. (Supplied: Matt White)

British palaeontologist Dean Lomax, who was not involved in the research, saw the discovery during a recent visit to Australia.

"It's one of the clearest examples ever discovered of a three-tier predator interaction and offers an unprecedented snapshot of behaviour in Australia's Cretaceous seas," he said.

"This extraordinary fossil records a trophic interaction between a pterosaur eaten by an ichthyosaur that was then partly consumed by a giant pliosaur.

"It gives us direct evidence of behaviour in the Eromanga Sea."

Dean Lomax recently inspected the discovery in Richmond. (Supplied: Dean Lomax)

Dr Lomax is recognised for his work studying ichthyosaurs and travelled across Queensland for a National Dinosaur Day initiative.

He said Queensland's fossil discoveries were globally significant because many species found in the region did not exist anywhere else.

World.title: Mural paints story of community's hope of turning tide on crime
World.content:
A masked police officer armed with a spray can aims the nozzle and squirts ochre-toned paint onto the shop wall; beside him, a teenage girl aims her can and sprays.

It is a scene that community elders and leaders hope will help turn the tide on crime for the 13,500 residents of Port Augusta, about 300 kilometres north-west of Adelaide, at the top of Spencer Gulf in South Australia.

Loading...

The pair helped paint a 65-metre-long artwork which was the brainchild of three police officers wanting to reduce crime and improve relationships with Aboriginal youth.

About 30 teenagers were involved over the stages of the mural, called This Place Is Us, Our Voice, Our Story, Our Way, covering 200 square metres of the back wall of a business.

The project was funded by the Port Augusta and Davenport Community Alliance, which is a three-year, $12 million joint federal and state government initiative launched in late 2024 to create a community-led road map towards a safer and more connected community.

The alliance includes traditional owners, elders, Aboriginal community-controlled organisations, young people and community service agencies, police and business representatives.

The mural features striking portraits and symbols of culture, youth and place. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jodie Hamilton)

Social issues

It was created to tackle social issues including a high crime rate compared to other regional centres.

There were 336 criminal offences recorded by police in Port Augusta and Port Augusta West in May this year, including 104 assault or harm-related charges.

OpenStats lists the 2022/2024 number of break-ins in Port Augusta at 709.8 per cent higher than the state average, and 552.4 per cent higher than the national average.

Juvenile offending

Far North Region Police Superintendent Paul Isherwood praised the community for the mural project and said juvenile offending was a major cause for concern in the town.

"Any relationship we can build with young people is important and we work very hard on that engagement," he said.

Scott Rathman was passionate about young people having their say in the mural project. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jodie Hamilton)

"It's not just about police being law enforcers, it's about them being community members, and continually trying to improve outcomes for everyone, living, working or passing through Port Augusta."

The seed for the mural was planted when Port Augusta Senior Community Constable Shirreen Jackson and a colleague, who has since died, noticed artist Scott Rathman painting another mural in the town.

"We thought let's do something for our kids, something that they can call their own and create themselves and basically look after," Senior Constable Jackson said.

Local SAPOL officers joined the teens on painting day in May.

"It was great to be able to have [police officers] involved, and that was the initial plan at the beginning," Senior Constable Jackson said.

Youth participant Ciara said the mural connected the knowledge of older generations to young people.

The mural project was the idea of Senior Community Constable Shirreen Jackson (second from right) and another colleague. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jodie Hamilton)

"It's really good we got the opportunity to put our own little piece into the community and to show what the younger generations are capable of," she said.

Fellow participant Romin said: "You just have to feel proud about it, you helped paint it, and you're a part of it to help your community."

Lead artist and Eastern Arrernte man Scott Rathman said the symbolism and story were developed in partnership with the teens and showed the importance of elders and the knowledge they passed down through the generations.

"The main concept of the mural is this idea of the legacy cloak and that Aboriginal people carry their culture with them," Rathman said.

Police joined in the painting session to help build relationships with young people. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jodie Hamilton)

The mural included the illustration of a smoke trail, symbolising the sharing of stories through generations, weaving across the artwork, and flowing between striking portraits of a child, a young woman and an elder.

There were symbols about choices in life, guiding young people, and community connections, as well as place, including the Flinders Ranges and the iconic Port Augusta bridge.

"There are many pathways we can take as individuals," Rathman said.

"The bridge connects people and the outback to the sea; it's what brings people together.

"If we nurture our young people through whatever challenges they have and we find a way that they don't end up dealing with SAPOL … or whatever, then they can become really powerful members of our community."

Superintendent Isherwood said the mural showed Port Augusta people were linked through community, culture and country.

"It's huge, and it's fabulous," he said.

The Port Augusta mural was a celebration of the community coming together to work on social issues and a common path forward. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jodie Hamilton)

A spokesperson for the Department of Human Services said the alliance placed the community in the driver's seat and brought people and organisations together to support local priorities, in line with Closing the Gap.

"Since forming in late 2024, the alliance has supported 14 community initiatives, including Mangrove Court, the Education and Wellbeing Hub, Operation Flinders on Adnyamathanha Country, and Return to Country, which has helped more than 545 people get home safely," they said.

"Projects like this give young people pride and a real stake in their community, along with the chance to build confidence and skills working alongside artists, elders and local police."

World.title: 'Not good enough': Dense breasts halting life-saving cancer diagnoses
World.content:
When Kate Clark's breast started leaking fluid, which she says was the colour of Fanta, she knew there was something wrong with her body.

She booked in for a mammogram and ultrasound in Canberra, and although both those tests came back negative for breast cancer, she felt she knew her body better.

Looking for answers, she went to a specialist, who sent her for an MRI.

"I'd had a mammogram and an ultrasound, and both had come back clear," Ms Clark said.

"[But] because of my leaking nipple, I didn't want to just leave it there."

Kate Clarke says if she had not pursued further testing she may have died of breast cancer. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

And her suspicion was vindicated when the MRI of her breasts "lit up like a Christmas tree", she said.

Then, in July 2024, she received the diagnosis that she feared: she had breast cancer. And by that time, it was found that the cancer had spread to her lymph nodes.

Because of Ms Clark's dense breasts, the original scans had come back without any signs that something was amiss.

"Had I not pursued it further, I could be in a much worse place now and perhaps not even be here," she said.

She is not alone.

Dense breasts a breast cancer risk factor

High breast density makes breast cancer harder to detect through routine mammograms and is a risk factor for developing breast cancer.

Breast density refers to the amount of fibrous and glandular tissue versus the amount of fatty tissue, and around 40 per cent of women in Australia fall into the category.

Cancer, represented by the white dot here, is harder to spot on mammograms of denser breasts. (ABC NEWS)

BreastScreen Australia, the national screening program funded by federal and state governments, provides free mammograms but previously had a policy of not recording or reporting patients' breast density.

In November 2024, BreastScreen Australia updated its national position to recommend that everyone screened be informed in writing of their breast density, and to encourage patients to have further discussions with their GP about additional screening options.

But despite the policy change, only BreastScreen services in New South Wales, Victoria, South Australia and Western Australia measure and report breast density.

Vicki Durston, the director of policy at Breast Cancer Network Australia, believes it is vitally important for people to be aware of their breast density.

She said that, despite the national position, some states and territories had been slow to implement measures to assess breast density status.

Breast Cancer Network Australia's Vicki Durston says it is essential that people are aware of their breast density. (ABC News: Patrick Rocca)

"We know that breast density is a risk factor for breast cancer, and we certainly know that approximately 40 per cent of women are at risk of high breast density," she said.

" So it's vitally important that women are notified of their status in order to know their risk. "

In the ACT, despite a commitment to the implementation a year ago, its local chapter of BreastScreen Australia, Breast Screen ACT, does not record breast density.

Policy recommending that breast density be reported also covers non-government-run imaging services, such as the ones Ms Clark used.

"This was a national position statement put out in 2024, and yet in the ACT and a number of other states, 20 months on, we are still waiting to see the prioritisation of this implementation," Ms Durston said.

'I burst into tears'

A typo in the email sent to Kate Clarke incorrectly informed her suspicious abnormalities had been detected in her breast scan. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Unfortunately for Ms Clark, the medical misdiagnoses did not stop at her first mammogram, which failed to show up cancer, or at the ultrasound that followed, but also at her first yearly check-up, while recovering from cancer.

She was on holiday with her family when she was emailed the results of another test.

"It said suspicious abnormalities found," she said.

" I read that, and straight away I burst into tears and went through [the results] with my husband. I couldn't quite believe it. "

After waiting for the Canberra imaging clinic to open, she was told the clinic had made a typo, and her scan was actually clear.

"Sure enough, they came back to me and said … it should have said no … and they amended the report," she said.

Kate Clark says she thinks the ACT government is letting down the community by not yet implementing breast density testing. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Ms Clark wants to use her experiences to warn other women of the potential dangers of dense breasts, and the possibilities of unreliable medical imaging.

She said she was disappointed to hear the ACT government had still yet to implement dense breast testing.

"I feel that it's not good enough … I think they are letting all of us women down by not implementing it," she said.

" Should they decide to implement it, it would be life-changing for so many. "

The ACT government said in a statement that assistive technology to support breast density reporting would be available in the first half of next year.

A Canberra Health Services spokesperson said plans to introduce breast density reporting following mammograms were in progress; however, they required significant technical upgrades.

"BreastScreen ACT is committed to introducing these changes responsibly and sustainably," the spokesperson said.

World.title: Search for missing baby to resume off SA coast amid community 'shock'
World.content:
A search for a missing three-month-old in South Australia's South East will today enter its third day, after the state's premier described the deaths of the boy's mother and sister as tragedies "that shock you to the core".

Dangerous weather conditions forced police to suspend the search near Port MacDonnell, at the south-eastern tip of the state, yesterday afternoon with no sign of the missing baby boy.

Police have conceded it is "very, very unlikely" he has survived, but have vowed to leave "no stone unturned".

SES volunteers have been heavily involved in the search. (ABC News)

The bodies of the boy's 23-month-old sister and 36-year-old mother, from Compton near Mount Gambier, were spotted in the water on Monday.

The alarm was raised that morning, when emergency services were called to a car park at the nearby headland of Cape Northumberland.

Police said the woman's car — a white Isuzu MU-X, with South Australian registration S592 BJR — was found "abandoned with its engine running", and the bodies of the woman and her daughter were later recovered.

The area is known for its rugged landscapes. (ABC News: Guido Salazar)

The circumstances have caused distress and grief within the South East, but also throughout the state.

"These types of tragedies are the ones that shock you to the core. There are a lot of unanswered questions here," South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas said on Tuesday.

"Wherever we see the loss of anybody, it's a tragedy. Where it involves children, that breaks your heart."

Mayor of the Southern Limestone Coast Council, Kylie Boston, said the community's thoughts were with the family.

Kylie Boston says the community is stunned. (ABC News: Guido Salazar)

"Everybody is just kind of stunned because you hope these things don't ever happen and it's just sad that something like this has happened," she said.

"Regional communities are really resilient, and we'll get behind everybody and support everybody.

"That's all we can all do."

Port MacDonnell post office manager Linda Driver said the region was "close knit", and she praised the efforts of local volunteers who had joined the search.

"Kudos to the community — the boys will always put their boats in, they'll always go out and have a look," she said.

"It's something that hits the whole town … [and] it does hit everything really hard.

"It's a ripple effect of what happens within the community, so everybody's going to be looking out for each other in the next few weeks."

Linda Driver says the community has been "hit hard". (ABC South East SA: Sam Bradbrook)

On Tuesday afternoon, local police said search teams would gather at first light on Wednesday and estimated the search would resume about 8am.

"We'll hold a briefing for our emergency services personnel and volunteers who are assisting, as well as the police," Superintendent Trent Cox said.

"The forecast is that it's not as extreme as today — still challenging. It's an exposed area."

Police said strong winds meant that yesterday's search, even before it was suspended, was confined to land.

The premier yesterday cautioned the public not to jump to conclusions about the circumstances of the case, which Superintendent Cox said remained under investigation.

"We are keeping a very open mind as to the circumstances that led to the mother and daughter being in the water, and the other child being missing," he said.

"There are a number of scenarios we're investigating."

Police have said there is nothing to suggest "any other persons are involved in the incident".

World.title: Victorian Labor leadership LIVE: Premier Ben Carroll mulls cabinet appointments following Jacinta Allan’s resignation

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson is confident Labor’s new commitment to calling a royal commission into corruption on Big Build construction sites will not undermine the Liberal’s prospects at the upcoming election.

Until Ben Carroll became premier on Monday and pledged to call a royal commission, it was a key differentiator between the major parties.

Opposition Leader Jess Wilson. Luis Enrique Ascui

World.title: Grenades, military-grade weapons seized from alleged Sydney safehouse
World.content:
NationalNSWCrime Grenades, military-grade weapons seized from alleged Sydney safehouse Daniel Lo Surdo July 29, 2026 — 7:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Grenades, military-grade weapons, more than 1000 rounds of ammunition and $3 million worth of drugs were uncovered in an alleged Sydney safehouse when the state’s anti-gang detectives raided the suburban property on Tuesday, raising renewed concerns about the spread of firearms in the city months after gun reforms passed the parliament. Taskforce Falcon detectives raided the Glenfield property on Tuesday morning, where they discovered six grenades, three semi-automatic weapons, four shotguns and a pistol. Six kilograms of cocaine, 15 kilograms of cannabis, 1.1 kilograms of heroin, 107 grams of MDMA, a kilogram of ketamine and $9000 in cash were also seized. Loading A 26-year-old man, dressed in black track pants and T-shirt, was led from the property in handcuffs, clutching a gold vape in his hand, before being taken to Campbelltown Police Station in a police truck. He was charged with a range of offences, including possessing a dangerous weapon with intent to injure, possessing more than three unregistered firearms without a licence, three counts of supplying a drug greater than a commercial quantity, and knowingly deal with proceeds of crime. The man was refused bail to appear at Campbelltown Local Court on Wednesday.



Several firearms and gun parts were discovered in a black duffle bag hidden in the alleged safehouse. NSW Police A 26-year-old woman, led from the alleged safehouse by a plain-clothed police officer, was charged with organising, conducting and assisting at a drug premises, and was bailed ahead of a court appearance in Campbelltown next month. NSW Police Minister Yasmin Catley said it was “awful to think what could have happened” if detectives failed to seize the weapons from the alleged safehouse. “We do not want to see these weapons in our communities and thanks to the hard work of police, they are now out of the hands of criminals,” Catley said. “To anyone thinking of taking part in this alleged vicious criminality, our message is: be prepared to spend a long time in a small cell.”



Three grenades were found at the property. NSW Police The state government rushed through gun reforms on Christmas Eve last year, less than two weeks after gunmen shot dead 15 people celebrating Hanukkah at Bondi Beach. The new laws implemented new limits on the number of firearms an individual can own – four, or 10 for farmers and sporting shooters – and also sought to strengthen firearms licence checks and oversight mechanisms. Assistant Commissioner Scott Cook, State Crime Commander, said the grenades and firearms discovered in the raid on the Glenfield property “have no place in suburban Sydney”. “The fact these items were located inside an alleged safehouse shows the level of violence these groups are prepared to engage in, and the level of risk they pose to the public,” Cook said.



“We will continue to target these networks relentlessly.” Taskforce Falcon was launched by NSW Police in May last year to crush simmering gangland conflicts across the city’s streets. World.title: FIFA president’s plan to sell World Cup stake met with fury
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesMergers & acquisitions FIFA president’s plan to sell World Cup stake met with fury Graham Dunbar July 29, 2026 — 7:12am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

FIFA President Gianni Infantino’s plan to create a $US20 billion ($28.7 billion) company running the World Cup with private investors including the Kushner family was announced — and immediately attacked by European soccer body UEFA. “It is not FIFA’s to sell,” UEFA said in a statement. “None of us are the owners of football.” The men’s World Cup that finished this month only deepened the political and personal ties between Trump and Infantino, and fuelled concerns about those ties including from UEFA. Getty Infantino’s plans to form a commercial subsidiary, which would be called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), running competitions like the World Cup and Club World Cup was first reported by The Times of London. FIFA said in a statement FFE would raise up to $US4.2 billion later this year to help fund development programs “based on an initial equity valuation of $US20 billion by carefully selecting long-term investors who will purchase minority, non-controlling interests.”



Related Article Trump's White House ‘I don’t have inside information’: How Donald Trump Jr is cashing in on dad’s presidency FIFA is working with JP Morgan while intended investors include Thrive Eternal launched by Joshua Kushner, whose brother Jared Kushner is a son-in-law of US President Donald Trump. The men’s World Cup that finished this month only deepened the political and personal ties between Trump and Infantino, and fuelled concerns about those ties including from UEFA. “The soul and governance of football are not assets to trade — especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially,” UEFA said, responding to the reports of selling stakes in FIFA competitions. FIFA is currently a Swiss-based not-for-profit association of its 211 national member federations worldwide.



Those members must approve any plan and would get the chance “to access up to $US20 million in one-off capital,” FIFA said. “This is about the democratisation of football worldwide,” Infantino said in a FIFA statement, which added that “a consultation process has begun.” The proposal deepens the divide between Switzerland-based FIFA and European soccer’s governing body UEFA, with Europe positioning itself as the custodian of the game while FIFA, a not-for-profit organisation, remains focused on broadening access with financial largesse. Getty Images UEFA, however, said it took reports of the project “extremely seriously. So should every national Football Association.” “This crosses a line that football’s governing institutions should never cross,” said UEFA, which comprises 55 of the FIFA members.



Britain’s new Prime Minister Andy Burnham joined critics of the plan, saying on social media that the sport does not belong to investors. “The World Cup is not a product. It is the greatest competition in world sport, and it was never anyone’s to sell,” Burnham wrote on X. “Dress the deal up however you like. Once you have sold a piece of it, you have sold out.” View post on X The outline of Tuesday’s surprise announcement was, FIFA said, detailed by Infantino to members who met in Manhattan on July 18 ahead of the World Cup final. There, Infantino promised to “unleash the commercial potential and opportunity that FIFA has.” FIFA’s statement about its proposed project led on how much money each of its 211 members could get through 2038 in the “FIFA Fast-Forward Program.”



Instead of the currently promised $US8 million each in development funds through the 2027-30 World Cup commercial cycle, it would be $US20 million, then $US22 million and $US24 million in the following cycles. FIFA banked record World Cup income of about $US12 billion from the 2026 tournament which had unprecedented high prices for tickets and hospitality across the US, Canada and Mexico. It already was unclear how that money could be matched from Spain, Portugal and Morocco co-hosting the 2030 men’s edition. A vehicle founded by Joshua Kushner, the brother of Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, is expected to be a lead investor in the enterprise, a source said. Bloomberg Member federations could choose if they wanted to take part in the new financial opportunities, FIFA said. “FIFA would retain sole control of FFE and exclusive authority over football governance, competitions, match calendar, and all regulatory and sporting decisions,” the soccer body said.



FIFA’s integrity standards were called into question during the World Cup, including by team coaches, Norway’s soccer federation and a top European public body, the Council of Europe. The project announced is the second time in Infantino’s increasingly controversial 11-year presidency he has tried to push through a multi-billion dollar deal with private backers. ‘The soul and governance of football are not assets to trade — especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially. None of us are the owners of football. It is not FIFA’s to sell.’ UEFA’s response to the plan In 2018, Infantino proposed a secretive $US25 billion offer over 12 years with SoftBank of Japan to create new global competitions, including an expanded men’s Club World Cup, seemingly backed by Saudi Arabian money. That ultimately failed after meeting fierce resistance from UEFA, which saw threats to its prize assets: the Champions League and the European Championship.



Infantino still built closer ties to Saudi soccer and the kingdom’s Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman. Saudi Arabia will host the 2034 World Cup and largely funded the revamped men’s Club World Cup hosted in the US last year. The financial success of the just-ended World Cup has looked likely to ensure Infantino is re-elected next year unopposed for a fourth and final term in office through 2031. At his re-election by acclaim in 2023 in Rwanda, Infantino suggested any CEO delivering similar financial results would be kept in the job forever. Speculation has swirled for years Infantino might want a different global role in soccer beyond his FIFA presidency, which is due to end when he is 61. The Times reported that a CEO-like commissioner role of the new FFE operation could be created for Infantino.

World.title: ASX set to rise ahead of inflation data, oil prices extend slide; Apple becomes a $US5tr company
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to rise ahead of inflation data, oil prices extend slide; Apple becomes a $US5tr company Stan Choe Updated July 29, 2026 — 6:28am ,first published 5:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Most of Wall Street rose, even as stocks of computer chipmakers continued to tumble worldwide. Oil prices, meanwhile, eased further from the two-month high they hit last week. The S&P 500 added 0.2 per cent, but the modest move masked big swings underneath the surface. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 537 points, or 1 per cent, while the Nasdaq composite slipped 0.2 per cent after briefly dropping 9.3 per cent below its record set last month. The slump in Wall Street’s AI stocks picked up pace on Tuesday. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures at 6.14am AEST pointing to a jump of 76 points, or 0.9 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.6 per cent on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was trading at US69.77¢. Inflation data is due out this morning. On Wall Street, Apple became just the second company ever to achieve a $US5 trillion ($7.2 trillion) market valuation.



Related Article Opinion

Property market Real estate agent’s viral posts show our property market angst Elizabeth Knight Business columnist The iPhone maker’s shares rose as much as 1.8 per cent to $US342.89 early in the session, pushing the company’s market capitalisation to above $US5 trillion for the first time before falling back below the mark as shares eased before closing at $US340.80. Nvidia closed at a record $US5.7 trillion on May 14, but it has since lost roughly $US1 trillion in valuation. Apple is now the biggest company in the S&P 500 Index. The majority of the US market rose after more companies delivered stronger profits for the spring than analysts expected. Coca-Cola climbed 5 per cent after its revenue rose 7 per cent despite what CEO Henrique Braun called “a dynamic consumer landscape.” Sherwin-Williams rallied 8.3 per cent, and Illinois Tool Works rose 3.6 per cent after both likewise reported stronger earnings for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Stock prices generally follow the trend of corporate profits over the long term, and expectations are high for this most recent round of reports with the US stock market still near its all-time high. Such expectations are weighing particularly heavily on stocks of chipmakers and other companies that have been huge winners from the boom in artificial-intelligence technology.



Micron Technology’s stock came into the day having more than tripled for the year following gangbuster growth, for example. During the three months through May 28, its revenue more than quadrupled from a year earlier. But worries are rising about whether such growth is sustainable. Big spenders on computer memory could pull back on investments if AI does not produce as much profit or productivity as promised. Lower-cost AI models from China could also mean less demand for memory and computing power than earlier expected. Micron dropped 8.9 per cent and was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. Others also helping to keep the market in check were Advanced Micro Devices, down 8.1 per cent, and Applied Materials, down 7.8 per cent. All told, the S&P 500 rose 15.60 points to 7,428.78. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 537.24 to 52,747.32, and the Nasdaq composite fell 55.17 to 24,876.91. The losses for chip stocks were even worse earlier in the day in other markets worldwide.



Sharp drops for SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics dragged South Korea’s Kospi index down 10.8 per cent. The market’s losses were so big that trading was temporarily halted at times in Seoul. “We believe the market was likely spooked by the progress of China’s chipmaking equipment capabilities, and was worried that this progress would threaten the competitive position of global chipmaking and chip equipment leaders,” said equity analyst Jing Jie Yu of Morningstar. “That said, we believe the sell-off today is largely a knee-jerk reaction and overdone,” he said. The dominant position of global chipmaking leaders is unlikely to be threatened meaningfully, he said. Several huge spenders on AI chips and data centres are scheduled to report their latest quarterly results this week, which could offer updates on how much they’re planning to invest. Meta Platforms and Microsoft are reporting on Thursday (AEST), while Amazon is due the following day. Because AI superstar stocks have grown so big, their movements carry more weight on the S&P 500 and other indexes than many other companies. But the broad US market could hold up despite their swings if other, less-loved areas are able to keep rising. It’s a rotation that some strategists have suggested could be healthy for the overall stock market.



In the oil market, the price for a barrel of Brent crude to be delivered in October fell 4.4 per cent to settle at $US82.08. It’s been falling since late last week, when the price for a barrel to be delivered in September briefly shot as high as $US102. Related Article Opinion

Global economy We might be sitting on a $2,600,000,000,000,000 bomb Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Pushing up on prices have been worries that worsening fighting in the Middle East could slow the global flow of oil. On the other side, though, are hopes that the United States and Iran could still negotiate something to allow oil tankers to use the Strait of Hormuz to move crude. Lower oil prices helped to ease Treasury yields in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.60 per cent from 4.65 per cent.



A weaker-than-expected reading on confidence among US consumers also weighed on yields. Fewer consumers are saying they feel good about current business conditions, according to the latest survey released by the Conference Board. The drop in oil prices helped push traders to trim their bets that the Federal Reserve could announce a hike to interest rates following its latest meeting on Wednesday. They’re forecasting a 31.5 per cent probability, down from more than 36 per cent a day before, according to data from CME Group. Higher rates could keep a lid on inflation, but they would also slow the economy by making it more expensive for US households and businesses to borrow. Long-term mortgage rates have already hit their highest level in nearly a year, chilling the housing industry. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: ‘Don’t need him to tell me that’: Trump rebukes Netanyahu as they meet on Iran
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaMiddle East at war ‘Don’t need him to tell me that’: Trump rebukes Netanyahu as they meet on Iran Michael Koziol Updated July 29, 2026 — 6:26am ,first published 3:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Donald Trump publicly rebuked Benjamin Netanyahu over plans for escalating the war in Iran as the two men met at the White House for the first time since the conflict commenced five months ago. The meeting came as the Israeli leader – and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky – visited Washington for the funeral of Republican senator Lindsey Graham, who was a staunch advocate for military aid to both countries. President Donald Trump, Vice President JD Vance and other dignitaries at the funeral of Lindsey Graham on Tuesday. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin At the White House, Netanyahu made an understated arrival using the West Wing’s side entrance, and his meeting with the US president and senior administration figures was closed to the media. But only a few hours earlier, Trump expressed frustration about reports that Netanyahu intended to present Israeli intelligence that Iran was fortifying Pickaxe Mountain – an underground nuclear site near its Natanz uranium enrichment facility.



“I don’t need Bibi to tell me that,” Trump told Fox News, using an affectionate term for the Israeli PM. “Bibi’s telling me that because he wants me to stay involved … We have the greatest cameras in the world focused on [Pickaxe Mountain], we know exactly what’s going on.” The New York Post reported on Tuesday (US time) that Netanyahu would use the visit to present evidence of ongoing Iranian nuclear activity and demonstrate that Tehran was not negotiating in good faith, citing a source in Jerusalem. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the funeral for Republican senator Lindsey Graham. AP Photo/Alex Brandon Netanyahu did not publicly declare what he intended to tell Trump, but the US president appeared to interpret the reporting as a statement from Netanyahu. “I heard Bibi announce that,” Trump told Fox News. “I said, ‘Why don’t you just tell it to me, why do you have to announce it to the world?’ I know exactly what’s going on at Pickaxe, it’s not a big problem.”



Trump repeated his threat to destroy the facility if a deal with the Iranians was not forthcoming. He also spoke about “competing factions” within the Republican Party, some of whom wanted him to escalate strikes and others who preferred a diplomatic solution. It was not clear whether Netanyahu actually presented Trump with intelligence about Pickaxe Mountain or any other Iranian nuclear site. The meeting lasted just over an hour. The meeting was closed to the media but the Israeli government distributed photos of the two leaders. Credit: Maayan Toaf / Israel Government Press Office Photographs from the meeting by the Israeli government showed Trump beaming, and there is no suggestion of a blow-up between the two leaders. But the president’s willingness to publicly push back on Netanyahu is indicative of a relationship that is more strained than before the war. Trump’s observation that Netanyahu “wants me to stay involved” – or seeks to prolong the war – is also a candid admission of the prevailing dynamic between the two leaders.



The Israeli prime minister is primarily in Washington for the funeral of Graham, who died suddenly this month at 71 from what medical reports said was an aortic tear. The long-serving senator was a close friend of Israel and Ukraine, and a cheerleader for US military intervention in Iran and elsewhere. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky also travelled to Washington for the funeral, and held a similarly private White House meeting with Trump just an hour before Netanyahu. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky meets with US President Donald Trump in the Oval Office. @ZelenskyyUa Zelenksy said it was a good meeting that included discussion about US plans to allow Ukraine to licence production of Patriot missile interceptors, “and several other ideas that could help” in the war against Russia. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said both meetings were “positive and productive”.



On Monday night, after arriving from Israel, Netanyahu and his wife, Sara, attended a private memorial dinner with Graham’s family, friends and several Trump administration officials at the Four Seasons Hotel in Washington. “America has lost a great patriot. Israel has lost one of its greatest friends and supporters. And I have lost a dear friend,” Netanyahu told the gathering, according to his office. Benjamin Netanyahu with US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth at the funeral for Lindsey Graham. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin Graham’s flag-draped casket is carried down the steps of the US Capitol. AP Photo/Mariam Zuhaib US news site Axios reported the dinner was hosted by Lebanese banker and film producer Antoun Sehnaoui and Trump’s former deputy Middle East envoy Morgan Ortagus.



Other attendees included Meta president Dina Powell McCormick, Trump aide Stephen Miller and his wife Katie, and a slew of Republican and Democratic senators – among them Darline Graham, who has taken her late brother’s Senate seat. Dozens of high-ranking dignitaries attended Tuesday’s funeral service at the Washington National Cathedral, including cabinet secretaries, top White House aides and members of Congress. They remembered a man whom Trump praised as “a giant of the Senate”. President Donald Trump delivering a eulogy for Republican senator Lindsey Graham, who died unexpectedly this month. Alex Brandon/AP Pool via AP News Corp and Fox chairman Lachlan Murdoch attended, as did former vice president Mike Pence and Fox News host Sean Hannity, who, like Trump, delivered a eulogy. The program featured contrasting messages about Graham, a well-known foreign policy hawk who urged Trump to attack Iran. “He was extremely hawkish,” the president told mourners. “He never saw a war that he didn’t like.”



Earlier, Trump told Fox News: “Lindsey liked war. I said, ’You’re a nice guy, how come you like war so much? He was a guy that liked war.” Related Article Analysis

US politics Lindsey Graham, the ‘Three Amigos’ and the shifting politics of Israel But Hannity said the common portrayal of Graham as a warmonger was wrong. “The truth is the opposite,” he said. “Lindsey desperately wanted – and talked to the president about – lasting peace in the Middle East. He wanted every country in the region on that path to peace. That was Lindsey’s dream. “[But] Lindsey had moral clarity. He knew – as President Trump knows, as Israel knows, as I know – there can be no path to peace until evil is defeated.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Idi Amin’s boxer grandson vows to win gold and be ‘the new king of Scotland’
World.content:
SportBoxingCommonwealth Games Idi Amin’s boxer grandson vows to win gold and be ‘the new king of Scotland’ Hannah Kennelly July 29, 2026 — 5:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The boxer grandson of Idi Amin has vowed to become the “king of Scotland” by winning gold for Uganda at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. Aziz Abdul, a heavyweight boxer for Uganda, will take on Englishman Damar Thomas on Thursday morning (AEST). Former Ugandan dictator Idi Amin, who died in 2003, and his grandson Aziz Abdul, who is competing in Glasgow. AP/Instagram But he has grabbed attention before even stepping in the ring with his comments to media over the last couple of days. “My idol is Mike Tyson, the baddest man on the planet,” Abdul told media earlier this week. “If I win the gold medal, I will be the baddest man in the Commonwealth, the baddest man in Glasgow and the new king of Scotland.”



Related Article Commonwealth Games First shoes, now speed suits: Australia joins arms race to get an edge in athletics Abdul’s reference hearkens back to his late grandfather Amin, who was married six times and fathered around 60 children. Amin was nicknamed “the Butcher of Uganda” – but also proclaimed himself the king of Scotland in 1976. He had a fixation for the country, sparked by his time as a soldier in the British colonial army, and often wore kilts and played the bagpipes. Also a one-time heavyweight boxing champion, Amin seized power on January 25, 1971, overthrowing president Milton Obote while Obote was abroad. Human rights groups say as many as 500,000 people were killed during Amin’s eight-year rule over Uganda until he was forced out of the country in 1979. He was never tried for his crimes in an international court and died in Saudi Arabia in 2003. “My grandfather’s achievements inspired me,” said Abdul, whose nickname is Ringo. “He was a heavyweight boxer like me, and I am so proud of him. Now we are not in Africa, we are in Europe. As my grandpa used to say, you need to win by knockout, so that’s what we have trained for and that’s what I hope to do.



“I believe in myself and I mean what I say. When I say I will do it, I will do it. Let them not doubt me. I am aiming for the gold medal.” Related Article Commonwealth Games Australia won 15 medals in the pool, but this Scottish swimmer with terminal cancer stole the show In a later interview with BBC Scotland, Adbul would not respond when asked if he was proud to be the grandson of the dictator, who also forced the expulsion of Uganda’s entire Asian minority, and whose rule led to total economic collapse. But Abdul did address how it feels to be linked to someone with such a sinister reputation. “Sometimes people say positive about him, but others say negative about him,” Abdul said. “That’s why I don’t want to talk more about him. “It’s not good to say something negative about someone who is not there, and it’s not good to say something about someone negative who was not there by the time when the incident happened, if it happened.”



Related Article Live

Commonwealth Games Commonwealth Games LIVE: Kennedy smashes record to win silver in 100m; Southam gold leads medal rush at the pool Abdul is 25, and according to the BBC Scotland report never met his grandfather. In the ring, he said, his big weapon is the “Ringo punch”. “I am not going to tell you about it – I will show you on the day if the right time comes,” he said. “You will see what the Ringo punch looks like. The big boys are here now. “Lions give back to lions. A lion cannot give back to a dog or a camel. A lion must resemble a lion. It is what it is. I am a real warrior. I am the son of the son.”

Getty Infantino’s plans to form a commercial subsidiary, which would be called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), running competitions like the World Cup and Club World Cup was first reported by The Times of London. FIFA said in a statement FFE would raise up to $US4.2 billion later this year to help fund development programs “based on an initial equity valuation of $US20 billion by carefully selecting long-term investors who will purchase minority, non-controlling interests.”



Related Article Trump's White House ‘I don’t have inside information’: How Donald Trump Jr is cashing in on dad’s presidency FIFA is working with JP Morgan while intended investors include Thrive Eternal launched by Joshua Kushner, whose brother Jared Kushner is a son-in-law of US President Donald Trump. The men’s World Cup that finished this month only deepened the political and personal ties between Trump and Infantino, and fuelled concerns about those ties including from UEFA. “The soul and governance of football are not assets to trade — especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially,” UEFA said, responding to the reports of selling stakes in FIFA competitions. FIFA is currently a Swiss-based not-for-profit association of its 211 national member federations worldwide.



Those members must approve any plan and would get the chance “to access up to $US20 million in one-off capital,” FIFA said. “This is about the democratisation of football worldwide,” Infantino said in a FIFA statement, which added that “a consultation process has begun.” The proposal deepens the divide between Switzerland-based FIFA and European soccer’s governing body UEFA, with Europe positioning itself as the custodian of the game while FIFA, a not-for-profit organisation, remains focused on broadening access with financial largesse. Getty Images UEFA, however, said it took reports of the project “extremely seriously. So should every national Football Association.” “This crosses a line that football’s governing institutions should never cross,” said UEFA, which comprises 55 of the FIFA members.



Britain’s new Prime Minister Andy Burnham joined critics of the plan, saying on social media that the sport does not belong to investors. “The World Cup is not a product. It is the greatest competition in world sport, and it was never anyone’s to sell,” Burnham wrote on X. “Dress the deal up however you like. Once you have sold a piece of it, you have sold out.” View post on X The outline of Tuesday’s surprise announcement was, FIFA said, detailed by Infantino to members who met in Manhattan on July 18 ahead of the World Cup final. There, Infantino promised to “unleash the commercial potential and opportunity that FIFA has.” FIFA’s statement about its proposed project led on how much money each of its 211 members could get through 2038 in the “FIFA Fast-Forward Program.”



Instead of the currently promised $US8 million each in development funds through the 2027-30 World Cup commercial cycle, it would be $US20 million, then $US22 million and $US24 million in the following cycles. FIFA banked record World Cup income of about $US12 billion from the 2026 tournament which had unprecedented high prices for tickets and hospitality across the US, Canada and Mexico. It already was unclear how that money could be matched from Spain, Portugal and Morocco co-hosting the 2030 men’s edition. A vehicle founded by Joshua Kushner, the brother of Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, is expected to be a lead investor in the enterprise, a source said. Bloomberg Member federations could choose if they wanted to take part in the new financial opportunities, FIFA said. “FIFA would retain sole control of FFE and exclusive authority over football governance, competitions, match calendar, and all regulatory and sporting decisions,” the soccer body said.



FIFA’s integrity standards were called into question during the World Cup, including by team coaches, Norway’s soccer federation and a top European public body, the Council of Europe. The project announced is the second time in Infantino’s increasingly controversial 11-year presidency he has tried to push through a multi-billion dollar deal with private backers. ‘The soul and governance of football are not assets to trade — especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially. None of us are the owners of football. It is not FIFA’s to sell.’ UEFA’s response to the plan In 2018, Infantino proposed a secretive $US25 billion offer over 12 years with SoftBank of Japan to create new global competitions, including an expanded men’s Club World Cup, seemingly backed by Saudi Arabian money. That ultimately failed after meeting fierce resistance from UEFA, which saw threats to its prize assets: the Champions League and the European Championship.



Infantino still built closer ties to Saudi soccer and the kingdom’s Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman. Saudi Arabia will host the 2034 World Cup and largely funded the revamped men’s Club World Cup hosted in the US last year. The financial success of the just-ended World Cup has looked likely to ensure Infantino is re-elected next year unopposed for a fourth and final term in office through 2031. At his re-election by acclaim in 2023 in Rwanda, Infantino suggested any CEO delivering similar financial results would be kept in the job forever. Speculation has swirled for years Infantino might want a different global role in soccer beyond his FIFA presidency, which is due to end when he is 61. The Times reported that a CEO-like commissioner role of the new FFE operation could be created for Infantino.

World.title: ASX set to rise ahead of inflation data, oil prices extend slide; Apple becomes a $US5tr company
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX set to rise ahead of inflation data, oil prices extend slide; Apple becomes a $US5tr company Stan Choe Updated July 29, 2026 — 6:28am ,first published 5:25am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Most of Wall Street rose, even as stocks of computer chipmakers continued to tumble worldwide. Oil prices, meanwhile, eased further from the two-month high they hit last week. The S&P 500 added 0.2 per cent, but the modest move masked big swings underneath the surface. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 537 points, or 1 per cent, while the Nasdaq composite slipped 0.2 per cent after briefly dropping 9.3 per cent below its record set last month. The slump in Wall Street’s AI stocks picked up pace on Tuesday. AP The Australian sharemarket is set to rise, with futures at 6.14am AEST pointing to a jump of 76 points, or 0.9 per cent, at the open. The ASX added 0.6 per cent on Tuesday. The Australian dollar was trading at US69.77¢. Inflation data is due out this morning. On Wall Street, Apple became just the second company ever to achieve a $US5 trillion ($7.2 trillion) market valuation.



Related Article Opinion

Property market Real estate agent’s viral posts show our property market angst Elizabeth Knight Business columnist The iPhone maker’s shares rose as much as 1.8 per cent to $US342.89 early in the session, pushing the company’s market capitalisation to above $US5 trillion for the first time before falling back below the mark as shares eased before closing at $US340.80. Nvidia closed at a record $US5.7 trillion on May 14, but it has since lost roughly $US1 trillion in valuation. Apple is now the biggest company in the S&P 500 Index. The majority of the US market rose after more companies delivered stronger profits for the spring than analysts expected. Coca-Cola climbed 5 per cent after its revenue rose 7 per cent despite what CEO Henrique Braun called “a dynamic consumer landscape.” Sherwin-Williams rallied 8.3 per cent, and Illinois Tool Works rose 3.6 per cent after both likewise reported stronger earnings for the latest quarter than analysts expected. Stock prices generally follow the trend of corporate profits over the long term, and expectations are high for this most recent round of reports with the US stock market still near its all-time high. Such expectations are weighing particularly heavily on stocks of chipmakers and other companies that have been huge winners from the boom in artificial-intelligence technology.



Micron Technology’s stock came into the day having more than tripled for the year following gangbuster growth, for example. During the three months through May 28, its revenue more than quadrupled from a year earlier. But worries are rising about whether such growth is sustainable. Big spenders on computer memory could pull back on investments if AI does not produce as much profit or productivity as promised. Lower-cost AI models from China could also mean less demand for memory and computing power than earlier expected. Micron dropped 8.9 per cent and was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500. Others also helping to keep the market in check were Advanced Micro Devices, down 8.1 per cent, and Applied Materials, down 7.8 per cent. All told, the S&P 500 rose 15.60 points to 7,428.78. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 537.24 to 52,747.32, and the Nasdaq composite fell 55.17 to 24,876.91. The losses for chip stocks were even worse earlier in the day in other markets worldwide.



Sharp drops for SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics dragged South Korea’s Kospi index down 10.8 per cent. The market’s losses were so big that trading was temporarily halted at times in Seoul. “We believe the market was likely spooked by the progress of China’s chipmaking equipment capabilities, and was worried that this progress would threaten the competitive position of global chipmaking and chip equipment leaders,” said equity analyst Jing Jie Yu of Morningstar. “That said, we believe the sell-off today is largely a knee-jerk reaction and overdone,” he said. The dominant position of global chipmaking leaders is unlikely to be threatened meaningfully, he said. Several huge spenders on AI chips and data centres are scheduled to report their latest quarterly results this week, which could offer updates on how much they’re planning to invest. Meta Platforms and Microsoft are reporting on Thursday (AEST), while Amazon is due the following day. Because AI superstar stocks have grown so big, their movements carry more weight on the S&P 500 and other indexes than many other companies. But the broad US market could hold up despite their swings if other, less-loved areas are able to keep rising. It’s a rotation that some strategists have suggested could be healthy for the overall stock market.



In the oil market, the price for a barrel of Brent crude to be delivered in October fell 4.4 per cent to settle at $US82.08. It’s been falling since late last week, when the price for a barrel to be delivered in September briefly shot as high as $US102. Related Article Opinion

Global economy We might be sitting on a $2,600,000,000,000,000 bomb Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist Pushing up on prices have been worries that worsening fighting in the Middle East could slow the global flow of oil. On the other side, though, are hopes that the United States and Iran could still negotiate something to allow oil tankers to use the Strait of Hormuz to move crude. Lower oil prices helped to ease Treasury yields in the bond market. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.60 per cent from 4.65 per cent.



A weaker-than-expected reading on confidence among US consumers also weighed on yields. Fewer consumers are saying they feel good about current business conditions, according to the latest survey released by the Conference Board. The drop in oil prices helped push traders to trim their bets that the Federal Reserve could announce a hike to interest rates following its latest meeting on Wednesday. They’re forecasting a 31.5 per cent probability, down from more than 36 per cent a day before, according to data from CME Group. Higher rates could keep a lid on inflation, but they would also slow the economy by making it more expensive for US households and businesses to borrow. Long-term mortgage rates have already hit their highest level in nearly a year, chilling the housing industry. AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.
