World.title: ‘Don’t need him to tell me that’: Trump rebukes Netanyahu as they meet on Iran
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaMiddle East at war ‘Don’t need him to tell me that’: Trump rebukes Netanyahu as they meet on Iran Michael Koziol Updated July 29, 2026 — 6:26am ,first published 3:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Washington: Donald Trump publicly rebuked Benjamin Netanyahu over plans for escalating the war in Iran as the two men met at the White House for the first time since the conflict commenced five months ago. The meeting came as the Israeli leader – and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky – visited Washington for the funeral of Republican senator Lindsey Graham, who was a staunch advocate for military aid to both countries. President Donald Trump, Vice President JD Vance and other dignitaries at the funeral of Lindsey Graham on Tuesday. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin At the White House, Netanyahu made an understated arrival using the West Wing’s side entrance, and his meeting with the US president and senior administration figures was closed to the media. But only a few hours earlier, Trump expressed frustration about reports that Netanyahu intended to present Israeli intelligence that Iran was fortifying Pickaxe Mountain – an underground nuclear site near its Natanz uranium enrichment facility.



“I don’t need Bibi to tell me that,” Trump told Fox News, using an affectionate term for the Israeli PM. “Bibi’s telling me that because he wants me to stay involved … We have the greatest cameras in the world focused on [Pickaxe Mountain], we know exactly what’s going on.” The New York Post reported on Tuesday (US time) that Netanyahu would use the visit to present evidence of ongoing Iranian nuclear activity and demonstrate that Tehran was not negotiating in good faith, citing a source in Jerusalem. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the funeral for Republican senator Lindsey Graham. AP Photo/Alex Brandon Netanyahu did not publicly declare what he intended to tell Trump, but the US president appeared to interpret the reporting as a statement from Netanyahu. “I heard Bibi announce that,” Trump told Fox News. “I said, ‘Why don’t you just tell it to me, why do you have to announce it to the world?’ I know exactly what’s going on at Pickaxe, it’s not a big problem.”



Trump repeated his threat to destroy the facility if a deal with the Iranians was not forthcoming. He also spoke about “competing factions” within the Republican Party, some of whom wanted him to escalate strikes and others who preferred a diplomatic solution. It was not clear whether Netanyahu actually presented Trump with intelligence about Pickaxe Mountain or any other Iranian nuclear site. The meeting lasted just over an hour. The meeting was closed to the media but the Israeli government distributed photos of the two leaders. Credit: Maayan Toaf / Israel Government Press Office Photographs from the meeting by the Israeli government showed Trump beaming, and there is no suggestion of a blow-up between the two leaders. But the president’s willingness to publicly push back on Netanyahu is indicative of a relationship that is more strained than before the war. Trump’s observation that Netanyahu “wants me to stay involved” – or seeks to prolong the war – is also a candid admission of the prevailing dynamic between the two leaders.



The Israeli prime minister is primarily in Washington for the funeral of Graham, who died suddenly this month at 71 from what medical reports said was an aortic tear. The long-serving senator was a close friend of Israel and Ukraine, and a cheerleader for US military intervention in Iran and elsewhere. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky also travelled to Washington for the funeral, and held a similarly private White House meeting with Trump just an hour before Netanyahu. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky meets with US President Donald Trump in the Oval Office. @ZelenskyyUa Zelenksy said it was a good meeting that included discussion about US plans to allow Ukraine to licence production of Patriot missile interceptors, “and several other ideas that could help” in the war against Russia. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said both meetings were “positive and productive”.



On Monday night, after arriving from Israel, Netanyahu and his wife, Sara, attended a private memorial dinner with Graham’s family, friends and several Trump administration officials at the Four Seasons Hotel in Washington. “America has lost a great patriot. Israel has lost one of its greatest friends and supporters. And I have lost a dear friend,” Netanyahu told the gathering, according to his office. Benjamin Netanyahu with US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth at the funeral for Lindsey Graham. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin Graham’s flag-draped casket is carried down the steps of the US Capitol. AP Photo/Mariam Zuhaib US news site Axios reported the dinner was hosted by Lebanese banker and film producer Antoun Sehnaoui and Trump’s former deputy Middle East envoy Morgan Ortagus.



Other attendees included Meta president Dina Powell McCormick, Trump aide Stephen Miller and his wife Katie, and a slew of Republican and Democratic senators – among them Darline Graham, who has taken her late brother’s Senate seat. Dozens of high-ranking dignitaries attended Tuesday’s funeral service at the Washington National Cathedral, including cabinet secretaries, top White House aides and members of Congress. They remembered a man whom Trump praised as “a giant of the Senate”. President Donald Trump delivering a eulogy for Republican senator Lindsey Graham, who died unexpectedly this month. Alex Brandon/AP Pool via AP News Corp and Fox chairman Lachlan Murdoch attended, as did former vice president Mike Pence and Fox News host Sean Hannity, who, like Trump, delivered a eulogy. The program featured contrasting messages about Graham, a well-known foreign policy hawk who urged Trump to attack Iran. “He was extremely hawkish,” the president told mourners. “He never saw a war that he didn’t like.”



Earlier, Trump told Fox News: “Lindsey liked war. I said, ’You’re a nice guy, how come you like war so much? He was a guy that liked war.” Related Article Analysis

US politics Lindsey Graham, the ‘Three Amigos’ and the shifting politics of Israel But Hannity said the common portrayal of Graham as a warmonger was wrong. “The truth is the opposite,” he said. “Lindsey desperately wanted – and talked to the president about – lasting peace in the Middle East. He wanted every country in the region on that path to peace. That was Lindsey’s dream. “[But] Lindsey had moral clarity. He knew – as President Trump knows, as Israel knows, as I know – there can be no path to peace until evil is defeated.” Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Idi Amin’s boxer grandson vows to win gold and be ‘the new king of Scotland’
World.content:
SportBoxingCommonwealth Games Idi Amin’s boxer grandson vows to win gold and be ‘the new king of Scotland’ Hannah Kennelly July 29, 2026 — 5:29am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The boxer grandson of Idi Amin has vowed to become the “king of Scotland” by winning gold for Uganda at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. Aziz Abdul, a heavyweight boxer for Uganda, will take on Englishman Damar Thomas on Thursday morning (AEST). Former Ugandan dictator Idi Amin, who died in 2003, and his grandson Aziz Abdul, who is competing in Glasgow. AP/Instagram But he has grabbed attention before even stepping in the ring with his comments to media over the last couple of days. “My idol is Mike Tyson, the baddest man on the planet,” Abdul told media earlier this week. “If I win the gold medal, I will be the baddest man in the Commonwealth, the baddest man in Glasgow and the new king of Scotland.”



Related Article Commonwealth Games First shoes, now speed suits: Australia joins arms race to get an edge in athletics Abdul’s reference hearkens back to his late grandfather Amin, who was married six times and fathered around 60 children. Amin was nicknamed “the Butcher of Uganda” – but also proclaimed himself the king of Scotland in 1976. He had a fixation for the country, sparked by his time as a soldier in the British colonial army, and often wore kilts and played the bagpipes. Also a one-time heavyweight boxing champion, Amin seized power on January 25, 1971, overthrowing president Milton Obote while Obote was abroad. Human rights groups say as many as 500,000 people were killed during Amin’s eight-year rule over Uganda until he was forced out of the country in 1979. He was never tried for his crimes in an international court and died in Saudi Arabia in 2003. “My grandfather’s achievements inspired me,” said Abdul, whose nickname is Ringo. “He was a heavyweight boxer like me, and I am so proud of him. Now we are not in Africa, we are in Europe. As my grandpa used to say, you need to win by knockout, so that’s what we have trained for and that’s what I hope to do.



“I believe in myself and I mean what I say. When I say I will do it, I will do it. Let them not doubt me. I am aiming for the gold medal.” Related Article Commonwealth Games Australia won 15 medals in the pool, but this Scottish swimmer with terminal cancer stole the show In a later interview with BBC Scotland, Adbul would not respond when asked if he was proud to be the grandson of the dictator, who also forced the expulsion of Uganda’s entire Asian minority, and whose rule led to total economic collapse. But Abdul did address how it feels to be linked to someone with such a sinister reputation. “Sometimes people say positive about him, but others say negative about him,” Abdul said. “That’s why I don’t want to talk more about him. “It’s not good to say something negative about someone who is not there, and it’s not good to say something about someone negative who was not there by the time when the incident happened, if it happened.”



Related Article Live

Commonwealth Games Commonwealth Games LIVE: Kennedy smashes record to win silver in 100m; Southam gold leads medal rush at the pool Abdul is 25, and according to the BBC Scotland report never met his grandfather. In the ring, he said, his big weapon is the “Ringo punch”. “I am not going to tell you about it – I will show you on the day if the right time comes,” he said. “You will see what the Ringo punch looks like. The big boys are here now. “Lions give back to lions. A lion cannot give back to a dog or a camel. A lion must resemble a lion. It is what it is. I am a real warrior. I am the son of the son.”

World.title: Double murder charge as two homes cordoned off on Auckland's North Shore
World.content:
A man has been charged with two counts of murder and one of attempted murder after incidents at two properties on Auckland's North Shore.

The 41-year-old is due to appear in the North Shore District Court on Wednesday morning.

Police were called to Seon Place in Birkdale shortly after 8.20pm on Tuesday after reports someone had been stabbed. They found a man with "moderate injuries".

The alleged offender was arrested at the same address.

"While speaking with this male, information has prompted us to dispatch a unit to a property at Lingfield Street in Glenfield to conduct a welfare check," police said in a statement.

A man and a woman were found dead at the second address.

Hato Hone St John says ambulances were called to Lingfield Street after 8pm on Tuesday. Nick Monro / RNZ

A scene guard was in place at both scenes and police would be conducting exmainations over the coming days.

A property on Linfield Street has been cordoned off. Nick Monro / RNZ

St John told RNZ it responded to the Birkdale address with an ambulance and a critical care unit around 8.25pm.

A person was taken to North Shore Hospital in moderate condition.

They were called to the Glenfield address at 8.50pm and were still at the scene shortly before 10pm.

"This is an awful set of events. I know this will leave many in our community unsettled, but what I can say at this early stage of the investigation is that the offender and victims are all known to each other," Acting Detective Inspector Megan Goldie said.

While there would be an increased police presence around Birkdale and Glenfield, there was no ongoing threat to the wider community, she said.

World.title: David Tamihere faces two-month wait to find out if he will be retried
World.content:
David Tamihere will have to wait another two months to find out whether he will be retried over the 1989 murder of two Swedish backpackers in Coromandel.

Tamihere appeared at the High Court in Auckland on Wednesday on the charges he was first convicted of in 1990 but which were quashed by the Supreme Court in March.

The Supreme Court said it was up to Crown prosecutors to decide whether to hold a trial again.

Crown prosecutor Alysha McClintock told the High Court on Wednedsay the Crown needed more time to decide whether it would try Tamihere again for the murder of Urban Höglin and Heidi Paakkonen.

Tamihere's lawyer James Carruthers said with a trial potentially a year away, the defence team was in the dark about the case.

They were dealing with events that happened 37 years ago and did not know what evidence or witnesses the prosecution was relying on.

Justice Mathew Downs agreed to the extension requested by the prosecution but gave it a deadline.

It must make a decision by the end of September, and Tamihere will appear again in October.

Arriving at court, Tamihere, who is now in his 70s, said he was feeling good but did not know what to expect.

He has been out of jail since 2010 when he was released on parole.

When the convictions were quashed, he was freed but is still facing the two murder charges.

The background

Höglin, 23, and Paakkonen, 21, were last seen in Thames in 1989.

Their disappearance and the subsequent trial was one of the country's highest profile crimes.

Many aspects remain a mystery.

Höglin's body was found in 1991, after Tamihere had been convicted, but Paakkonen's body has never been found.

At the time the couple went missing, Tamihere had been living in the bush in the Coromandel for about three years, in hiding from police over a prior rape charge.

Much of the Crown's original case was circumstantial.

It included evidence that Tamihere had been seen driving around the Coromandel region in the couple's ute.

Tamihere admitted dumping or selling their possession but maintained he had never met them.

The Crown's case also relied on testimony from former inmate Robert Conchie Harris who said Tamihere told him he killed the Swedes. However Harris was convicted of perjury over evidence in 2017.

The appeals

Tamihere first appealed his convictions in 1992, after Höglin's body was found wearing a watch that a prosecution witness had initially said he had seen at Tamihere's house.

The body was also 70km away from where the Crown first suspected he had been killed.

That appeal was unsuccessful but the 2017 perjury conviction of Harris prompted a new round of appeals from Tamihere.

In 2024, the Court of Appeal declined to quash the convictions, saying despite the problems with some crown evidence, there was still enough to safely say Tamihere was guilty.

The Supreme Court released its decision in March that finally quashed the convictions.

It said Harris's evidence meant the trial was fundamentally unfair, and that there had been a "radical recasting" of the crown case since the original trial.

That effectively meant the case had never truly been tested by a jury.

The court said it was possible a jury would still find Tamihere guilty, but that could only be decided in a retrial.

Timeline

April 1989 - Heidi Birgitta Paakkonen and Sven Urban Höglin are last seen in Thames. Tamihere was on the run from police and living rough in the bush after pleading guilty to raping a woman three years earlier.

May 1989 - David Tamihere is arrested over an earlier rape. That same day, the couple are reported missing.

December 1990 - Tamihere is convicted of murdering the couple and sentenced to life imprisonment.

1991 - Höglin's body is found near Whangamatā.

1992 - The Court of Appeal rejects Tamihere's appeal.

1994 - Tamihere is denied leave to appeal to the Privy Council.

1995 - Witness C - later revealed as Roberto Conchie Harris - swears an affidavit retracting his evidence.

1996 - Harris retracts his retraction.

2010 - Tamihere is released on parole.

2016 - A private prosecution alleges Harris lied at Tamihere's trial.

2017 - Harris is sentenced after being found guilty of perjury and not guilty of perverting the course of justice.

2017 - Harris appeals the perjury convictions and sentence and fights to keep his identity hidden.

2018 - Harris drops his appeal against the perjury convictions.

2018 - The High Court revokes suppression order for Witness B, another prison informant.

2020 - Justice Minister Andrew Little announces Tamihere's case is going back to the Court of Appeal after a Royal Prerogative of Mercy is granted.

November 2023 - The Court of Appeal hears Tamihere's case.

July 2024 - The Court of Appeal declines to quash Tamihere's convictions.

December 2024 - The Supreme Court grants leave for the case to be heard there.

August 2025 - The case heads to the Supreme Court sitting in Auckland.

World.title: Auckland hits the negatives as freezing temperatures continue
World.content:
Freezing temperatures are persisting around the country but have warmed up from the beginning of the week.

It was a frosty start to the week with temperatures plummeting below -7C in some places in both the north and south islands.

MetService meteorologist Alwyn Bakker said of the main centres at 5am Wednesday morning, Taupō was the main standout at -4.1C, up from -5.6C at the same time Tuesday.

He said at 8am, Dunedin was -2.1C, as was Hamilton at 6am this morning.

Christchurch, he said, dipped below freezing to -0.1C at the airport.

Wellington and Auckland were "a little bit balmier", Bakker said.

At 5am, Auckland was -1.9C, which he said was "pretty cold for Auckland".

Wellington, he said, was at a "comparably tropical" 4.1C at 2am this morning.

Bakker said a ridge of high pressure had gradually started to drift off to the east giving a bit of a lift in temperatures.

World.title: Commercial fishing could be banned in parts of Northland under mātaitai reserve plan
World.content:
Commercial fishing could be banned along Northland's Bream Bay and in part of Whangārei Harbour if a proposed mātaitai reserve gets a green light.

Fisheries NZ is currently consulting on the proposal and will hold a public meeting at Marsden Yacht and Boat Club in One Tree Point, south of Whangārei, from 6pm on Thursday.

Recreational fishing can't be banned in mātaitai reserves - but they do allow future bylaws to be created, which could, for example, set seasonal restrictions or quotas.

The main proposal is for a mātaitai the length of Bream Bay and extending up to two nautical miles offshore.

The reserve also hugs the southern side of Whangārei Harbour as far as Oakleigh on the Mangapai River.

In total, the reserve, if approved, would cover 115 square kilometres.

A second, much smaller reserve of one square kilometre would cover Marsden Bank and Mair Bank, two well-known sandbanks off Marsden Point where taking shellfish is already under a rolling two-year ban.

Patuharakeke Rohe Moana Committee put forward the main proposal, which covered the hapū's entire rohe moana (traditional marine area).

The aim, as stated in the application, was to "protect and restore customary fisheries for present and future generations".

Spokeswoman Juliane Chetham said the hapū had been considering how it could use customary fisheries management tools, available under the Fisheries Act and kaimoana regulations, since at least 2009.

While this week's public meeting was aimed at recreational fishers, recreational fishing could not be banned in a mātaitai reserve.

Juliane Chetham. SUPPLIED

"In the future, we could apply to put bylaws in place, but we're not doing that now, and that would have to follow the same consultation process, and a decision by the Minister, as we're going through now."

Chetham, who heads the hapū's resource management unit, said the only immediate change if a mātaitai was brought in would be a ban on commercial fishing.

Only a handful of commercial fishers still worked inside Whangārei Harbour, and it was not clear how much commercial fishing occurred close to shore in Bream Bay.

"But if there are some commercial fishers who are going to be adversely affected, we're keen to talk to them and discuss making exemptions or potentially changing the boundary."

Chetham said the hapū spoke to commercial fishers last year and got some general comments, but not the kind of information that could help guide decision-making.

She described the proposals as "a first pou in the ground" with much consultation and kōrero to come.

Chetham said there had been "a bit of concern" around the country when mātaitai reserves had been proposed.

Supplied / Fisheries NZ

Part of that was fuelled by misinformation that recreational fishers were going to be shut out.

"We're just trying to set ourselves up with the best tools available to us as kaitiaki to manage our fisheries going forward. And I think a lot of the recreational sector will share the same concerns that we do. Unfortunately, from what I see on social media, it's turned into more of a race-based kōrero, instead of a sustainable fisheries kōrero. It's very, very unfortunate."

The strongest concerns had been around finfish.

"We're not actually interested at this point in time in finfish. Not that we think they're necessarily in a healthy state, but Fisheries NZ is managing sustainability measures in that space. Shellfish are our priority."

The kaimoana beds at Marsden Bank and Mair Bank had already been closed by Fisheries NZ due to plummeting shellfish numbers, but that closure had to be renewed every two years.

"We've been monitoring pipi in particular, and they haven't recovered to a level that we and the scientists we work with consider to be abundant enough to support harvesting being opened up again," she said.

"Nonetheless, we do see little pockets of recovery, and as a longer-term solution, a mātatai and then a bylaw would allow us a more nuanced approach rather than this sort of blunt tool of saying, right, the whole thing's closed for two years. In future we'd like to be able to say, 'well, maybe we can open it for a short season'."

Chetham said a mātaitai, if granted, would have no effect on proposals to expand Northport or mine for sand off Bream Bay, both of which Patuharakeke opposed.

Those projects were covered by RMA or fast-track legislation, and in any case the sandmining would take place further offshore.

Langs Beach RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

Fisheries Minister Shane Jones said the hapū were entitled to apply for a mātaitai under the Treaty of Waitangi Fisheries Act - but the Crown would make the final decision.

"I have never in my entire political career encountered an application of this scale … Mātaitai fishing reserves refer to discrete areas, and obviously we'll take advice whether a discrete area is consistent with Oakleigh to Bream Head," he said.

He encouraged Northlanders to take part in the consultation process.

The final decision would take account of all interests associated with the coastline, and was unlikely to happen before the election.

Consultation was open until 21 August.

Fisheries NZ defined a mātaitai reserve as "an identified traditional fishing ground which tangata whenua have a special relationship with".

The application for the smaller mātaitai reserve had been made by Ngā Tangata Kaitiaki o Te Rerenga Parāoa, which brought together Ngāti Tu, Te Parawhau, Ngāti Kahu o Torongare and Patuharakeke.

The biggest existing mātaitai in the country, off Cape Runaway, near East Cape, measures 70 square kilometres and came into force in 2020.

World.title: 'Left to rot': Auckland residents say Kainga Ora ghost homes attracting illegal dumping
World.content:
'Left to rot': Akl residents on stalled Kainga Ora development Morning Report Download MP3 4m

A resident on a central Auckland street say multiple boarded up houses and vacant lots have been "left to rot", after a major Kainga Ora project was stopped last year.

And a city councillor says the community feels "abandoned" after the government pulled the plug on the development, but the housing minister and Kainga Ora say some social homes are being planned.

Hundreds of homes were set to be built on O'Donnell Avenue, as part of the housing agency's Wesley West development.

Demolition began before the agency undertook a nationwide re-set last year.

Resident Stu Harwood said there were more than 30 empty Kainga Ora lots or houses on the street, and some had been fenced or boarded up for two years.

"They've effectively been left to rot.

"Because these houses are just degrading in plain view of everyone in the neighbourhood - it's now become a target for illegal dumping, they haven't been looked after at all. There's rubbish collecting, all up and down the street."

An old suitcase, mattress, spare tyre and mound of building materials are among items RNZ saw had been tossed onto the sections, or grass berms outside them.

An old suitcase and other items. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

Stu Harwood said signs urging against dumping and regular calls to the council hadn't stopped the dumping.

Auckland Council told RNZ it had 56 call-outs for illegal dumping on the street in the last financial year.

Harwood said there was a view among residents that the street had "gone downhill".

"It's a real shame, this street's got a school on it, Wesley Primary, you know it's a great neighbourhood, and it's a real shame to see these properties not used."

Stu Harwood. RNZ/Marika Khabazi

Kainga Ora's general manager of urban development and delivery, Nick Howcroft, said the agency had plans to transform 36 state house sites into 331 new medium-high density social and private market units in the area.

Residents were moved out between May 2024 and February 2025, and some demolition started, he said.

But following a government re-set of the agency last year, $72 million from the project was re-prioritised.

Howcroft said Kainga Ora is instead planning 39 2-4 bedroom state homes across four sites, predominantly for families, and had lodged a resource consent application with Auckland Council, with construction expected to start in late spring.

Kainga Ora had plans to build hundreds of homes on O'Donnell Avenue, but that was stopped last year. RNZ/Marika Khabazi

Albany-Eden-Puketapapa councillor Julie Fairey said that's a fraction of what had been imagined.

"It was going to be quite a much larger scale of redevelopment. They were talking about creating effectively a new town centre at the intersection of Sandringham and Stoddard Road.

"There was a lot of discussion with council about the council facilities that would be needed, potentially a new park in the area."

The Cityvision-backed councillor said the Wesely community felt abandoned after the development stopped, while thousands of others across the city needed housing.

"There's nothing happening with these sections...so they're attracting illegal dumping, there could be issues with rats or vermin, so not only is it an under-utilisation of land, but the community feel really abandoned, and that sucks."

Auckland councillor Julie Fairey. RNZ/ The Detail - Sharon Brettkelly

Howcroft said Kainga Ora was regularly monitoring the sites for illegal dumping and doing regular ground maintenance on the properties.

"If neighbours are aware of any issues with people illegally accessing the sites or dumping rubbish, we would appreciate them letting us know."

'Big challenge'

Wesley Primary School principal Andy Crowe said he was expecting his school to grow from about 150 to 600 students.

The school was gearing up for multiple stages of development too - and in 2023 moved into new buildings ahead of major construction.

But plans for three more large hubs - the equivalent of 12 extra classrooms - ground to a halt.

O'Donnell Avenue. RNZ/Marika Khabazi

He said families in the social houses were forced to move out of the area, including to Ōtāhuhu and Karaka.

"They basically are getting shipped everywhere else but staying in our community. Transience is a really really big challenge.

"One of the key drivers for our kids success, regardless of what school or socio-economic background, is that they get to stay in education, and they get to stay in the community that's supporting them."

Crowe said it's been difficult to re-set as a school, while meeting the strategic objectives of the curriculum.

He said he was pleased to hear the new homes being built on O'Donnell Avenue were predominantly for families, and might contribute to roll growth.

Overngrown grass on O'Donnell Avenue. RNZ/Marika Khabazi

Data from the Ministry of Cities, Environment, Regions and Transport show there are currently 9356 people on Auckland's social housing register.

Fairey said she thought Kainga Ora staff wanted the larger development to go ahead.

"I think that a lot of the people at Kainga Ora would love to be able to progress this, but they do not have support from their minister, they do not have support from this government or Cabinet."

Housing Minister Chris Bishop said while the original development was paused, hundreds of homes had been built in the wider Mt Roskill area - with state homes still coming for Wesley.

"It's a gain in terms of social homes, yes. I mean we have tried to re-focus the Wesley component of the wider Mt Roskill project towards social houses.

"The large scale projects are a mixture of urban renewal for social houses, but also fundamentally just market houses. Just private sector market sales."

Housing Minister Chris Bishop. RNZ / Mark Papalii

Bishop said he'd stressed to officials that empty state homes or land must be looked after to prevent rubbish dumping.

He said Kainga Ora owned 78,000 houses throughout the country and at any given point there would be demolition, sales, and vacancies.

At the end of March 2026 there were 400 empty Kainga Ora homes, down from 1300 when National went into government, he said.

World.title: Arrowtown residents rally against proposed fast-track housing development
World.content:
Locals sceptical about plans to build 1200 homes near Arrowtown Morning Report Download MP3 3m

Queenstown's mayor says the government's fast-track process is allowing developers to sidestep years of planning work, leaving councils and communities to pick up the bill.

It comes as Arrowtown residents rally against a proposed housing development they claim could choke roads, harm local tourism and ultimately be a "folly of history".

Ridgeburn Ltd is seeking fast-track consent to build a neighbouring community rivalling the historic township in size - comprising 1210 houses and a commercial precinct between Lake Hayes and the Kawarau River.

A meeting about the proposal organised by the newly formed group Queenstown Smart Growth Initiative (QSGI) drew more than 120 residents to the Arrowtown Rugby Club on Tuesday night.

QSGI spokesperson Hanna Petit said the primary concern was that Queenstown Lakes District Council had already identified well-located, serviced land capable of accommodating growth in its spatial plan - whereas Ridgeburn was about six kilometres beyond the boundary, in a place where traffic congestion was already all too common.

"The issue that we've got with Queenstown is that we live within a basin. So we're restricted in terms of we can't continue to sprawl and we can't build roads to fix the issues that we have with the traffic infrastructure," she said.

"The spatial plan is more than just red tape. It is really a plan that ensures development can happen in the right ways."

The meeting saw frustrations aired not just about Ridgeburn, but also that it was one of 11 major fast-track proposals either flagged or submitted in the district.

Queenstown Smart Growth Initiative spokesperson Hanna Petit says her group wants to challenge claims made about the proposed Ridgeburn development. RNZ / Katie Todd

Queenstown Lakes District Mayor John Glover said those concerns were valid.

"At a holistic level, it's a bit like conservation. If you work in any conservation field, right plant, right place is absolutely key. And what we're seeing are developments which are not the right plant in the right place - and they're not going to thrive," he said.

"The costs that get imposed downstream, down the road, on the community are quite significant. And we have spent literally millions of dollars of ratepayers money coming up with plans for where growth should happen."

He said conversations with other mayors suggested a rising tide of discontent with the fast-track process - and how it was undermining the careful planning work councils had already undertaken.

"We have a government that's stood on localism and allowing local councils to make decisions. And of course this completely bypasses that," he said.

Ridgeburn Ltd has pitched its project as a way to quell the district's housing shortage, and pledged to rent 135 of the houses below market rate, with a further 45 houses offered to mana whenua or sold "at more affordable price points".

Its substantive application, submitted in March, set out plans to fully fund and build private wastewater and stormwater systems, and establish a community park, sports field and reserve land.

This month fast-track panel convener Jane Borthwick said the project was not ready to be passed to an expert panel for a final decision due to "significant information gaps" identified by local councils.

Ridgeburn Ltd agreed to provide most of the outstanding information, including a more robust transport assessment and an environmental risk assessment, by 10 August.

Queenstown Lakes District Mayor John Glover. RNZ / Nate McKinnon

Petit said she believed Ridgeburn could be a major burden on local roads, ratepayers and the tourism economy.

"The way that fast-track is designed is that it puts the economic benefit at the forefront of the application...unfortunately, you cannot quantify the impact that a development like this would have on our tourism economy," she said.

"We do know that the number one reason people come to Queenstown is because of the scenery and the number one reason that people don't like coming to Queenstown is because of the traffic. And Ridgeburn plays into both of those reasons. And once it's gone, it's gone, there's no coming back."

Resident Mark Cole said he was concerned the developer appeared to be pursuing financial gain at the expense of the existing community.

"We live in the area ... we're the ones that are going to have to live with the outcomes," he said.

"This area ... is a very special area. We've all flown over it as we approach and depart this very special place. This is not the place to be doing this type of development. It's not."

Gibbston resident Ken Mackenzie said he wanted to see the Ridgeburn development rejected before it set a precedent.

He said he was worried it could pave the way for a proposed 900-house development near him, also listed under the fast-track process.

"We've got to start with this one, and hopefully shut this one down, otherwise the Gibbston one will be the next boil on the bum," he said.

Petit said QSGI was set up to make sure the fast-track panel had access to clear, credible evidence so it could understand the true impacts such a large development would have on the region.

In lieu of an opportunity to make public submissions on the application, the group had assembled a team of independent experts to present to the panel and challenge the developers' claims, she said.

"It's not necessarily just the community's view because obviously the community doesn't really have any bearing on the fast-track process. It's more about ensuring that both sides of the coin are presented to the panel," she said.

World.title: How researchers say we could make New Zealanders richer
World.content:
Academic: How financial literacy could help Kiwis' wealth Morning Report Download MP3 3m

There could be a simple way to make some New Zealanders 25 percent more wealthy, new research suggests: Make them more financially literate.

AUT professor Bart Frijns has co-authored research looking at the long-term impact of financial literacy on wealth.

He said it sought to examine whether financial literacy was a cause or a consequence of financial success.

"Very often what we see is that people that are wealthier tend to be more financially literate but that's simply because they have more money and therefore invest more in financial literacy. What we really wanted to figure out is, is there a really clear relationship between improvement in financial literacy and then better financial outcomes later in life?"

He used longitudinal data on Dutch households and connected financial literacy measured in 2011 with financial outcomes in 2019 for 475 individuals.

People were asked questions about the conception of inflation, diversification and other basic financial literacy questions.

"It's a good proxy for what people know about money," he said.

Frijns said the results were striking.

What's good debt, what's bad debt and how do I tell the difference? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 11m

"An increase in financial literacy led to a 12 percent increase in income and a significant impact on savings as well, on wealth accumulation by 25 percent.

"There's definitely a push from the literacy to becoming better off. A push from literacy into financial success but it also shows those people that invested in financial literacy in 2011 were still benefiting from that financial literacy 8 years on."

He said a one-point increase in financial literacy in 2011 was observed to lead to annual income increases of €4,644 (about NZ$7900 or a 12 percent increase relative to the average income in the sample), and savings increased by €12,540 (NZ$21,000 or a 25 percent increase relative to the average savings in the sample).

He said it aligned with predictions that up to 40 percent of wealth inequality at retirement could be due to differences in financial knowledge.

He said the research also showed differences in how financial literacy was used.

Younger people tended to earn higher incomes when they were financially literate while older people were more likely to accumulate more savings.

"This suggests that people apply financial knowledge in ways that reflect their changing financial priorities over the life course. As a result, financial education may be most effective when tailored to specific life stages.

"Programmes aimed at younger people could focus on career development, income growth and early financial decision-making, whereas programmes for older adults may be better directed towards retirement planning and wealth accumulation."

The gender differences

There were gender differences, though that did not bode as well for women.

The researchers found that while financial literacy had strong associations with higher income and savings among men, there were no significant relationships for women.

Frijns said the results suggested that gender differences may extend beyond financial literacy levels themselves.

They said that could be because traditional gender roles, unequal influence over household finances, labour market inequalities and other factors could be limiting how much women could turn their knowledge into decisions.

Previous research has consistently shown that women report lower levels of financial literacy than men.

He said the experience was likely to be similar in New Zealand.

"I don't see a reason why you would expect different results in the relationship between financial literacy and wellbeing… I think it's an important discussion for New Zealand."

He said the results supported government initiatives for financial literacy education in schools.

"That financial education is likely better targeted at maximising income, as our results show that is how young adults use their financial knowledge."

He said it was also important for KiwiSaver.

"One could think about what this could mean for KiwiSaver balances if New Zealanders were provided with more targeted financial literacy education on their retirement savings.

"Finally, with average household debt at 90.6 percent of GDP, compared with the UK at 73.9 percent and the US at 68 percent, improved financial literacy may result in better debt management strategies… Based on our findings that a one-point increase in financial literacy leads to a 25 percent increase in savings and the theoretical predictions that differences in financial knowledge can lead to a 30 percent to 40 percent wealth gap at retirement, improving financial literacy of those with the lowest financial knowledge could help close this gap.

"For all New Zealanders the message is clear: learning about and understanding your finances can lead to substantial improvements in wealth."

World.content:
Commonwealth Games: Lewis Clareburt clinches gold for 400m IM Morning Report Download MP3 2m

Swimmers Lewis Clareburt and Erika Fairweather will try to grow their medal haul in the pool on day 5 at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games.

World.title: 'Very bad look': Brisbane defender given three-game ban
World.content:
Brisbane defender Ty Gallop has been suspended for three games for a serious misconduct act he admits is a "very bad look".

Gallop pleaded guilty at the AFL Tribunal on Tuesday night for what he described as retaliation on Mitch Georgiades after the Port Adelaide forward grabbed his broken thumb.

The 20-year-old had tackled Georgiades to the ground during Sunday's clash in Brisbane and, after the ball left the area, shoved the Port attacker face-first into the turf.

Gallop played the match with strapping on a broken right thumb.

"Mitch has grabbed my thumb as I have gone to stand up," Gallop said, adding Georgiades' action was intentional.

But Gallop expressed remorse for retaliating, saying he had phoned Georgiades to apologise.

"Looking back now and watching the footage, I understand that the retaliation to what happened wasn't fair," he said.

"I have gone out of my way to push him down, which I am sorry for and I do regret. I'd like to have that time over again.

"It's a very bad look and there's no room for it in footy."

Gallop said his retaliation was an "immediate reaction".

"I have grabbed the back of his jersey and pushed him back into the ground," he said.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"I think I play a hard brand of footy but I play a very fair brand of footy as well … it was purely out of retaliation."

Under questioning from the AFL's counsel Nick Pane, Gallop agreed his act was totally unreasonable and unacceptable.

Pane asked the tribunal for a three-game suspension.

"Georgiades' head made forceful contact with the ground," Pane said. "The action had significant potential to cause serious injury."

The Port spearhead wasn't hurt in the incident.

Gallop's counsel Adrian Anderson said the 23-gamer had "lashed out" but argued for a two-match ban.

"There is a context here," Anderson said.

"It's different where someone has a broken thumb and it's grabbed and they react in the heat of the moment."

After hearing just over one hour of evidence, tribunal chairman Jeff Gleeson KC and members Darren Gaspar and Scott Stevens returned a verdict some 50 minutes later.

AFL Saturday live North Melbourne survives a nervy finish to break a decade-long drought against Essendon as star ruckman Tristan Xerri rubs blood on Andrew McGrath's face in a heated exchange.

Gleeson said the tribunal gave no weight in its deliberations to Gallop's thumb being grabbed before his misconduct.

"The vision of the serious misconduct is startling in the degree to which it is unsportsmanlike," he said.

Gallop is the sixth AFL player suspended on a serious misconduct charge and the second this season, following North Melbourne ruckman Tristan Xerri's three-game ban for wiping blood onto the face of Essendon captain Andrew McGrath in a match in March.

Gallop will now miss Brisbane's games against Carlton, Hawthorn and Gold Coast, and will not be available until the round 24 games against Collingwood at the MCG.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Country footy player charged after 'ugly' scenes in southern WA
World.content:
A country football player has been charged with assault and choking after clashes during a game in southern Western Australia.

The man was allegedly involved in two incidents during Sunday's Lower South West Football League clash in Kojonup between the hometown Cougars and the Bridgetown Bulldogs.

Footage of two incidents during the game prompted public outcry and a police investigation.

A WA Police spokesperson confirmed Kojonup Police, with assistance from Busselton detectives, charged the man, from Cowaramup, with assault occasioning bodily harm and "impeding another person's breathing or blood circulation by applying pressure to the neck".

The Cowaramup man is accused of choking an opposing player. (Supplied)

On Tuesday WA Police Commissioner Col Blanch said violence on the football field was "not on".

"You are not immune on the sporting field," he said.

"We understand there are normal contacts in the spirit of play, but if it is outside of play and a deliberate targeted attack, then it is an assault."

Loading...

Game 'turned ugly'

Kojonup Football Club vice-president Matt Marinoni said the top-of-the-table clash was a "tense and fiery" game that "turned ugly".

He said the umpires did not see the off-ball incident.

"Then there was a lot of noise in the crowd," Mr Marinoni said.

"From there there was a bit of a wrestle and melee because we saw one of our teammates was on the ground, unconscious."

That player is in good spirits and recovering from his facial injuries and concussion, but is "shaken", according to the club.

A spokesperson from the Lower South West Football League told the ABC it was aware of the incident.

"The matter has been referred to the Country Football WA tribunal process and will be dealt with in accordance with the applicable rules and procedures," the spokesperson said.

The league declined to comment further, in order to "preserve the integrity and fairness of the tribunal process".

The Bridgetown Football Club said the matter was being dealt with by Country Football WA.

"[We] do not condone the behaviour shown during Sunday's game," the club said in a statement.

"This has no place in football and does not reflect the true values of our club."

The 23-year-old is due to face the Katanning Magistrates Court in August.

World.title: Joint spares Aussie blushes on tough day at Memphis Open
World.content:
Rising star Maya Joint has spared Australia's blushes at the WTA's hard-court event in Memphis.

On a day when the Australian challenge fizzled, the world number 77 won her round-of-16 clash against wildcard Whitney Osuigwe in straight sets.

The 20-year-old needed a tick over 90 minutes for a 6-4, 6-1 win against the American.

Joint will now meet the winner of top-seed Ekaterina Alexandrova or fellow Russian Kristina Liutova for a place in the quarterfinals.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Already boasting tournament victories in Rabat and Eastbourne last year, which helped her climb to a career-best number 28 in the world in February this year, Joint lost her serve twice in the opening set but did enough to take it in 45 minutes.

The second set proved more comfortable and Joint, who famously eliminated Serena Williams in the opening round of Wimbledon this year, broke three times to advance.

There was no such joy for Talia Gibson and Storm Hunter though.

Gibson was soundly beaten by German Tatjana Maria 6-0, 6-3, while compatriot Storm Hunter succumbed 7-5, 7-5 to fifth-seeded Colombian Camila Osorio.

World number 66 Kimberly Birrell, who lost her first-round doubles clash alongside American Peyton Stearns to Ingrid Martins and Ekaterina Ovcharenko 6-4, 6-7 (7/4), 11-9, takes on China's Ma Yexin in the singles draw on Tuesday.

In the shock of the day, Swiss third seed Viktorija Golubic was eliminated in three sets by Katie Volynets of the US, while all three unseeded Russian players in action were victorious.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Embattled LIV Golf tour asks to defer payment to Adelaide golf club
World.content:
The financially struggling LIV Golf tour has asked for an extension on a payment to Kooyonga Golf Club, raising doubts over whether next year's Adelaide event will go ahead.

Kooyonga in Adelaide's western suburbs is scheduled to host LIV Golf Adelaide in 2027 before the tour moves to a newly redeveloped North Adelaide Golf Course in 2028.

But the future of the league has been under a cloud since Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) announced it would be pulling its reported billions in funding at the end of the 2026 season.

The Grange Golf Club has previously hosted the LIV event in Adelaide. (ABC News: Rory McClaren)

South Australian Premier Peter Malinauskas said he was made aware last week that LIV Golf had asked for an extension on a payment to Kooyonga Golf Club.

"An extension was sought by LIV as they're working through programming next year for those payments to be made in September," he said.

"That extension was granted."

SA Premier Peter Malinauskas says he is aware LIV Golf has asked for an extension. (ABC News)

Mr Malinauskas indicated there would "presumably" be enough time for Kooyonga to prepare for the March 2027 event, given the club had granted the payment extension.

The deferred payment is worth $500,000, Adelaide radio station FIVEaa reported.

In a statement, Kooyonga Golf Club confirmed it "evaluated and approved" a "short operational extension regarding its initial venue payment" to LIV Golf.

Deputy Liberal leader Josh Teague said the government needed to be more transparent about the event's future.

SA's deputy Liberal leader Josh Teague wants more transparency about the event's future. (ABC News: Olivia Mason)

"Those who've bought tickets, those who are committing all sorts of other ways to the holding of the event are going to be left mightily disappointed … if all of a sudden LIV Golf goes from hero to zero," he said.

"If there's one thing you need to host successful international events, it's confidence and it's the capacity for everybody to get behind something because you know that it's actually going to happen and not just be shrouded in doubt.

"That's unfortunately where we stand right now."

The ABC has contacted LIV Golf for comment.

The shift to North Adelaide has been controversial. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

The premier has previously said the state government would need a "clear indication" from LIV Golf about the event's future by October.

Can the SA government justify a $45m golf course upgrade without LIV Golf? The Malinauskas government took a calculated risk to redevelop the North Adelaide Golf Course in time for LIV Golf in 2028. It might not pay off.

The state government has a contract with LIV Golf until 2031 and pays an undisclosed fee for the tour to host an annual event in Adelaide.

LIV Golf's success at the Grange Golf Club was also the catalyst for the government to fund a controversial $45 million redevelopment of the North Adelaide Golf Course.

The project has been subject to protests over the felling of 585 trees.

The government has since secured the Australian Open golf tournament to be hosted at the North Adelaide Golf Course from 2028 to 2034.

World.title: The sun has set on the British Empire, and yet this celebration remains
World.content:
"It's just a square."

That's the three-star review of Nelson Mandela Place in Glasgow by someone named Katie Nicholson on Google.

Katie isn't entirely wrong. A statue for the freedom fighter and former South African president is set to be unveiled in October, but for now there's not a whole lot to see at the spot, listed as a tourist attraction on Google Maps.

But the couple of street signs tacked to buildings on West George Street, not far from the city centre, sit as an elegant and understated middle finger to apartheid South Africa.

The South African consulate left this location for some reason. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

In 1986, while Mandela was still in prison on Robben Island, the Glasgow City Council changed the name of St George's Place to Nelson Mandela Place.

It meant that the South African consulate under the then-ruling National Party was forced not only to see the name of one of their chief antagonists as they entered the Stock Exchange building every day, but also send out correspondence bearing his name.

They opted to use a PO Box address before moving from the location in the early 90s.

After Mandela was released, he came to the city to thank the people for their solidarity in 1993.

Nelson Mandela thanked Glasgow in 1993, between being released from prison and becoming president of South Africa. (Getty Images: Chris Bacon/PA)

"While we were physically denied our freedom in the country of our birth, a city 6,000 miles away, and as renowned as Glasgow, refused to accept the legitimacy of the apartheid system, and declared us to be free."

That cry of freedom is as synonymous with the Scottish as it is with Mandela himself.

So, how does a celebration of this Commonwealth sit with a city and country that has always had a fraught relationship with oppressors generally and the English specifically?

ABE – Anyone but England

Andy Murray got to represent Scotland in the 2022 Battle of the Brits. (Getty Images: Mark Runnacles/Battle of the Brits)

Tennis great Andy Murray once perplexed some (read: Americans) less au fait with the unique rivalries within the UK when he was asked who he'd be supporting at the 2006 FIFA World Cup and replied: "Anyone but England."

Scotland isn't on its own in this regard.

In the Ashes last summer, Australia's injury-plagued men's Test team scored a triumphant professional 4-1 victory, but more Australian joy was derived from watching another epic capitulation of an England team that had declared itself the saviour of Test cricket, teaching us all how to entertain, if not actually win much of anything.

We cheered every humiliating faceplant and fumble at least as much as we celebrated the all-time world-class performances of Travis Head and Mitchell Starc.

The recently completed World Cup was another reminder of the collective glee shared by so many in watching England stumble.

The Sun has set on the British Empire, and yet this celebration remains. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

There's just something about the schadenfreude for Scots, Aussies and dozens of other nations in watching England lose.

Sure, you've got the Parthenon Sculptures and Rosetta Stone, but we've got Ellyse Perry and Steve Smith.

"There is this standard, reflexive idea of that they would prefer almost everybody to win other than England, as the most powerful part of the United Kingdom," Western Sydney University emeritus professor of culture and research David Rowe told ABC Sport.

"I think for some people it's serious, for some people it's just a bit of fun."

Loading Instagram content

There are jokes to be made, but also reflections on the very real subjugation that went on for centuries, and arguably only ended in 1997 when Hong Kong gained its independence.

This celebration of empire remains a peculiarity as calls grow to decolonise our language and our lives.

For a perfect example, the Parthenon Sculptures mentioned earlier are more famously known as the Elgin Marbles, named for the lord who nicked them from Greece and brought them back to Old Blighty at the start of the 19th century.

"I mean, the Commonwealth of Nations is, let's face it, anachronistic," Rowe said.

Flags that don't always get to fly wave prominently at the Commonwealth Games. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

"There are people who … don't know much about it or, if they schooled up on it, educated themselves about it, would realise that this is an anachronistic organisation based on an empire that no longer technically exists."

Although, many in the still-constituent Scotland would tell you the legacy, if not the actuality, of the empire remains in many ways.

"There are plenty of people in Scotland, including its leading Scottish National Party, who really would prefer to separate from the United Kingdom and who are mightily displeased by Brexit," said Rowe, a sports sociologist who consulted on the Glasgow Life team tasked with helping boost the city's standing on the global sporting stage.

"There are plenty of Scots who felt a greater affinity with the European Union than with England."

Strange, anomalous and anachronistic

A time machine is perhaps a fitting vehicle of entry of an event harking back to the past. (AAP: Andrew Milligan/PA Wire)

At the opening ceremony of the 2026 Commonwealth Games, King Charles III and Queen Camilla were warmly welcomed by the packed crowd at Glasgow's Hydro, perhaps surprisingly considering the same crowd's hearty refrains of Flower of Scotland barely an hour later.

The Scottish anthem retells Robert the Bruce's legendary victory over King Edward II of England at the Battle of Bannockburn in 1314.

The thrust of the rousing choon, and Scotland's identity more broadly, is about how this small but mighty land of hard folk repelled the crown time and again on the back of sheer grit and pride.

So ingrained in their identity is sticking it to the English that, instead of tearing down statues of old royals and dignitaries like the Duke of Wellington, they have simply given up on removing the traffic cones placed on his head.

The Games have never opened like this – maybe they always should The 2026 Commonwealth Games are like no other that came before them and the opening ceremony was similarly unique in a way that will make it hard to go back.

And yet, twice in the past 12 years, Glasgow has gone out of its way to host what is correctly dubbed the Friendly Games, welcoming dozens of nations whose primary unifying theme is that they were once conquered by the "bastards" from that anthem.

"It does strike me as something of an irony that it's not that very long ago that Scotland had a referendum to sever its ties with the United Kingdom and the British Crown, and now it's hosting a Commonwealth Games," Rowe said.

"I think it's having a bit of fun, all the kilts and all the Scottish culture, reminding people that Scotland has its own identity and has not just been subsumed by the United Kingdom."

The Commonwealth Games has the royal seal of approval. (Getty Images: Aaron Chown/WPA Pool)

If you need more evidence of the strange bedfellows in effect, Rowe said you need only look at the event's original name.

It was called the British Empire Games from 1930 to 1950, the British Empire and Commonwealth Games until for the next four editions, and the British Commonwealth Games until 1972.

"So even more coded British," Rowe told ABC Sport.

"And it's a strange body in some ways, if you consider that it is a monument to colonialism and imperialism. And yet the members, most of whom were formerly under the jurisdiction of the British crown, were colonised, have now voluntarily agreed to join an organisation which was formed out of that imperial arrangement."

It also provides those in the British Isles a chance to beat England while representing Scotland, Wales, Northern Ireland, Guernsey, Jersey or the Isle of Man.

Scottish knights of the British Empire Chris Hoy and Andy Murray have won a combined 13 Olympic medals for Great Britain.

Duncan Scott is Team GB's most decorated Olympic swimmer, Mark Cavendish has won a world championship and Olympic silver with the Union Jack next to his name, but both turned around to beat the English while flying the Scottish saltire and Isle of Man's triskelion during the Commonwealth Games.

Duncan Scott has won more Olympic medals than any other British swimmer. (Supplied: Commonwealth Sport)

So how does the home crowd feel watching their sporting heroes flying those flags?

"I think it means more to them to compete for Scotland," one Glasgow local, Peter, told ABC Sport.

"You can see it in their faces when they do better. It does mean a lot more to them to represent their home country."

There's perhaps a hint of personal projection in this fan's assessment, as summed up by his mate, Pat.

"I would hope that it does [mean more] for them, because it would for me," he said.

Duncan Scott with the 2014 and 2026 mascots, the latter sporting a traffic cone for a horn. (Getty Images: Jane Barlow/PA Images)

No amount of raucous crowd support or national pride is going to turn a 45-year-old bricklayer who's had a hot dog for breakfast into a 10-flat 100m runner. But at the tippy-top of sport, where the margins are at their finest, it's got to be worth a few hundredths of a second.

Angharad Evans swam for Team GB at the 2025 world championships in Singapore, missing the semifinals and finishing a brutal 18th overall in the 100m breaststroke as she went almost two seconds slower than her time at the national trials.

She carried those scars with her until she exorcised them with a spectacular victory at the Tollcross International Swimming Centre, winning her first international gold medal and thanking the crowd for getting her to the wall 0.12 of a second ahead of Aimee Canny.

Angharad Evans said the Tollcross crowd carried her for the final 10 metres. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

"Scotland was there to witness that and that was a very, very special moment for me," she said.

"I thanked them because leading into competitions it's so easy for doubts and negative thoughts to play a part in my mindset leading up, and I walk out and they just really uplift me and give me the confidence I need and boost me up.

"They often talk about how proud they are of us bringing back gold medals and PBs, but I'm immensely proud to have the Tartan Army supporting me in the crowd.

"Wearing the blue and white, hearing the crowd, being part of Scotland just carries you to the end. I don't think I would have had the strength and the courage I did in the last 10 metres if I wasn't in the blue and white and didn't have that crowd behind me.

"They absolutely helped me get to the end and finish in first place. So it's a medal for me but it's also a medal for Scotland."

All that from an English-born 23-year-old who is still learning the words to that famous Scottish anthem.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: Quick hits: Davies makes history, Diamonds clap back in uni debate
World.content:
Rose Davies runs a "race of a lifetime" to make Australian history, and the Diamonds remain in the spotlight even off the court.

Here are the quick hits from day four of the Commonwealth Games.

1. Davies makes history on the track

Rose Davies celebrated Australia's first athletics gold of the Games. (Getty Images: Michael Steele)

The eagerly anticipated athletics program finally got underway on the fourth day of competition in Glasgow, and it wasn't long before Australia claimed its first gold on the track.

Rose Davies sat back for much of the women's 10,000m but timed her move to perfection, waiting until less than a kilometre remained before galloping ahead of Kenya's Diana Wanza.

And Davies eventually won in a canter, crossing the finish line almost 11 seconds before silver medallist Wanza.

Australian commentary great Bruce McAvaney called it "the race of a lifetime" during the Network Seven broadcast.

Davies became the first Australian woman to win the 10,000m at a Commonwealth Games.

"These moments come once in a lifetime, and I'm so happy I got to achieve this," Davies told the Seven Network.

2. From a cancer diagnosis to a Games final

Archie Goodburn did not win a medal but won the respect of everyone as he competes while dealing with brain tumours. (Getty Images: SNS Group/Ross MacDonald)

When people say the phrase "there are more important things in life than sport" they're probably speaking about Scotland's Archie Goodburn.

The 25-year-old breaststroke specialist had a chance to compete at the Paris Olympics when he was diagnosed with three inoperable brain tumours in 2024.

But speaking after his race in the final, where he finished seventh, his interview put everything in perspective and made it very hard not to get emotional watching him.

"My dream was to make the final. But outside the pool I dream, like, of a future where brain cancer isn't the biggest killer of those under 40," he said.

"[A dream] where the UK government establish a national brain cancer lead to make that change, and I'd much prefer that that change was made and that dream is completed than any of my personal goals in the pool.

"Because what families and young people are going through out there is really beyond the comprehension of many people out here and certainly far harder than anything I've ever had to do as a world-class sportsman."

3. Welsh sisters twinning in bronze

Seeing double? (Getty Images: PA Images/Owen Humphreys)

Wales has not been flush with supreme gymnasts at the Commonwealth Games.

But given their national colour, perhaps it's no surprise that at these Scottish Games that two have come along at once, like lithe, smiling versions of red London buses.

Both Abi Roper and Emily Roper were in action in the vault, with Abi claiming a bronze medal with a score of 13.433, just a fraction ahead of her identical twin sister who scored 13.283 after being penalised 0.3 for her landing on her second vault.

Then, an hour or so later, Emily put her disappointment behind her to deliver a display worthy of a medal, also winning bronze behind Australian gold medal winner Katie McDonald.

In a heartening display of sisterly love, Abi could be seen roaring her support from the stands, her own bronze medal dangling around her neck, as her sister delivered the performance of her life to win Wales its first-ever medal on that apparatus at a Commonwealth Games.

"Sometimes we bicker because we are competitive, so we are constantly fighting to see who is better," Emily told a BBC interviewer in 2025.

Who knows how much bickering there would have been had Emily come away from Glasgow empty-handed.

4. Diamonds can't help being icons, even on a day off

After winning their first two matches, our netball world champions had day four off in Glasgow. But everyone's still talking about the Diamonds: just not for the broadcast-related reason you might expect.

Diamonds disappointed first two games only live on streaming service Diamonds fans are disappointed to discover Australia's dominant netball team's Glasgow matches are only being aired live on Seven's online streaming service.

Folks online have been debating Australia's netball uniform, which rides up during play and often ends up looking more like a singlet.

Some are worried the poor design is distracting our goal shooters, who have to take their shots before readjusting the awkward uniform (lest they be penalised for a held ball!).

Currently competing in her third Commonwealth Games, Courtney Bruce has worn a few iterations of the kit over the years, and she says the team isn't too worried about the 2026 uniform.

"It is what it is, there's literally nothing we can do about it, [so] we don't think about it," she told the ABC.

In a video posted on social media Commonwealth Games debutant Sophie Garbin poked fun at what she described as "the most talked about" aspect of the Glasgow event.

Loading...

All it takes is one look at the comment section to see people on either side of the heated debate: from supporters saying shorter dresses are easier to play in, to those who reckon the Diamonds look "silly".

Responding to haters, Bruce says it's a "good thing we're strong … fit, and we train hard".

I mean, it's not like they aren't wearing shorts under the dress. (Getty Images: Lintao Zhang)

5. Mollie O'Callaghan pulls out of the backstroke

Mollie O'Callaghan has withdrawn from the 50m backstroke. (Getty Images: Adam Pretty)

Coming into this Commonwealth Games, Mollie O'Callaghan revealed she was managing a back injury, and it cost her a chance in her backup event the 50m backstroke.

The 22-year-old was worried that she might not even be able to compete in Glasgow after scans revealed stress fractures and bone bruising on her lumbar spine.

She was, however, cleared by a specialist to compete.

"Things might look a little different for me at the Commonwealth Games and Pan Pacs, but I'll give everything I have and do my absolute best every time I race," O'Callaghan said in an Instagram post before the Games.

Some things remained the same though, the Queenslander claiming yet another gold medal for her burgeoning collection in the 200m freestyle and 4x100m freestyle relay.

However, she withdrew from the mixed 4x100m freestyle relay and did not line up in the 50m backstroke heats on Monday morning to focus on the 100m freestyle final that evening.

World.title: Sabalenka, Djokovic lead mixed doubles teams for US Open
World.content:
Top-ranked Aryna Sabalenka and 24-time Grand Slam champion Novak Djokovic headline the initial list of 16 teams entered into the US Open mixed doubles championship.

The tournament was overhauled last year, with a $US1 million ($1.43 million) prize going to the winners, in an effort to get top singles players to compete. Many of those types of stars were listed among the teams announced Monday by the US Tennis Association.

Iga Świątek and Casper Ruud, the runners-up in 2025, are entered again, along with Elena Rybakina and Taylor Fritz, the Japanese duo of Naomi Osaka and Kei Nishikori, along with Jessica Pegula and Jack Draper.

The main draw will be played over two days on August 25-26, with all the matches set to be held in Arthur Ashe Stadium and Louis Armstrong Stadium, the two biggest venues at the US Open.

Teams can enter up until August 17, when the six duos with the best combined singles rankings at the time will be automatically entered into the main draw.

That means Sabalenka, the two-time defending US Open women's champion and Djokovic, still ranked number five on the men's tour at age 39, will be safely into the field.

Eight teams will be given wild cards by the USTA, and two other teams will play their way into the field through a qualifying tournament to be held from August 24.

Defending champions win US Open mixed doubles final Italian pair Sara Errani and Andrea Vavassori accomplish their "mission" by winning the US Open mixed doubles title for the second straight year in a controversially revamped format.

The remainder of the teams that were entered as of Monday:

Mirra Andreeva and Andrey Rublev; Belinda Bencic and Flavio Cobolli; Diana Shnaider and Daniil Medvedev; Amanda Anisimova and Learner Tien; Alex Eala and Felix Auger-Aliassime; Leylah Fernandez and Frances Tiafoe; Taylor Townsend and Alexander Zverev; Elena-Gabriela Ruse and Nuno Borges; Sara Errani and Andrea Vavassori; Katerina Siniakova and Henry Patten; and siblings Peyton Stearns and Preston Stearns.

Errani and Vavassori are the two-time defending US Open champions. The Italians needed a wild card to get into last year's event because their singles ranking was too low, and that will be the case again this year.

The US Open was initially criticised last year because the format of the event shut out doubles specialists such as Errani and Vavassori, but the tournament certainly seemed a success, helping draw 78,000 fans to the grounds and selling out Ashe both days.

"Any time you can bring women and men together on the same team, you showcase tennis at its best. This is exactly what the mixed doubles championship does," USTA CEO Craig Tiley said in a statement.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"The mixed doubles championship is an innovation that will engage new audiences and give our fans another opportunity to see the biggest stars compete together."

Errani and Vavassori were the only traditional doubles team in last year's tournament.

There is a chance for more this year — Siniakova and Patten are doubles specialists — with the addition of the eight-team qualifying tournament, which will include six direct entries and two wild cards.

The format will be best-of-three-set matches with sets to four games, tiebreakers at 4-all and a 10-point match tie-break instead of a third set, through the semifinals. The final will be standard scoring with sets to six games and a tiebreaker at 6-all, and a 10-point match tiebreaker if necessary.

AP

Tech.title: AI leaders sign statement asking the government to do something about automated AI
Tech.content:
Employees of OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as Google, Meta, Thinking Machines, Microsoft, Mistral, and other leading AI labs, have written a statement to the US government supporting a potential slowdown of sorts for frontier AI development — or at least a speed-up of global coordinated governance efforts.

“Al could help create a dramatically better future, but that outcome is not guaranteed,” the employees wrote in a statement. “The world’s leading Al companies believe they could be close to automating Al research. It is hard to predict exactly how much this will accelerate Al progress, but there is a real risk that capability development rapidly accelerates beyond our ability to understand or control the resulting systems.”

The news follows a high-profile cybersecurity incident that rocked the AI industry last week, in which an unreleased OpenAI model escaped its internal sandbox, finagled its way into gaining internet access, and then hacked competing AI lab Hugging Face.

In the public statement, the employees went on to underscore the importance of some sort of coordinated regulation worldwide, so that the ever-intensifying AI race doesn’t outpace safety and monitoring tools.

“To realize Al’s potential, industry, government, and society at large may need the option to buy time to address emerging risks, develop security measures, and strengthen oversight,” they wrote. “But each company—and country—is under intense competitive pressure not to unilaterally slow that acceleration. And today, the world lacks the technical and governance tools to deliberately pace frontier-wide progress. Building on work already underway to monitor frontier model releases: We request that the U.S. government support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated Al development.”

Some of the OpenAI executives or co-founders who have signed the statement include CRO Mark Chen, Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki, co-founder John Schulman, and co-founder Wojciech Zaremba. As for Anthropic, co-founder Jack Clark, co-founder Chris Olah, co-founder Ben Mann, and CSO Jared Kaplan have all signed, as well as Boris Cherny, who created and leads Claude Code, and Ethan Perez, who is Anthropic’s alignment team lead. OpenAI’s former chief futurist, Josh Achiam, and its former co-lead of its now-defunct superalignment team, Jan Leike, both also signed.

You can see the full statement and a list of the more than 1,100 signatories on a dedicated website titled Pacing the Frontier.

Tech.title: Is it illegal to trick the US government into wiping your phone during a questionably legal search?
Tech.content:
A Georgia man was charged with a felony for allegedly wiping his phone while being questioned by Customs and Border Protection. Samuel Tunick had something in common with others who have had their devices searched at airports: He was an activist.

Unlike others who have had their phones seized with no explanation, Tunick was told that CBP needed to search his device to determine whether it contained child sexual abuse material, according to court filings. But Tunick’s attorneys argue that the search “was a pretext for a fishing expedition” into his connections with the Stop Cop City protests in Atlanta, in which dozens of people were charged under state RICO laws, which were later dismissed. A few protesters are still facing domestic terrorism and arson cases.

According to a motion to suppress evidence filed in March, Tunick didn’t consent to a search and repeatedly asked to speak to his attorney, but CBP officers told him they didn’t need a warrant to search his phone. Tunick ultimately gave the agents the password to his phone, but when they entered it, “the screen went blank, flashed several times and the phone appeared to restart,” court records say. Prosecutors allege that Tunick used the GrapheneOS “duress password” to wipe his phone, therefore deleting evidence.

Travelers’ devices have come under increased scrutiny since Donald Trump’s return to office — and the courts don’t agree on the legality of these warrantless searches. As a result, travelers have little clarity about how their rights apply at airports and other ports of entry. This gray area has allowed the Department of Homeland Security to target people perceived to be criticizing the president or the policies of his administration.

The confusion comes from a patchwork of federal rulings. The Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit ruled in United States v. Payne that law enforcement can forcibly unlock a person’s device with their fingerprint, facial recognition, or other biometric markers without running afoul of the Fifth Amendment’s protection against self-incrimination. But people can’t be forced to provide or enter their passcode, since it’s a form of “testimonial” evidence — information that requires a person to reveal their thoughts.

Those rulings, however, weren’t issued with airports in mind, and CBP claims that the Constitution doesn’t apply at ports of entry. Judicial opinion is mixed on that, too. The Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit — which oversees federal courts in Maryland, North Carolina, South Carolina, Virginia, and West Virginia — recently ruled that border agents don’t need a warrant to manually search travelers’ phones. (More advanced forensic searches, however, do require a warrant.) A separate appeals court whose jurisdiction includes Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island, and Puerto Rico ruled that agents can conduct manual and forensic searches without a warrant. Meanwhile, a federal judge in New York’s Eastern District determined that CBP agents can’t conduct any device searches without a warrant.
